domain.title: Algorithms & Data Structures
domain.tag: beyond the interview grind · what's actually used in systems
domain.why: Knowing an algorithm's name and being able to explain why real systems actually use it are two different skills. Anyone can memorize 'binary search is O(log n).' Fewer people can tell you why a search engine's autocomplete uses one data structure and a video game's collision detection uses a completely different one, or why sometimes the 'worse' algorithm on paper is faster in practice because of how computer memory actually works. That second kind of understanding is what this domain builds.

concepts.t: Asymptotic notation: what O, Omega and Theta actually claim

L0.body:
f(n) = O(g(n))      iff  exists c>0, n0.  for all n >= n0:  f(n) <= c*g(n)     # upper bound
f(n) = Omega(g(n))  iff  exists c>0, n0.  for all n >= n0:  f(n) >= c*g(n)     # lower bound
f(n) = Theta(g(n))  iff  f = O(g) and f = Omega(g)                             # tight

3n^2 + 100n + 7  =  O(n^3)   TRUE  (loose, but true)
                 =  Theta(n^2) TRUE  (tight)
                 =  Omega(n)   TRUE
L0.cloze: $f = O(g)$ is an {{c1::upper}} bound, $f = \Omega(g)$ is a {{c2::lower}} bound, $f = \Theta(g)$ means {{c3::both}}. So $3n^{2}$ is $O(n^{3})$: {{c4::true}}, because $O$ does not claim tightness.

concepts.L1: Three separate claims about how a function grows, each an assertion that a constant $c$ and a threshold $n_{0}$ exist. $O$ bounds from above, $\Omega$ from below, $\Theta$ both. None of them say anything about any particular finite $n$.
concepts.L2: $O$ is not the running time; it is a set of functions that a running time belongs to, so $3n^{2} = O(n^{3})$ is perfectly true and useless. People say $O$ when they mean $\Theta$, then argue about whether an algorithm is 'really' $O(n^{2})$ when both speakers are correct about different claims.
concepts.L3: Take $f(n) = 3n^{2} + 100n + 7$. To show $f = O(n^{2})$ pick $c = 4$ and find $n_{0}$ with $100n + 7 \leq n^{2}$: at $n = 101$, $100 \cdot 101 + 7 = 10107 \leq 10201$, and the gap only widens, so $n_{0} = 101$, $c = 4$ works. The definition is satisfied by exhibiting one pair, which is why the bound says nothing at $n = 50$. The same $f$ is also $O(n^{3})$ with $c = 1$, $n_{0} = 106$. Both statements are true because $O$ is a membership claim, not a measurement. Only $\Theta$ forbids the loose answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $f(n) = {a}n^{{2}} + {b}n + 5$, exhibit a constant $c$ and threshold $n_{{0}}$ proving $f = O(n^{{2}})$. Give $c$ and the smallest integer $n_{{0}}$ that works for your $c$.
L4.answer: Pick c = a+1. Then the requirement is b*n + 5 <= n^2, i.e. n^2 - b*n - 5 >= 0, so n0 = ceil((b + sqrt(b^2+20))/2). For a=3,b=100: c=4, n0=101. For a=5,b=40: c=6, n0=41. Any larger c with a matching n0 is equally valid: the definition asks for existence, not for the best pair.
L4.explanation: The point of the exercise is that a big-O claim is discharged by exhibiting one (c, n0) pair. There is no canonical pair, and no claim at all about small n. That is exactly why a Theta(n log n) algorithm can lose to a Theta(n^2) one at n = 30.

L4.prompt_tpl: True or false, and why: an algorithm with worst-case running time $\Theta(n\log n)$ also has worst-case running time $O(n^{{{k}}})$.
options: True - O is an upper bound and n log n grows slower than n^k for k >= 2, so the claim holds and is simply loose.
False - a Theta bound is exact, so no other bound can be stated.
False - O(n^k) would imply the algorithm is slower than n log n.
L4.answer: True - O is an upper bound and n log n grows slower than n^k for k >= 2, so the claim holds and is simply loose.
L4.explanation: Loose upper bounds are true statements. The habit of reading O as 'is exactly' is the single most common notation error; Theta is the notation that forbids looseness, and almost nobody uses it in conversation.

L4.prompt_tpl: For f(n) = 2n^2 + {B}n, prove f = O(n^2) using c = 3. What is the smallest positive integer n0 such that f(n) <= c*n^2 holds for every n >= n0?
L4.answer: c=3 turns the requirement 2n^2 + Bn <= 3n^2 into Bn <= n^2, i.e. n(n - B) >= 0, which for positive n holds exactly when n >= B: no rounding is needed because Bn = n^2 has the exact integer root n = B. So n0 = B. For B=15: n0=15 (check: n=15 gives 225<=225; n=14 gives 210<=196 is false). For B=30: n0=30. For B=60: n0=60.
L4.explanation: Choosing c one larger than the leading coefficient cancels the n^2 term exactly, leaving a linear inequality Bn <= n^2 whose exact integer solution is n0 = B. This is the same technique L3 uses on 3n^2+100n+7, just with the algebra made to land on a whole number instead of needing a ceiling.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which statement correctly defines f(n) = Omega(g(n))?
L4.answer: There exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that f(n) >= c*g(n) for all n >= n0.
L4.explanation: Omega mirrors O with the inequality reversed: a lower-bound existence claim that has to hold from some threshold onward, not everywhere. It says nothing about small n, and it does not require closeness to g - that stronger, symmetric claim is what Theta adds.
options: There exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that f(n) >= c*g(n) for all n >= n0.
There exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n <= n0.
f(n) and g(n) are equal up to a constant factor for every value of n, including small n.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone claims f(n) = n^{p} is O(n) because at n=1, n^{p} = 1 = n. Is this a valid proof that f = O(n)?
L4.answer: No: O requires f(n) <= c*g(n) to hold for every n at or beyond some threshold n0, forever afterward. Matching at one convenient point proves nothing, and here no c works past any threshold because n^p / n = n^(p-1) grows without bound.
L4.explanation: A single satisfied value never proves an eventually-forever claim; the definition quantifies over all n past n0, not over some n. For p >= 2 the ratio n^p/n is unbounded, so no constant c can rescue the claim no matter which n0 is tried.
options: No: O requires f(n) <= c*g(n) to hold for every n at or beyond some threshold n0, forever afterward. Matching at one convenient point proves nothing, and here no c works past any threshold because n^p / n = n^(p-1) grows without bound.
Yes: the existence clause in the definition is satisfied by any single value of n where the inequality holds.
No: but only because the constant c must be exactly 1, and no larger constant is permitted.

L4.prompt_tpl: For f(n) = n^2 and g(n) = {k}*n, which integer n is the smallest one where f(n) is strictly greater than g(n), i.e. where n^2 > {k}*n, and why does n = {k} itself not count?
L4.answer: n = {k} + 1: at n = {k} the two sides are exactly equal ({k}^2 = {k}*{k}), so n = {k} satisfies n^2 >= {k}*n but not the strict >; the next integer up is the first to exceed it.
L4.explanation: This is the sign/strictness trap hiding inside O's own definition: <= is non-strict, so equality at the boundary satisfies O but never counts as one function strictly exceeding the other. Confusing >= with > at the crossover point is exactly the error this item is built to catch.
options: n = {k} + 1: at n = {k} the two sides are exactly equal ({k}^2 = {k}*{k}), so n = {k} satisfies n^2 >= {k}*n but not the strict >; the next integer up is the first to exceed it.
n = {k}: the inequality is satisfied by equality too, so the point where the two functions first meet already counts as f(n) being greater than g(n).
n = {k} - 1: strict inequalities always cross one integer earlier than the algebraic solution, the same way a non-strict bound would.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that f(n) = n^{p} is not O(n^{q}) when p > q, by giving the argument that no constants c and n0 can work. (Consider what happens to f(n) / n^q as n grows.)
L4.answer: Suppose for contradiction that constants c > 0 and n0 exist with n^p <= c*n^q for all n >= n0. Dividing both sides by n^q (positive for n > 0) gives n^(p-q) <= c: a fixed upper bound on a quantity that must hold for every n past n0. But p - q >= 1, so n^(p-q) grows without bound as n increases, eventually exceeding any fixed c, however large. That contradicts the supposed inequality holding for all n >= n0, so no such (c, n0) pair exists and n^p is not O(n^q). The same unbounded-ratio argument is what rules out collapsing a genuinely worse recurrence into a better asymptotic class in 'Divide and conquer as a cost recurrence'.
L4.explanation: Formally negating a big-O claim goes through the ratio f(n)/g(n): if that ratio is unbounded as n grows, no constant can cap it, however large the constant. This limit-based contradiction is the standard tool for proving one polynomial degree is not interchangeable with another, and it generalizes directly to comparing divide-and-conquer recurrences.

concepts.t: The word RAM model and what it quietly assumes

L0.body:
# The cost model behind every 'O(n) time' claim you have ever read:
#   memory is an array of w-bit words, w >= log2(n)
#   +  -  *  /  &  |  ^  <<  >>  compare  load  store   ->  1 unit of time each
#   arrays are random access: a[i] costs 1 regardless of i

# Consequence: sorting n integers is NOT bounded below by n log n in this model.
radix_sort(a, w=64, r=16)   # 4 passes, O(n) time, because we may look at bits.
L0.cloze: The RAM model charges {{c1::1}} unit for any arithmetic on a {{c2::w}}-bit word, and assumes $w \geq$ {{c3::\log_{2} n}} so an index fits in a word. Under it, an $a[i]$ access costs {{c4::1}} no matter what $i$ is.

concepts.L1: The unstated machine underneath every complexity claim: memory as an array of $w$-bit words with $w \geq \log_{2} n$, unit cost for one arithmetic operation or one memory access, and no cost difference between $a[0]$ and $a[10^{9}]$.
concepts.L2: Two of its assumptions are false on real hardware, one is false in theory. Random access is not unit cost, which is what the cache-oblivious literature exists to repair. Radix sort escapes the $n\log n$ comparison bound not by multiplying but by unit-cost shift and mask reading a key's bits directly, which the model allows.
concepts.L3: The $w \geq \log_{2} n$ assumption is not a technicality. If a word could not hold an index, you could not address the input in constant time and pointer arithmetic would itself be logarithmic. Granting it also grants you $O(1)$ operations on $\log n$ bits at once, which is where van Emde Boas trees, fusion trees and radix sort get their speed: they beat comparison lower bounds by reading the bits of a key rather than only comparing keys. The comparison lower bound is a statement about a weaker model, not about sorting. Change the model and the bound goes with it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Radix sort runs in $O(n)$ time on $n$ integers of {w} bits with radix $2^{{16}}$. The comparison-sort lower bound is $\Omega(n\log n)$. Explain why these do not contradict each other.
L4.answer: They are statements about different models. The Omega(n log n) bound holds for algorithms whose only access to keys is pairwise comparison; the decision tree has n! leaves and depth at least log2(n!). Radix sort never compares two keys - it indexes buckets by extracted bit fields, which the word RAM model permits at unit cost. Weaken the model to comparisons only and radix sort is not expressible.
L4.explanation: This is the cleanest example of a lower bound being a property of a model rather than of a problem. The right follow-up question in an interview is always 'lower bound in which model?'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Sorting $n = 10^{{9}}$ keys of {w} bits by LSD radix sort with radix $r = {r}$ bits: how many passes, and how large is the count array per pass?
L4.answer: passes = ceil(w/r); count array = 2^r entries. w=32,r=8: 4 passes, 256 counters. w=64,r=8: 8 passes, 256. w=32,r=16: 2 passes, 65536 counters. w=64,r=16: 4 passes, 65536 counters. Each pass is one streaming read plus one scattered write of n keys.
L4.explanation: Bigger r means fewer passes but a count array that may fall out of L1/L2 and a scatter with worse TLB behaviour. r = 8 or 11 is the usual practical optimum, which is a cache-model argument the RAM model cannot express at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: The word RAM model requires $w \geq \log_2 n$ so a single word can hold an index into an array of n elements. For n = {n} elements, what is the minimum word size w in bits, i.e. $w = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$?
L4.explanation: This turns the assumption into arithmetic: w must be at least this many bits for THIS n, or an index does not fit in one word and a[i] stops being a single unit-cost step. A 64-bit word covers every n up to 2^64, which is why it is the default in practice.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a machine with w = {w}-bit words, which single operation costs exactly 1 unit of time under the word RAM model's own accounting, regardless of how large n is?
L4.answer: A random access a[i] into an array of n elements
L4.explanation: The model charges 1 unit only for a single arithmetic op, comparison, load or store on one w-bit word. Finding a max or sorting are built from many such unit-cost steps, so their total cost grows with n; only a[i] is a single primitive.
options: A random access a[i] into an array of n elements
Finding the maximum of an unsorted array of n elements
Sorting n arbitrary w-bit integers by pairwise comparison

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with gcc at -O0, this C fragment counts elements into a plain 32-bit int and then adds one more: `int n = {n}; int next = n + 1; printf("%d\n", next);` What does it print for n = {n}, and which word-RAM assumption does the 32-bit int silently fail to meet once a true count needs more than 31 bits?
L4.answer: n=2147483646 -> prints 2147483647 (no wrap, INT_MAX not yet reached). n=2147483647 (INT_MAX) -> next wraps to -2147483648: verified with gcc 13, x86-64 Linux, -O0 (and with -fwrapv, so this is the actual two's-complement wrap, not just UB in principle). The bug: int is fixed at 32 bits regardless of the machine's real word size w=64, so once the count needs log2(n) > 31 bits it silently violates w >= log2(n) and 'index+1' becomes negative instead of erroring.
L4.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in the C standard, but on this concrete platform gcc emits a plain wraparound add. The lesson for this concept: the word-RAM model's w is a property of the machine, but a C int nails w at 32 regardless of the machine, so the assumption can break silently long before the real hardware word is exhausted.

L4.prompt_tpl: The decision-tree argument gives a comparison-sort lower bound of $\lceil \log_2(n!) \rceil$ comparisons. Using Stirling's approximation $\log_2(n!) \approx n\log_2 n - n\log_2 e + 0.5\log_2(2\pi n)$, estimate this lower bound for n = {n}. Answer with the estimated number of comparisons.
L4.answer: log2(n!) is approximated by n*log2(n) - n*log2(e) + 0.5*log2(2*pi*n) (Stirling). n=1,000 -> about 8,529; n=100,000 -> about 1,516,704; n=1,000,000,000 -> about 28,454,657,829. Compare radix sort's actual cost: Theta(n) word-RAM operations, not Theta(n log n) comparisons - the gap is exactly this bound, escaped by reading bits instead of comparing.
L4.explanation: This is a plug-in estimate, not a derivation: two formulas given verbatim, evaluated for a specific n. Compare the result against radix sort's Theta(n) word-RAM cost to see how large the gap the model change buys really is.

L4.prompt_tpl: The decision-tree argument shows any comparison sort needs at least $\lceil \log_2(n!) \rceil$ comparisons in the worst case, because its execution traces a binary tree with one leaf per distinguishable input permutation and n! permutations need that much depth to tell apart. Radix sort sorts n w-bit keys in Theta(n) word-RAM operations, far below this bound for large n. This is not a contradiction. Identify the specific assumption the decision-tree bound depends on that radix sort does not make, and name the Whetstone concept where the bound itself is proved.
L4.answer: The decision-tree bound applies only to comparison sorts: algorithms whose sole way to learn about the input is a pairwise comparison between two keys, one per tree node. Radix sort never compares a key against another key; it reads a key's own bits directly via unit-cost shift and mask under the word-RAM model, which the decision-tree model does not offer as a primitive. Since the bound is a property of the comparison model, not of sorting itself, an algorithm that uses a different primitive is not bound by it. The bound is proved in full in 'Lower bounds: comparison sorting and the cell-probe model'.
L4.explanation: The gap the Stirling estimate quantifies numerically is explained here: it is not that radix sort is 'faster at comparing', it is that radix sort does not compare at all, so a bound about comparisons cannot apply to it.

L4.prompt_tpl: The word RAM model charges a[i] the same 1 unit of time for any i. Name the concrete assumption this makes about memory hardware, and explain how the concept 'I/O and cache-oblivious models' changes the cost function to repair it.
L4.answer: It assumes every memory cell is equally far from the processor: no caches, no DRAM row buffers, no page table walk, one flat array with uniform access latency. The I/O (external-memory) and cache-oblivious models replace the unit-cost access with a charge only for block transfers of size B between memory levels, so an algorithm's cost becomes a function of cache lines or disk blocks touched rather than raw operation count - which is why a B-tree beats a balanced BST in practice even though both cost O(log n) comparisons under word RAM.
L4.explanation: This is the concept's own L2 point made explicit and pushed one concept forward: word RAM is not wrong so much as silent about memory hierarchy, and the I/O model is the theory that fills exactly that silence, with B-trees as its headline example.

concepts.t: Recursion and induction are the same argument

L0.body:
def sum_to(n):                 # claim: returns n*(n+1)//2 for all n >= 0
    if n == 0: return 0        # BASE:  0 == 0*(0+1)//2                 ok
    return n + sum_to(n - 1)   # STEP:  assume correct for n-1, then
                               #        n + (n-1)n//2 = n(n+1)//2       ok

# The base case of the code IS the base case of the proof.
# The recursive call IS the induction hypothesis.
# Termination = the argument strictly decreases toward the base.
L0.cloze: In a recursive function the base case is the {{c1::base case}} of the induction, the recursive call is the {{c2::induction hypothesis}}, and termination requires an argument that {{c3::strictly decreases}} toward the base.

concepts.L1: A recursive procedure and an inductive proof have the same three parts: a base case, a step that assumes the result for smaller inputs, and a well-founded decreasing measure. Writing the recursion is writing the proof; you just do not write the proof down.
concepts.L2: Strong induction, not ordinary induction, is what most recursive code needs: the call is often on $n/2$ or on an arbitrary smaller subproblem, not on $n-1$. And the decreasing measure is a separate obligation from correctness. Code that is correct whenever it returns can still loop forever.
concepts.L3: Merge sort needs strong induction. The step assumes correctness on both halves, of sizes $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2 \rceil$; for $n \ge 4$ neither equals $n-1$ (only for $n \le 3$ does one half coincide with $n-1$). Ordinary induction only ever reaches $n-1$ and so cannot discharge the general step. The measure that decreases is the subarray length, and it is well founded because it is a non-negative integer, which is why recursion on a real number domain, or on a graph without a visited set, is the standard way to write a non-terminating recursive function that is otherwise perfectly correct. When you cannot find the measure, you have not found a bug yet, but you have found where the bug will be.

L4.answer: The induction has one base case, n == {b}, but the step decreases by both 1 and 2, so some branches skip over {b} entirely (landing on the value 1 away from it) and then keep recursing through 0 into negative n with no base case ever matched: fib(10) never terminates on those branches. A step that reaches n-2 needs base cases at two consecutive values (n == 0 and n == 1), not a single threshold.
L4.explanation: The rule generalises: the base cases must cover every value the step can land on below the threshold. A recursion that decreases by up to k needs k base cases, or a guard that clamps. This is the single most common recursion bug and it is a proof error, not a coding error.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove by induction that a binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^{{h+1}} - 1$ nodes, taking a single node to have height {h0}. Give the base case and the step.
L4.answer: Base: h = 0 is a single node, 1 <= 2^1 - 1 = 1. Step: a tree of height h has a root plus two subtrees of height at most h-1, each with at most 2^h - 1 nodes by the hypothesis, so at most 1 + 2(2^h - 1) = 2^(h+1) - 1. Equality holds exactly when both subtrees are perfect of height h-1.
L4.explanation: This is the bound behind every 'a balanced tree has height O(log n)' claim: invert it and n <= 2^(h+1) - 1 gives h >= log2(n+1) - 1. The inductive step is the same shape as the recursive traversal you would write.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using the recursive `sum_to` function from the L0 example, what does `sum_to({n})` evaluate to?
L4.answer: sum_to(n) = n(n+1)/2 by the induction traced in L0. sum_to(5) = 15, sum_to(9) = 45, sum_to(12) = 78, sum_to(20) = 210.
L4.explanation: sum_to(n) is the L0 example: base case n=0 returns 0, and the step adds n to the recursive result for n-1. The closed form n(n+1)/2 is exactly the induction hypothesis the code relies on at every call, so evaluating it directly checks the same claim the recursion proves.

L4.prompt_tpl: The induction above proves a binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. For h = {h}, what is this numeric bound?
L4.explanation: This is the closed form proved in the derive item above: a tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1)-1 nodes, with equality when every level is full. Plugging in h checks you can use the proved bound as a formula, not just trace the induction that produced it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Merge sort splits an array of n = {n} elements into two halves of size floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2). What is floor(n/2) for this n?
L4.explanation: Merge sort's step (see L3) splits n elements into floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2), neither of which is n-1, which is exactly why the correctness induction on merge sort must be strong induction rather than ordinary induction on n-1.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three proposed measures are meant to strictly decrease toward a base case, to argue a recursive function terminates. Exactly one does not actually guarantee termination. Which one, and why?
L4.answer: A positive real number that is halved on every call, with the base case triggered only when it equals exactly 0 - not well-founded: halving a positive real never reaches exactly 0.
L4.explanation: A strictly positive real that keeps halving approaches 0 but never equals it in finitely many steps, so a base case that only fires at exactly 0 is never reached and the recursion never terminates. A well-founded measure needs no infinite strictly-decreasing chain, which the reals under a base case of exact equality can supply.
options: A non-negative integer that decreases by at least 1 each call - well-founded, since there is no infinite strictly-decreasing chain of non-negative integers.
The count of unsorted elements remaining, which strictly decreases each call and reaches 0 - well-founded for the same reason: a finite starting integer count.
A positive real number that is halved on every call, with the base case triggered only when it equals exactly 0 - not well-founded: halving a positive real never reaches exactly 0.

L4.prompt_tpl: Merge sort's correctness (this concept) and its running-time bound $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$, analysed in 'Divide and conquer as a cost recurrence', are both proved by induction on subproblem size. State concretely what each induction proves, and explain why solving the recurrence for $T(n)$ does not by itself establish that the algorithm is correct.
L4.answer: The correctness induction (this concept) proves a predicate: the output is sorted, for every input of size n, using the hypothesis that both smaller subcalls already return sorted output. The recurrence's induction proves a number: that the running time on n elements is at most c n log n for some constant c, using the hypothesis that the smaller subcalls already run within that bound. Solving $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$ only bounds cost, and does so by assuming the merge step behaves as claimed; a merge sort that ran in exactly the predicted time but merged elements wrongly would still satisfy the recurrence while failing correctness, so the two inductions have to be discharged separately.
L4.explanation: Two different inductive hypotheses live on the same recursion tree: one is a predicate (sorted output), one is a number (running time). A merge sort with a subtly wrong merge step can still satisfy the cost recurrence exactly while failing correctness, which is why the two inductions are separate obligations, never one.

concepts.t: Divide and conquer as a cost recurrence

L0.body:
# Every divide-and-conquer algorithm is three numbers:
#   a  = number of subproblems
#   b  = factor by which the input shrinks
#   f(n) = cost to split and to combine
#
#   T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n)

mergesort   a=2 b=2 f=n      -> T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
binsearch   a=1 b=2 f=1      -> T(n) = 1T(n/2) + 1
karatsuba   a=3 b=2 f=n      -> T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n
strassen    a=7 b=2 f=n^2    -> T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2
L0.cloze: Karatsuba multiplication makes {{c1::3}} recursive calls on halves, giving $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n)$ and running time $n^{{{c2::\log_{2} 3}}} \approx n^{{{c3::1.585}}}$.

concepts.L1: Any divide-and-conquer algorithm reduces to three numbers: how many subproblems $a$, how much smaller each is by factor $b$, and the non-recursive split-plus-combine cost $f(n)$. The recurrence $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ is the whole design, and the algorithm is an implementation detail of it.
concepts.L2: The interesting design lever is $a$, not $f$. Strassen does more combine work than naive block multiplication and wins anyway, because it cut $a$ from $8$ to $7$. Optimising the merge step of merge sort cannot change its exponent; changing how many recursive calls you make is the only thing that can.
concepts.L3: Draw the recursion tree: level $i$ has $a^{i}$ nodes of size $n/b^{i}$, so its cost is $a^{i}f(n/b^{i})$, and there are $\log_{b} n$ levels with $a^{\log_{b} n} = n^{\log_{b} a}$ leaves. Three regimes follow: work grows down the tree and the leaves dominate ($T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_{b} a})$), work shrinks and the root dominates ($T(n)=\Theta(f(n))$), or every level costs the same, giving $T(n)=\Theta(f(n)\log n)$. Merge sort is balanced: $\log_{2} n$ levels each merging $n$ elements. Karatsuba is leaf-dominated at $n^{\log_{2} 3} = n^{1.585}$. Binary search is also balanced, not root-dominated: $f(n)=\Theta(1)=n^{\log_{2} 1}$, so every level costs $\Theta(1)$ and $T(n)=\Theta(1\cdot\log n)=\Theta(\log n)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: An algorithm makes {a} recursive calls on inputs of size $n/2$ and does $\Theta(n)$ work to split and combine. What is $T(n)$ in $\Theta$ terms?
L4.answer: Compare n^(log2 a) against n. a=2: log2 2 = 1, balanced, T = Theta(n log n). a=3: log2 3 = 1.585 > 1, leaves dominate, T = Theta(n^1.585). a=4: log2 4 = 2, T = Theta(n^2). a=5: log2 5 = 2.322, T = Theta(n^2.322).
L4.explanation: Only a = 2 gives the extra log factor; every a > 2 gives a strictly polynomial answer with no log. Verify: 3^log2(1e6) = (1e6)^log2(3) = (1e6)^1.585 ~= 3.2e9, against 1e6*log2(1e6) ~= 2.0e7 for a = 2.

L4.prompt_tpl: Strassen replaces {n8} multiplications of $n/2 \times n/2$ blocks with 7, at the cost of about 18 block additions instead of 4. Why is that a win asymptotically?
L4.answer: Additions are Theta(n^2) and multiplications drive a. The recurrence goes from T(n)=8T(n/2)+Theta(n^2), where n^log2(8) = n^3 dominates, to T(n)=7T(n/2)+Theta(n^2), where n^log2(7) = n^2.807 still dominates. Extra Theta(n^2) combine work cannot change a leaf-dominated exponent; only a can.
L4.explanation: log2(7) = 2.8074. The crossover in practice is usually n in the hundreds to low thousands, because the constant and the numerical stability both get worse - a concrete case of the constants-win concept applying to an asymptotic win.

L4.prompt_tpl: A divide-and-conquer algorithm makes {a} recursive calls on subproblems of size n/2, down to a base case of size 1, starting from n = {n} (a power of 2). How many leaves does its recursion tree have? Give the exact integer.
L4.answer: leaves = a^log2(n), since the tree has log2(n) levels and each level multiplies the node count by a. a=2,n=16: 2^4=16. a=3,n=64: 3^6=729. a=4,n=16: 4^4=256.
L4.explanation: The recursion tree has log2(n) levels (halving n down to 1), and node count multiplies by a at every level, so leaves = a^(number of levels) = a^log2(n) = n^log2(a) by the same identity used for Karatsuba's n^1.585.

L4.prompt_tpl: A divide-and-conquer algorithm halves its input at every recursive call and does Theta(n) work to split and combine: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. For n = {n} (a power of 2), how many levels does its recursion tree have, from the root (level 0) down to the base case?
L4.answer: levels = log2(n), since each level halves the subproblem size and there are log2(n) halvings from n down to 1. n=1024: 10. n=4096: 12. n=65536: 16.
L4.explanation: Halving n a total of log2(n) times reaches size 1, so the tree has log2(n) levels below the root -- the same count that gives merge sort its log2(n) merge passes.

L4.prompt_tpl: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^{p}. For p = {p}, which of the three recursion-tree regimes (leaves dominate, root dominates, every level equal) applies, and what is T(n) in Theta terms?
L4.answer: log2(a) = log2(2) = 1 sets the balance point. p=0: f(n)=n^0=1 grows slower than n^1, so leaves dominate: T(n)=Theta(n^1)=Theta(n). p=1: f(n)=n matches n^log2(2), every level costs the same: T(n)=Theta(n log n) (this is merge sort). p=2: f(n)=n^2 grows faster than n^1, root dominates: T(n)=Theta(n^2).
L4.explanation: Comparing the exponent p of f(n) against log2(a)=1 is exactly the master-theorem comparison: below it the leaves win, at it every level ties, above it the root wins. p=0 is a constant-work halving recurrence (like binary search but with a=2 instead of a=1), not the same case as p=1's merge sort.

L4.prompt_tpl: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n, with base case T(1) = 1. First classify which recursion-tree regime this falls into (leaves dominate, root dominates, or every level ties), then use that to derive T(n) exactly, as an integer, for n = {n} (a power of 2). Account for every level, including the n^2 base-case leaves themselves, not just the levels above them.
L4.answer: a=4, b=2, so log2(a)=2 and f(n)=n has degree 1 < 2: leaves dominate. Level i (i=0..log2(n)-1) costs 4^i*(n/2^i)=n*2^i, a geometric series with ratio 2 summing to n*(2^log2(n)-1)=n*(n-1). The n^2 base-case leaves each cost T(1)=1, adding a separate n^2 term. Total: T(n) = n*(n-1) + n^2 = 2n^2-n. n=16: 2*256-16=496. n=64: 2*4096-64=8128. n=256: 2*65536-256=130816.
L4.explanation: The geometric series over the levels above the base case gives only the combine cost; the recursion tree also has n^2 base-case leaves whose own cost (T(1)=1 each) must be added separately -- the internal-cost-plus-leaf-cost decomposition CLRS uses. Both terms are Theta(n^2), so leaves dominate overall, but the exact constant needs both, not just the geometric series.

L4.prompt_tpl: T(n) = a(n) * T(n/2) + n, where a(n) = log2(n) grows with n instead of being a fixed constant. Why does the geometric-series argument that gives T(n) = Theta(n^log2(a)) break down here?
L4.answer: The recursion-tree method relies on the number of nodes multiplying by the same constant factor a at every level, which is what turns the level sizes into a geometric series with a single ratio. If a depends on n, the branching factor is different at every level (level i has a(n)*a(n/2)*...*a(n/2^(i-1)) nodes, not a^i), there is no single ratio, and the closed form a^log_b(n) = n^log_b(a) no longer applies. This is not the case 'The master theorem, and where it fails' names either: its Akra-Bazzi extension handles unequal splits with constant coefficients (e.g. T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n), not a branching factor that itself varies with n -- Whetstone does not currently name a technique for this case.
L4.explanation: A varying a(n) breaks the single-ratio geometric series the recursion-tree method depends on, which is also why Akra-Bazzi (built for a fixed number of terms with constant coefficients) does not generalize to it -- an honest gap rather than a named technique to look up.

concepts.t: The master theorem, and where it fails

L0.body:
T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n),   a >= 1, b > 1.   Let  c_crit = log_b(a).

case 1  f(n) = O(n^(c_crit - eps))            -> T(n) = Theta(n^c_crit)      leaves win
case 2  f(n) = Theta(n^c_crit * log^k n), k>=0 -> T(n) = Theta(n^c_crit log^(k+1) n)
case 3  f(n) = Omega(n^(c_crit + eps))         -> T(n) = Theta(f(n))         root wins
        and regularity:  a*f(n/b) <= d*f(n) for some d < 1

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log n      <- NO CASE APPLIES.  Answer is Theta(n log log n).
L0.cloze: Let $c = \log_{{b}} a$. If $f$ is polynomially {{c1::smaller}} than $n^{{c}}$ the leaves dominate and $T = \Theta(n^{{c}})$. If $f = \Theta(n^{{c}})$ the answer gains a factor of {{c2::\log n}}. Case 3 additionally needs the {{c3::regularity}} condition.

concepts.L1: A closed form for $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ that decides which level of the recursion tree dominates by comparing $f(n)$ to $n^{\log_{b} a}$. Three cases: leaves win, all levels tie, root wins.
concepts.L2: The gap in case 1 and case 3 is polynomial, not merely asymptotic, and recurrences fall into it. $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/\log n$ matches no case: $n/\log n$ is smaller than $n$ but not by any $n^{\varepsilon}$.
concepts.L3: Sum the tree directly for $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/\log n$. Level $i$ has $2^{i}$ subproblems of size $n/2^{i}$, each costing $(n/2^{i})/\log(n/2^{i})$, so the level costs $n/(\log n - i)$. Summing $i$ from $0$ to $\log n - 1$ gives $n\sum_{j=1}^{\log n} 1/j = \Theta(n\log\log n)$ by the harmonic series. No case produces a $\log\log$ factor, which is the tell. For unequal splits use Akra-Bazzi: find $p$ with $\sum a_{i}b_{i}^{p} = 1$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{p}(1 + \int_{1}^{n} f(u)/u^{p+1}\,du))$. For $T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n$, $p$ solves $(1/5)^{p} + (7/10)^{p} = 1$, which is $p = 1$ minus a bit, and the integral gives $\Theta(n)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give $\Theta$ for $T(n) = {a}T(n/{b}) + n^{{{k}}}$.
L4.answer: c = log_b(a). a=2,k=1: c=1, f=n^1=n^c, case 2, Theta(n log n). a=2,k=2: c=1 < 2, case 3, Theta(n^2). a=4,k=1: c=2 > 1, case 1, Theta(n^2). a=4,k=2: c=2 = 2, case 2, Theta(n^2 log n). a=8,k=1: c=3, case 1, Theta(n^3). a=8,k=2: c=3 > 2, case 1, Theta(n^3).
L4.explanation: The three cases hang only on comparing c = log_b(a) to f's exponent, never on the recursion's shape. a=8,k=2 is standard block matrix multiplication (8 subproblems, O(n^2) merge), case 1, Theta(n^3); Strassen's a=7 instead gives Theta(n^log2(7)) approx Theta(n^2.807). Always compute log_b(a) first and compare the exponent, never pattern-match the shape.

L4.prompt_tpl: A candidate applies the master theorem to $T(n) = {a}T(n/2) + n/\log n$ and answers $\Theta(n\log n)$. What went wrong and what is the true answer?
L4.answer: No case applies. c = log2(2) = 1, and n/log n is asymptotically smaller than n^1 but not by a factor n^eps for any eps > 0, so it falls in the gap below case 2 and above case 1. Summing the recursion tree gives n * sum_{j=1..log n} 1/j = Theta(n log log n).
L4.explanation: The harmonic sum is the giveaway: log log n factors never come out of the master theorem. When f differs from n^c only by a polylog factor that is not of the case-2 form, sum the tree by hand or use Akra-Bazzi.

L4.prompt_tpl: A divide-and-conquer algorithm makes {a} recursive calls, each on an input of size n/{b}. Compute the critical exponent c = log_b(a) to two decimal places.
L4.answer: c = log(a)/log(b) (change of base; the result does not depend on which log you use). a=3,b=3: c=1.00. a=9,b=3: c=2.00. a=10,b=3: c=2.10 (log 10 / log 3 = 2.0959...).
L4.explanation: log_b(a) is the only number that decides the case, so compute it exactly rather than eyeballing whether a looks like a power of b. It need not be an integer: a=10,b=3 gives a non-integer c, and case 1/2/3 still applies to whatever f(n) you are given.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^2(\log n)^{k}$, the generalized case 2 gives $T(n) = \Theta(n^2(\log n)^m)$. Give $m$ as a plain integer.
L4.answer: m = k+1 in every case: the recursion tree ties at n^2 on every level, and summing (log n)^k over the log n levels adds exactly one power of log n. k=0 gives the textbook case-2 statement, m=1; k=1 -> m=2; k=2 -> m=3; k=3 -> m=4.
L4.explanation: The exponent on n never moves in case 2 - only the log power gains one factor, because summing a constant (log n)^k term over log n levels of the recursion tree is itself a sum of log n equal terms. Forgetting the plus-one is the single most common master-theorem slip.

L4.prompt_tpl: Binary search halves the array and does O(1) work per level, so T(n) = T(n/2) + Theta(1). Which case of the master theorem applies, and what is T(n)?
L4.answer: Case 2 (tie): Theta(log n)
L4.explanation: a=1,b=2 gives c=log_2(1)=0, and f(n)=Theta(1)=Theta(n^0) matches n^c exactly with k=0, so case 2 applies and adds one log factor: T(n)=Theta(log n), the familiar binary-search bound.
options: Case 1 (leaves win): Theta(sqrt(n))
Case 2 (tie): Theta(log n)
Case 3 (root wins): Theta(n)

L4.prompt_tpl: Take $T(n) = T(n/2) + n(2 - \cos n)$. Here $a=1$, $b=2$, so $c = \log_2 1 = 0$, and $f(n) = n(2-\cos n)$ stays between $n$ and $3n$, so it is $\Omega(n^1)$: case 3's growth test is satisfied. Does the regularity condition $af(n/b) \le d f(n)$, $d<1$, hold for every large $n$, and can you still conclude $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$?
L4.answer: No. At n = 2*pi*k with k odd, cos(n) = 1 so f(n) = n, while cos(n/2) = cos(pi*k) = -1 so f(n/2) = (n/2)(2-(-1)) = 1.5n. Then a*f(n/b) = 1*f(n/2) = 1.5n = 1.5*f(n), so no d<1 works for these arbitrarily large n: regularity fails infinitely often. Case 3's growth test alone is not enough; the master theorem gives no conclusion here.
L4.explanation: Regularity rules out functions that spike on some recursive calls even though they satisfy the growth bound overall. n(2-cos n) passes the case-3 growth test but a*f(n/b) exceeds f(n) at infinitely many n, so no constant d<1 works: case 3 does not apply, and you must analyze the recurrence some other way (e.g. bound T(n) directly).

L4.prompt_tpl: For the median-of-medians recurrence $T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n$, the Akra-Bazzi characteristic equation is $(1/5)^p + (7/10)^p = 1$. Evaluate the left side at $p = {p}$ to three decimal places.
L4.answer: f(p) = (1/5)^p + (7/10)^p. f(0.5)=1.284, f(0.8)=1.028, f(0.84)=1.000, f(1.0)=0.900. f is strictly decreasing in p (both bases are under 1), so the root sits near p=0.840; since 1/5+7/10=0.9<1, p must be below 1, confirming the recursion's subproblems shrink fast enough overall.
L4.explanation: This is exactly the recurrence for Selection: quickselect, median of medians, introselect. Because the root p is under 1, Akra-Bazzi's T(n)=Theta(n^p(1+integral of u/u^(p+1))) has the n^(1-p) term dominate the n^p prefactor, and the whole expression collapses to Theta(n): linear-time selection.

L4.prompt_tpl: Quicksort with a fixed-ratio pivot always splits n elements into fractions {frac} (they add to 1), giving $T(n) = T(\alpha n) + T((1-\alpha)n) + n$ where alpha is the smaller fraction. Akra-Bazzi's characteristic equation is $\alpha^p + (1-\alpha)^p = 1$. Show why $p=1$ satisfies this for every alpha strictly between 0 and 1, then use this concept's own Akra-Bazzi Theta formula to derive $\Theta(T(n))$.
L4.answer: p=1 works for every alpha because alpha^1+(1-alpha)^1 = alpha+(1-alpha) = 1 by definition, and alpha^p+(1-alpha)^p is strictly decreasing in p (both bases are in (0,1)), so p=1 is the unique root regardless of how skewed alpha is. Plugging p=1 into T(n)=Theta(n^p(1+integral_1^n u/u^(p+1) du)) gives integral_1^n (1/u) du = ln n, so T(n)=Theta(n(1+ln n))=Theta(n log n).
L4.explanation: Any two-way split into fixed nonzero fractions of n, however lopsided (even 1:99), gives Theta(n log n): this is why quicksort with any fixed-ratio pivot is Theta(n log n), the bound used in Quicksort: partitioning, pivot choice, and why it wins. Only a ratio that itself shrinks with n (not fixed), as in median-of-medians, pushes p below 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: Redo the harmonic-sum derivation for $T(n) = {a}T(n/{a}) + n/\log n$ (same trick as the base-2 case, different base). What is $\Theta(T(n))$, and why does the base not matter?
L4.answer: Theta(n log log n), for every a>1. Level i (i=0..log_a n - 1) has a^i subproblems of size n/a^i, each costing (n/a^i)/log(n/a^i), so the level total is n/(log n - i*log a). Summing over the recursion's depth gives (n/log a) * sum_{k=1}^{log_a n} 1/k, a harmonic sum again: Theta(n * log(log_a n)/log a) = Theta(n log log n), because log_a n = (log n)/(log a) differs from log n only by the constant factor 1/log a, which Theta absorbs.
L4.explanation: Changing the branching factor only rescales the harmonic sum's upper limit and a leading constant, and Theta swallows both. This is why the phenomenon in this concept's own L3 is not a quirk of base 2: any recurrence with c_crit=1 and f(n)=n/log n produces the same log log n factor, regardless of a and b.

concepts.t: Amortized vs average vs worst case

L0.cloze: A dynamic array append is {{c1::amortized}} $O(1)$ - a hard bound over any sequence. A hash lookup is {{c2::average}} $O(1)$ - a bound in expectation that an {{c3::adversary}} can break. An array index is {{c4::worst-case}} $O(1)$.

concepts.L1: Amortized is a worst-case guarantee over a sequence of operations, with no probability involved. Average case is probabilistic over inputs. These are routinely conflated and they are not the same guarantee.
concepts.L2: Dynamic array append is amortized O(1) — a hard guarantee. Hash table lookup is average O(1) — a probabilistic one that adversarial input can break. In a latency-sensitive system, that difference is the entire story.
concepts.L3: Amortized bounds are proved by charging: give each append $3$ credits, spend $1$ to write the element and bank $2$; when the array of size $k$ doubles, the $k/2$ elements added since the last resize have banked $k$ credits, exactly paying for the $k$ copies. No probability appears anywhere, so no input can defeat it. A hash table's $O(1)$ is an expectation over the hash function or over the input distribution. Fix the hash function, publish it, and an attacker computes colliding keys until every lookup walks an $n$-element chain: this is the HashDoS attack, and it is why modern runtimes seed SipHash per process. The two bounds fail in completely different ways, which is the entire point.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service has a p99 latency budget of {ms} ms. One design uses a dynamic array with amortized $O(1)$ append; another uses a hash table with average $O(1)$ insert. Which guarantee is more fragile under adversarial input, and which is more fragile at the tail?
L4.answer: The hash table is fragile under adversarial input: average-case is an expectation over inputs or over the hash seed, and a chosen-key attack collapses it to O(n) per lookup. The dynamic array is fragile at the tail: amortized O(1) is a hard total bound but one individual append costs Theta(n) when it resizes, which lands in p99 or p999 directly.
L4.explanation: Both answers are 'the array', for different reasons, and that is the useful distinction. Amortized says nothing about any single operation, so amortized structures are the wrong default in latency-sensitive paths; incremental or chunked-growth structures exist precisely for this.

L4.prompt_tpl: Starting from capacity 1 and doubling, how many element copies occur in total while appending $n = {n}$ elements, and what is the largest single append cost? Answer with the total number of element copies.
L4.answer: Copies total = 2^ceil(log2(n)) - 1 (the sum 1+2+4+...+2^(k-1) of all resizes). n=1000: 1023 copies. n=1024: 1023. n=1000000: 1048575. Largest single append copies the whole array at the last resize: 512, 512, and 524288 respectively.
L4.explanation: Total copies < 2n, so amortized cost is under 3 writes per append - a hard bound. But the worst single append copies n/2 elements. Amortized O(1) and worst-case Theta(n) are simultaneously true, which is exactly the confusion the concept names.

L4.prompt_tpl: A separate-chaining hash table has {m} buckets and stores {n} keys placed by simple uniform hashing (each key independently and equally likely to land in any bucket). What is the expected number of keys examined during an unsuccessful search, not counting the search key itself? Answer with that expected count.
L4.answer: By linearity of expectation, each of the m buckets holds n/m keys on average, so an unsuccessful search of one bucket examines n/m keys in expectation. m=50,n=10: 0.2. m=80,n=25: 0.3125. m=120,n=40: 0.3333. This is what 'average O(1)' means precisely: an expectation over the hash function's placement of keys, not a bound on any single search.
L4.explanation: Average-case O(1) for a hash table is an expectation over the random placement of keys (or over the hash function), computed here as n/m. It says nothing about one particular search: a fixed hash function plus chosen keys can put every key in one bucket, making that same search Theta(n).

L4.prompt_tpl: An initially empty stack supports push(x), costing 1, and multipop(k), which pops min(k, current size) elements at a cost equal to the number popped. Over a sequence of {n} operations total, where each operation is one push or one multipop call, what is the largest possible total number of individual pop actions across the whole sequence? Answer with that maximum total.
L4.answer: Every element popped was pushed exactly once, so total pops can never exceed total pushes. With n operations split between pushes and multipops, pushes are maximized by using exactly one multipop call, at the very end, draining everything: n-1 pushes then 1 multipop gives n-1 pops. n=10: 9. n=50: 49. n=500: 499.
L4.explanation: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so summed over the whole sequence, pop cost is bounded by push count, at most n-1 out of n operations. That is the aggregate-method proof that multipop is amortized O(1) per operation even though one multipop call alone can cost Theta(n).

L4.prompt_tpl: A dynamic array starts at capacity {c0} and, instead of doubling, grows its capacity by {c0} more slots every time it fills up, so capacity goes {c0}, then 2 times {c0}, then 3 times {c0}, and so on. While appending n = {n} elements (n a multiple of {c0}), what is the total number of element copies performed across every resize? Answer with that total copy count.
L4.answer: Resizes happen at sizes c0, 2*c0, ..., (k-1)*c0 where k=n/c0, copying that many elements each time: total = c0*(1+2+...+(k-1)) = c0*k*(k-1)/2 = n*(n-c0)/(2*c0). n=100,c0=10: 450. n=200,c0=20: 900. n=400,c0=50: 1400.
L4.explanation: Fixed-increment growth makes total copies Theta(n^2) instead of Theta(n), so per-append cost becomes Theta(n), not O(1). The amortized O(1) guarantee for dynamic-array append depends on geometric growth specifically, not on growing at all; change the growth rule and the guarantee this concept names breaks.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dynamic array doubles capacity when full, starting from capacity 1. Consider the append that finds the array full with size equal to capacity, both equal to {c}, so it must resize. Define potential Phi as 2 times current size minus current capacity. Using that definition, derive Phi immediately before this append (size {c}, capacity {c}) and Phi immediately after (size {c}+1, capacity 2 times {c}). The append's actual cost is {c} element copies plus 1 insert. What is the amortized cost of this append, defined as actual cost plus the change in potential (Phi after minus Phi before)? Answer with that amortized cost.
L4.answer: Phi before = 2*c - c = c. Phi after = 2*(c+1) - 2*c = 2. Amortized cost = actual + (Phi after - Phi before) = (c+1) + (2-c) = 3, for every c. c=4: Phi before=4, Phi after=2, amortized = 5 + (2-4) = 3. c=16: Phi before=16, Phi after=2, amortized = 17 + (2-16) = 3. c=1024: Phi before=1024, Phi after=2, amortized = 1025 + (2-1024) = 3.
L4.explanation: The potential method reproduces exactly the '3 credits per append' charging argument in this concept's mechanism, invariant of array size: the potential drop at a resize (from near-2n back to near-0) exactly cancels the resize's real cost. See The potential method for the general technique this specializes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A trading system needs a hard worst-case bound on lookup latency for a small in-memory key set, not just a good average. A chaining hash table gives average $O(1)$ lookup; cuckoo hashing gives worst-case $O(1)$ lookup (at most 2 probes) but only expected $O(1)$ insertion, with load factor kept under about 50 percent. Which guarantee should govern the read path's design, and why can cuckoo hashing offer a worst-case bound that plain chaining structurally cannot?
L4.answer: Design the read path around the worst-case bound: cuckoo hashing's 2-probe worst case is what a latency-sensitive read path needs, and its expected-O(1) insertion cost can be paid off the hot path. Chaining cannot offer a worst-case O(1) bound because an unsuccessful search must walk the whole bucket, and a bucket's chain length is unbounded in the worst case (all n keys can collide into one bucket); cuckoo hashing fixes the number of candidate slots per key at exactly 2, so a lookup is always 2 probes, independent of n or of insertion order.
L4.explanation: The same average-versus-worst-case distinction this concept opens with, applied to a design choice: chaining's average O(1) can degrade to O(n) per lookup (this concept's own HashDoS case), while cuckoo hashing (Pagh and Rodler, 2001) bounds every lookup by construction, not by expectation. See Cuckoo hashing and the cuckoo filter for the mechanism.

L0.body:
Phi : State -> R>=0,   Phi(initial) = 0,   Phi(s) >= 0 always

amortized_cost(op) = actual_cost(op) + Phi(after) - Phi(before)

# Dynamic array, doubling, with size s and capacity c:
Phi = 2*s - c        # 0 right after a resize, equals s when the array is full
#   cheap append:  actual 1, dPhi = +2   -> amortized 3
#   resize append: actual s+1, dPhi = 2(s+1)-2c - (2s-c) = -c+2 -> amortized 3
L0.cloze: Amortized cost is actual cost {{c1::plus}} the change in potential. The potential must start at {{c2::0}} and never go {{c3::negative}}, which makes the sum of amortized costs an {{c4::upper bound}} on the sum of actual costs.

concepts.L1: Define a potential function on the data structure state; amortized cost = actual cost + change in potential. Proves the dynamic array and splay tree bounds cleanly.
concepts.L2: Worth being able to do, because it's the tool that makes amortized analysis rigorous rather than hand-wavy, and it comes up in tree and heap analysis.
concepts.L3: The telescoping is the whole trick. Summing amortized costs over a sequence gives $\sum c_{i} + \Phi_{\mathrm{end}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{start}}$, and since $\Phi_{\mathrm{start}} = 0$ and $\Phi \geq 0$, the total amortized cost is at least the total actual cost. Verify the dynamic array with $\Phi = 2s - c$: on a cheap append $s$ rises by one so $\Phi$ rises by two, giving amortized $1 + 2 = 3$. On a resize at $s = c$, actual cost is $c + 1$ copies-plus-write, $c$ doubles to $2c$, and $\Phi$ goes from $2c - c = c$ to $2(c+1) - 2c = 2$, a change of $2 - c$, so amortized is $(c + 1) + (2 - c) = 3$. Every operation is $3$, and the bound is now a theorem rather than an assertion about averages.

L4.prompt_tpl: Define a potential for a binary counter of {k} bits under increment, and use it to prove the amortized cost of increment is $O(1)$.
L4.answer: Let Phi = number of 1 bits. An increment that flips t trailing ones to zero and one zero to one has actual cost t+1 and changes Phi by 1 - t. Amortized cost = (t+1) + (1-t) = 2. Phi starts at 0 and is never negative, so n increments cost at most 2n bit flips regardless of k.
L4.explanation: The bound is independent of the counter width, which the aggregate argument also shows (bit i flips every 2^i increments, total sum n/2^i < 2n) but far less reusably. The potential generalises to Fibonacci heaps and splay trees; the counting argument does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone proposes $\Phi = c - s$ (free capacity) for a dynamic array with capacity $c$ and size $s$, growth factor {g}. Why does the proof fail?
L4.answer: Phi = c - s decreases on a cheap append, so the amortized cost of a cheap append is 1 - 1 = 0, but on the resize step Phi jumps from 0 to c, giving amortized cost about 2c. The potential must be large exactly when an expensive operation is imminent and must pay for it by dropping; this one grows when the expensive operation happens. It also violates nothing formally - it is still non-negative - it simply proves a useless bound.
L4.explanation: The design rule: Phi should measure stored-up work. 2s - c is zero right after a resize and rises to s when full, so it holds exactly the credits needed. Choosing Phi is the creative step; verifying it is mechanical.

L4.prompt_tpl: An operation has actual cost {actual}. Using amortized_cost(op) = actual_cost(op) + Phi(after) - Phi(before), with Phi(before) = {phi_before} and Phi(after) = {phi_after}, what is the amortized cost of this operation?
L4.answer: amortized = actual + Phi(after) - Phi(before). actual=5, Phi(before)=3, Phi(after)=7: 5+7-3=9. actual=12, Phi(before)=10, Phi(after)=2: 12+2-10=4. actual=40, Phi(before)=0, Phi(after)=15: 40+15-0=55.
L4.explanation: This is the definition applied directly. The whole craft of the method is choosing Phi so this number comes out the same on every real operation; with arbitrary numbers like these it will not, which is the point of practicing the substitution on its own first.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dynamic array grown only by doubling has capacity c = {c} and currently holds s = {s} elements (doubling guarantees c/2 < s <= c). Using the potential Phi = 2*s - c, what is Phi right now?
L4.explanation: Phi rises by 2 with every cheap append (s up by 1, c fixed) and resets to a small constant at every resize; this is that formula being evaluated directly, the same arithmetic used to get the amortized-3 result in the concept's own worked example.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary counter starts at 0 (so Phi = 0, the number of one-bits) and undergoes n = {n} increments with no overflow, each bit flip costing O(1) in the word-RAM model. Using the potential-method bound that every increment has amortized cost 2, what is the maximum possible total number of bit flips over all n increments? Answer with that number.
L4.answer: Total actual cost = total amortized cost - Phi(end) + Phi(start) <= 2n - 0 + 0 = 2n, since Phi(start)=0 and Phi(end)>=0. n=10: at most 20 flips. n=100: at most 200. n=1,000,000: at most 2,000,000.
L4.explanation: The telescoping sum turns a constant per-operation amortized cost into a linear total bound, and it holds for any counter width k because k never appears in the derivation - only the popcount Phi does.

L4.prompt_tpl: A k-bit binary counter (fixed width, no growing) reaches all-ones and is incremented once more, wrapping to all-zero the way a real hardware counter does (the overflow bit is discarded). Using Phi = number of one-bits, does the amortized-cost-2-per-increment bound survive this wraparound? Work out the amortized cost of the wraparound increment itself, for k = {k}.
L4.answer: Yes, it survives. On wraparound the actual cost is k (every one-bit flips to zero, and none flips to one, since the counter discards the overflow instead of growing a new bit). Phi(before) = k (all ones), Phi(after) = 0, so amortized cost = k + (0 - k) = 0, even cheaper than the usual 2. Phi still starts at 0 and never goes negative regardless of k, so the telescoping argument is untouched and the total-cost bound of 2n over n increments still holds.
L4.explanation: The per-increment formula t+1 actual, 1-t change in Phi assumed a 0 bit is always available to flip to 1; overflow breaks that assumption, but the proof never actually needed that specific formula to repeat identically - only Phi >= 0 and Phi(start) = 0, which wraparound does not disturb.

L4.prompt_tpl: A student computes amortized cost as actual_cost(op) - (Phi(after) - Phi(before)) instead of plus, for a dynamic array's resize step at capacity c = {c} (actual cost c + 1, Phi rising from c to 2, a true change of 2 - c). What number does the sign error produce, and why does the mistake show up immediately?
L4.answer: actual - (Phi(after) - Phi(before)) = (c+1) - (2-c) = 2c - 1. c=8: 15. c=64: 127. c=256: 511 - a number that grows linearly with c instead of staying constant. A correctly chosen Phi makes the amortized cost O(1) (here exactly 3) independent of c; an answer that scales with array size is an immediate sign that the plus became a minus.
L4.explanation: Subtracting instead of adding the change in potential is the most common mechanical slip in this method. It is self-diagnosing: the entire reason to pick this Phi was to cancel the size-dependence out, so a size-dependent result on a resize step is the tell.

L0.cloze: A linear scan of {{c1::1000}} contiguous ints touches about {{c2::63}} cache lines, which the hardware {{c3::prefetcher}} streams. A ten-hop tree search takes ten {{c4::dependent}} loads that cannot be overlapped.

concepts.L1: Cache-line effects give array traversal a 10-50x constant advantage over pointer chasing. A linear scan of a contiguous array beats a binary search tree for n well past intuition — often into the thousands.
concepts.L2: This is the single most practically important gap between algorithm theory and systems work. B-trees exist because of it. Flat arrays with linear scan beat hash maps at small n for the same reason.
concepts.L3: Count cache lines, not operations. A 64-byte line holds 16 32-bit ints, so scanning 1000 of them is 63 line fills, and the prefetcher issues them ahead of use so they overlap: effective cost is bandwidth-limited, roughly a few nanoseconds per line. A balanced tree over the same 1000 keys is about 10 comparisons but 10 dependent loads, each of which must complete before the next address is known. If the nodes are not resident, that is 10 serialised misses at roughly 80-100 ns, so about 1 microsecond against about 200 nanoseconds. The tree does one-hundredth the comparisons and loses by 5x.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {L} MiB array of 4-byte ints is scanned linearly. Cache line is 64 B and streaming bandwidth is {bw} GB/s. How many line fills, and roughly how long does the scan take?
L4.answer: Lines = L MiB / 64 B = L * 16384. Time = L MiB / bw. L=1,bw=20: 16384 lines, 1.049 MB / 20 GB/s = 52 us. L=4,bw=20: 65536 lines, 210 us. L=64,bw=50: 1048576 lines, 67.1 MB / 50 GB/s = 1.34 ms. The per-element comparison cost is invisible next to the transfer.
L4.explanation: The scan is bandwidth-bound, so its cost depends only on bytes touched, not on the number of comparisons. That is why halving the element size often beats halving the algorithmic work, and why struct-of-arrays layouts win.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must look up a key in a set of {n} 8-byte integers, many times, in a hot loop. Rank: sorted array with binary search, flat array with linear scan, and a pointer-based balanced BST.
L4.answer: n=8: linear scan on one or two cache lines wins outright; binary search's branches mispredict and the BST is absurd. n=64: 512 bytes is 8 lines - linear scan is still competitive and branch-free SIMD scan wins; binary search is close. n=1000: 8 KB fits L1, binary search wins on comparisons but a branchless/eytzinger-laid-out search wins more; the pointer BST loses at every size because of dependent misses.
L4.explanation: The BST never wins on a static set. Its value is ordered dynamic updates. The crossover between linear scan and binary search sits in the tens to low hundreds of elements on modern cores and depends on branch predictability, not on n alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: A balanced binary search tree holds {n} keys and none of it is cache-resident, so every pointer hop is a DRAM miss costing {lat} ns. Using ceil(log2(n)) hops for a successful search, how long does one search take? Answer with the number of nanoseconds.
L4.answer: hops = ceil(log2(n)). n=1000: hops=10, so 800 ns at lat=80 or 1000 ns at lat=100. n=100000: hops=17, so 1360 ns at lat=80 or 1700 ns at lat=100. n=1000000: hops=20, so 1600 ns at lat=80 or 2000 ns at lat=100.
L4.explanation: Each hop is a dependent load: the CPU cannot know the next address until the current one returns from DRAM, so misses serialize instead of overlapping the way a prefetched linear scan's line fills do. Total time is simply hops times per-miss latency.

L4.prompt_tpl: A contiguous array holds {n} elements of {sz} bytes each. A cache line is 64 bytes. How many 64-byte lines does one full linear scan touch (round up for a partial line at the end)? Answer with the number of lines.
L4.explanation: The scan's real cost is bytes touched divided into 64-byte transfers, not the element count directly - doubling the element size roughly doubles the line count and the scan time, which is why packing data tightly (smaller sz) is a direct performance lever.

L4.prompt_tpl: Now suppose both structures are fully cache-resident (everything already sits in L1, no DRAM misses either way), so a comparison costs about {c1} ns for the array and about {c2} ns for the BST (its extra cost is branch mispredicts on the unpredictable left/right choice). For n = {n} keys, the array scan averages n/2 comparisons and the BST averages log2(n). By what multiple is the resident BST now faster than the resident array? Answer with that multiple.
L4.explanation: Constants only win because pointer chasing normally pays a roughly 100 ns DRAM tax per hop that a streamed scan avoids. Remove that tax by keeping both structures cache-resident and the comparison costs converge to nanoseconds, so the O(log n) versus O(n) gap reasserts itself and grows without bound as n grows - the opposite of the concept's headline claim, and exactly the condition under which it stops applying.

L4.prompt_tpl: A B-tree node is sized to hold {B} keys, so a search needs about ceil(ln(n)/ln(B)) node visits, one cache-line-scale fetch each; a plain binary tree needs about ceil(log2(n)) pointer hops for the same n keys. For n = {n} keys, compute the binary tree's hop count divided by the B-tree's node-visit count. Answer with that ratio (see I/O and cache-oblivious models for the general external-memory version of this argument).
L4.answer: n=1000000,B=16: bst hops=ceil(log2(1e6))=20, b-tree visits=ceil(ln(1e6)/ln(16))=5, ratio=4. n=1000000,B=64: hops=20, visits=4, ratio=5. n=16000000,B=16: hops=24, visits=6, ratio=4. n=16000000,B=64: hops=24, visits=4, ratio=6.
L4.explanation: This is the same one-fetch-per-node-not-per-comparison idea generalized: making each node exactly one cache-line (or disk-block) wide cuts the number of expensive fetches by the log of the branching factor. B-trees are this trick engineered on purpose rather than discovered by accident, which is why they, not BSTs, are the standard on-disk and often in-memory index structure.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C++, std::set<int> is usually a red-black tree (pointer-chasing, like the BST above) while a sorted std::vector<int> searched with std::binary_search is a flat array. For {n} stored ints looked up repeatedly in a hot loop, which container wins in practice, and why do so many C++ programmers reach for std::set anyway?
L4.answer: The sorted std::vector plus std::binary_search wins at essentially every n for a read-mostly workload, for the same cache-line reasons as the array-vs-BST case above: contiguous storage and far fewer cache misses per lookup. std::set earns its cost only when the set itself is mutated often (inserts and erases interleaved with lookups) or when stable iterators into a changing structure are required; programmers default to it out of habit and because its interface matches the abstract ordered-set idea, not because it is faster.
L4.explanation: std::set trades lookup speed for O(log n) insert and erase without invalidating other elements' iterators - a real requirement sometimes, but a lookup-only workload never needs it. cppreference documents this tradeoff on each container's page, and it is one of the most common misapplied data-structure choices in production C++.

L0.body:
# output-sensitive: cost depends on how much you produce
convex_hull(points)        # O(n log h), h = hull size   (Chan's algorithm)
grep -o pat file           # O(n + z), z = number of matches

# parameterized: cost is exponential only in a structural parameter k
vertex_cover(G, k)         # O(2^k * n)     FPT in k
treewidth_dp(G, tw)        # O(2^tw * n)    FPT in treewidth
sat_solve(cnf)             # exponential in theory, seconds on real instances
L0.cloze: Output-sensitive bounds charge for the answer as well as the input: Chan's hull is {{c1::O(n \log h)}}, matching is $O(n + m + z)$ where $z$ counts {{c2::matches}}. Fixed-parameter tractable means the exponential factor touches only {{c3::k}}, giving $f(k) \cdot n^{O(1)}$.

concepts.L1: Bounds in terms of output size or a structural parameter rather than input size. Treewidth-parameterized algorithms make NP-hard problems tractable on structured instances.
concepts.L2: 'NP-hard' is often used to end a conversation. The useful follow-up is which parameter is small in practice — most real instances of hard problems have structure that admits a practical algorithm.
concepts.L3: Fixed-parameter tractable has a precise definition that people skip: running time $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$, where the exponential is confined to $f(k)$ and the dependence on $n$ is polynomial with an exponent independent of $k$. $O(n^{k})$ is not FPT; it is XP, and the difference is the difference between a solver that works and one that does not. Vertex cover is FPT: branch on an edge, one of its two endpoints must be in the cover, giving a depth-$k$ binary tree and $O(2^{k}n)$. At $k = 20$ that is a million times $n$, entirely feasible, while the naive $\binom{n}{k}$ enumeration at $n = 10^{4}$ is astronomically larger.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare $\binom{{n}}{{k}}$ brute force against $O(2^{{k}}n)$ FPT branching for vertex cover with $n = {n}$ and $k = {k}$.
L4.explanation: The gap is the entire content of parameterized complexity. Note also that O(n^k) - which people often mistake for FPT - is 1000^10 = 1e30 at n=1000, k=10: as hopeless as brute force. Confining the exponential to k is the definition.

L4.prompt_tpl: An interviewer says a scheduling problem is NP-hard. Give the two follow-up questions that turn that into an engineering conversation, with a concrete example of each for {dom}.
L4.answer: First: which parameter is small on real instances? Register allocation is NP-hard in general but linear on the interval graphs produced by a linear scan, and chordal for SSA form. Second: what approximation ratio or output-sensitivity is acceptable? Query planners search a restricted space (left-deep joins) and accept a plan that is good rather than optimal.
L4.explanation: NP-hardness is a statement about worst-case instances over all inputs. Almost no production system faces that distribution. Naming the structural parameter - treewidth, interval structure, number of joins, backdoor size - is what distinguishes an engineering answer from a complexity-class recitation.

L4.prompt_tpl: The command `grep -o pat file` scans a file of n = {n} bytes and finds z = {z} matches. Under the output-sensitive time bound O(n + z), how many total steps does the bound predict?
L4.explanation: The bound is linear in two separate terms: scanning cost n plus a unit of work per match reported, z. This is why claims that grep is 'just linear' need to say whether z stays small (typical) or can approach n (pathological, e.g. matching every byte).

L4.prompt_tpl: A treewidth-parameterized DP visits every bag of a tree decomposition and keeps a table of size 2^tw per bag, giving a total bound of O(2^tw * n) table entries for a graph with n = {n} vertices and treewidth tw = {tw}. Compute the number of table entries the bound predicts.
L4.explanation: Treewidth plays the same role here as k does for vertex cover: the exponential blow-up is confined to tw, not n. At n=100000, tw=15 the bound is already about 3.3 billion entries, near the edge of feasibility - which is exactly why treewidth-based algorithms are used only where tw is genuinely small.

L4.prompt_tpl: A note claims: since the exponent k is fixed for any given input, an O(n^k) algorithm counts as fixed-parameter tractable. Find the flaw in this claim, and compute n^k for n = {n}, k = {k} to show the practical cost.
L4.answer: The flaw: FPT requires the exponent of n to be a constant that does not depend on k, i.e. running time f(k) * n^c for fixed c. In O(n^k) the exponent IS k, so growing k grows the polynomial's own degree - that is precisely the class XP, not FPT, and XP is strictly larger. Computed: n=100,k=3 -> 1,000,000; n=100,k=5 -> 10,000,000,000; n=1000,k=3 -> 1,000,000,000; n=1000,k=5 -> 1,000,000,000,000,000. Even at k=5 and n in the hundreds, this is already worse than any practical FPT bound.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common misreading of FPT: seeing a fixed k in the exponent and assuming that makes the algorithm fine. The definition requires the exponent on n to be constant and independent of k; O(n^k) fails that test and belongs to XP, where the blow-up hits the polynomial itself rather than a separate factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: Chan's convex hull algorithm runs in O(n log h), where h is the number of hull vertices, on an input of n = {n} points. Describe the kind of input that forces h to its maximum relative to n, and state whether the output-sensitive bound then still beats a plain O(n log n) hull algorithm.
L4.answer: h is maximized, h = n, when every point lies on the hull - for example n points placed on a circle, or the vertices of a convex polygon in general position. Then O(n log h) = O(n log n): Chan's algorithm degenerates to the same asymptotic cost as a plain n log n hull algorithm such as Graham scan, so the output-sensitive bound buys nothing here. The advantage shows up only when h = o(n): a clustered or near-collinear point set can have h as small as 3, giving O(n log 3) = O(n), a real asymptotic win a non-output-sensitive algorithm cannot match.
L4.explanation: Output-sensitivity is a win that depends entirely on how small the output actually is on the instances you care about, not a universal improvement - exactly the parameter-dependence theme that runs through this whole concept, from hull size h to treewidth tw to vertex-cover k.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the O(2^k * n) bound for the vertex cover branching algorithm: state the invariant that makes branching on an uncovered edge safe, explain why the recursion depth cannot exceed k, and compute the number of leaves in the search tree for k = {k}.
L4.answer: Invariant: for any edge (u,v), a vertex cover must contain u or v - an uncovered edge means neither endpoint was chosen, which is exactly what a vertex cover forbids - so branching into 'put u in the cover' and 'put v in the cover' loses no candidate solution; it is exhaustive, not a heuristic. Each branch spends one unit of the budget k, so a branch that has used k vertices without covering every edge can be abandoned, giving depth at most k with branching factor 2, hence at most 2^k leaves. Each node costs O(n) to find an uncovered edge and update the remaining graph, so total work is O(2^k * n). Leaves: k=15 -> 32768; k=25 -> 33554432.
L4.explanation: This is the bounded search tree technique, the workhorse of elementary FPT algorithms: branching that is exhaustive but shallow, where shallow means bounded by the parameter rather than by n. The same technique gives FPT algorithms for feedback vertex set and cluster editing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tree-decomposition DP for weighted independent set keeps, at each bag, a table of which bag vertices are chosen: 2^w entries for a bag of width w, giving the O(2^tw * n) bound for treewidth tw = {tw}. Justify why this is the same design principle taught in 'Dynamic programming, structurally' rather than a new idea, and compute the per-bag table size.
L4.answer: 'Dynamic programming, structurally' teaches that a DP's state is 'enough information about the part already decided to extend it correctly', and the recursion follows the problem's own decomposition - a chain of indices for array DP, here a tree decomposition for graph DP. Treewidth DP is the same idea generalized from a chain to a tree: the state at each bag is exactly enough information (which bag vertices are in or out) to combine child-bag answers correctly, and the table size 2^w is just that state space, not a new idea specific to parameterized complexity. Per-bag table size: tw=6 -> 64 entries; tw=12 -> 4096 entries.
L4.explanation: Seeing treewidth DP as an instance of ordinary DP, not a separate technique, is what makes O(2^tw * n) intuitive rather than memorized: the exponential factor is just the size of the DP state, confined to tw because the state is defined per bag rather than per vertex.
