L0.body:
External memory model (Aggarwal-Vitter):  M = cache size,  B = block size
   scan n items          Theta(n/B)             transfers
   sort n items          Theta((n/B) log_{M/B}(n/B))
   B-tree search         Theta(log_B n)
   binary search on sorted array   Theta(log_2 n - log_2 B) = Theta(log(n/B))

Cache-oblivious: same bounds, algorithm never mentions M or B.
   van Emde Boas layout  Theta(log_B n)        funnelsort  Theta((n/B) log_{M/B}(n/B))
L0.cloze: In the external-memory model you count {{c1::block transfers}}, not operations. A B-tree searches in $\Theta({{c2::\log_{B} n}})$ transfers while binary search on a sorted array takes $\Theta(\log(n/B))$. A {{c3::cache-oblivious}} structure achieves the same bound without knowing $B$.

concepts.L1: Count block transfers between memory levels rather than operations. B-trees are optimal in the external memory model. Cache-oblivious structures (van Emde Boas layout, funnel sort) achieve it without knowing block size.
concepts.L2: This model explains real system design far better than the RAM model does, and almost nobody brings it up. It's the theoretical justification for B-trees, for LSM trees, and for why matrix tiling works.
concepts.L3: Put numbers on it. Take $n = 2^{30}$ keys and a 64-byte line holding 8 eight-byte keys, so $B = 8$. Binary search costs $\log_{2} n - \log_{2} B = 30 - 3 = 27$ transfers, because the last three levels finally land inside one line. A B-tree with the same $B$ costs $\log_{8} 2^{30} = 10$. Widen to a 4 KiB page, $B = 512$: binary search is $30 - 9 = 21$, the B-tree is $\log_{512} 2^{30} = 3.3$. The B-tree gets better as $B$ grows; binary search barely moves, because it only benefits from $B$ at the very bottom. That single arithmetic gap is why B-trees dominate disk indexing, though LSM-trees (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra's SSTables) trade this same I/O accounting for lower write amplification instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: With $n = 2^{{{e}}}$ keys and block size $B = {B}$ keys, how many block transfers does binary search on a sorted array cost, and how many does a $B$-way search tree cost?
L4.explanation: Binary search gains an additive log2(B); the B-tree gains a divisive log2(B). That is the whole argument for high fanout, and it is why doubling the page size helps a B-tree far more than it helps a sorted array.

L4.prompt_tpl: Matrix multiply of two $n \times n$ matrices, $n = {n}$, in a cache of $M$ words with block $B$. Why does tiling change the transfer count from $\Theta(n^{{3}})$ to $\Theta(n^{{3}}/(B M^{{1/2}}))$?
L4.answer: Naive ijk streams a whole row and a whole column per output element; the column has no locality, so each of the n^3 multiply-adds can cost a transfer once n exceeds the cache. Tiling into t x t blocks with 3t^2 <= M keeps three tiles resident: each tile product does t^3 work for t^2/B transfers per tile loaded, so total transfers are (n/t)^3 * 3t^2/B = 3n^3/(tB), and t = Theta(sqrt(M)) gives the bound.
L4.explanation: This is the model justifying every GEMM blocking scheme and every attention tiling strategy - FlashAttention is exactly this argument applied to softmax(QK^T)V, reducing HBM traffic rather than FLOPs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Scanning n = {n} items sequentially with block size B = {B} items, how many block transfers does the scan cost? Answer with the number of block transfers.
L4.answer: Theta(n/B) transfers, exactly ceil(n/B): a stream of n items packed B per block always needs one more block for any remainder. n=1000000,B=256: 3907; n=1000000,B=4096: 245; n=50000000,B=256: 195313; n=50000000,B=4096: 12208.
L4.explanation: A sequential scan never revisits a block, so the cost is just how many blocks the n items occupy, rounded up. It is the cheapest access pattern in the model and the baseline every other bound below is compared to.

L4.prompt_tpl: External merge sort of n = {n} items with block size B = {B} items and memory M = {M} items needs P = ceil(log(n/B) / log(M/B)) passes over the data, each pass reading and writing every block once. What is the total number of block transfers? Answer with the total transfer count.
L4.explanation: Each of the P passes streams the whole file once in each direction (read+write), costing 2n/B transfers per pass; multiplying by the pass count from the sort formula in L0 gives the real transfer budget an external sort pays.

L4.prompt_tpl: Binary search over a sorted array of n = {n} items with block size B = {B} items costs ceil(log2(n)) - floor(log2(B)) block transfers by the raw formula. That raw formula can go negative once B is large relative to n, but the real cost is never less than 1 transfer. What is the actual number of block transfers? Answer with the number of block transfers.
L4.explanation: Theta(log(n/B)) is only meaningful for B <= n; when B is small relative to n the raw ceil/floor formula already gives the right transfer count, but once B grows past n the same formula would go negative, so the real cost floors at 1 instead. The max(1, ...) clamp is what keeps the formula honest across both regimes.

L4.prompt_tpl: The external-memory binary-search bound is log2(n) - log2(B) transfers, for n = {n} items. What does this bound become when B = 1, meaning every item is its own block and there is no blocking at all?
L4.answer: log2(n) transfers -- the model degenerates exactly to ordinary binary search in the comparison model, because log2(1) = 0
L4.explanation: log2(1) = 0, so the bound collapses to log2(n): with B=1 there is no blocking to exploit, and the external-memory model matches the plain comparison-model bound for binary search, exactly as the word RAM model would predict.
options: log2(n) transfers -- the model degenerates exactly to ordinary binary search in the comparison model, because log2(1) = 0
0 transfers, because log2(1) cancels the whole expression
n transfers, because with no blocking every item needs its own transfer regardless of the search pattern

L4.prompt_tpl: A B-tree indexes n = {n} keys at page capacity B = {B} keys (fanout B), costing log_B(n) block transfers per worst-case lookup. Working out log base B of n minus log base 2B of n for these values gives a page-read savings under 1 if you double the page capacity to 2B. The sibling concept 'Sizing a B-tree node: fanout arithmetic' shows tree height is a step function of fanout: most page-size doublings buy zero actual tree levels, while every node read at 2B moves twice the bytes of a read at B. Given a lookup savings under one page read and no guarantee the tree height actually drops, should you double B purely to speed up point lookups?
L4.answer: No: the fractional savings is often not enough to remove even one tree level, since height only drops at specific fanout thresholds, while doubling B always doubles the bytes transferred per node read -- the increase is not justified by lookup speed alone.
L4.explanation: log_B(n) - log_{2B}(n) computed here is always under one full transfer for these n, B (verify: 0.476, 0.222, 0.714, 0.333, 0.952, 0.444 across the six draws), and the sibling fanout-arithmetic concept shows height changes only at integer thresholds, so most doublings buy zero levels while doubling bytes read per node -- both facts together, not either alone, make doubling unjustified for point lookups.
options: No: the fractional savings is often not enough to remove even one tree level, since height only drops at specific fanout thresholds, while doubling B always doubles the bytes transferred per node read -- the increase is not justified by lookup speed alone.
Yes: any positive savings in page reads compounds across enough lookups to be worth the extra bytes per node, regardless of whether the tree height changes.
It depends only on the storage device's raw bandwidth, not on whether the tree height actually decreases.

concepts.t: Lower bounds: comparison sorting and the cell-probe model

L0.body:
# Comparison sorting: any correct algorithm is a binary decision tree.
#   n! possible permutations  ->  n! leaves  ->  depth >= log2(n!)
#   log2(n!) = n log2 n - n log2 e + O(log n)      (Stirling)
log2(100!)  = 524.76 comparisons   (vs 100*log2(100) = 664.39)

# Cell-probe model: only memory probes are charged. Everything else is free.
#   predecessor search, n keys of w bits, S space:
#   Theta( min( log_w n , log(w - log n)/ log( (w-log n)/ log(S/n) ) ) )  -- Patrascu-Thorup
L0.cloze: A comparison sort is a {{c1::decision tree}} with $n!$ leaves, so its depth is at least $\log_{{2}}(n!) \approx n\log_{{2}} n - {{c2::1.4427}}n$. The {{c3::cell-probe}} model charges only memory probes and is where unconditional data structure lower bounds are proved.

concepts.L1: A lower bound is a theorem about a model of computation, not about a problem. Comparison sorting needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons because a binary decision tree distinguishing $n!$ outcomes has depth $\geq \log_{2}(n!)$.
concepts.L2: The cell-probe model is deliberately absurd: computation is free, only reading and writing memory cells costs anything. That is what makes its bounds unconditional - they cannot be dodged by a cleverer algorithm, only by using more space.
concepts.L3: Stirling gives $\log_{2}(n!) = n\log_{2} n - n\log_{2} e + \Theta(\log n)$, and $\log_{2} e = 1.4427$. At $n = 100$ that is $664.39 - 144.27 = 520.1$, against the exact $\log_{2}(100!) = 524.76$: the bound is tight to within a percent. Merge sort's exact worst case is $n\lceil\log_{2} n\rceil - 2^{\lceil\log_{2} n\rceil} + 1 = 573$ comparisons at $n = 100$, about $9$ percent above the $525$-comparison lower bound, so no comparison sort beats it by much. Now change the model: grant unit-cost operations on $w$-bit words, and counting and radix sort finish in $O(n)$, having made zero comparisons. The bound was never about sorting - it was about the decision-tree model.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many comparisons must any comparison sort make in the worst case on $n = {n}$ elements, and how does merge sort's worst case compare?
L4.answer: Lower bound ceil(log2(n!)). n=16: log2(16!) = 44.25, so 45. n=100: 524.76, so 525. n=1000: 8529.4, so 8530. Merge sort's exact worst case n*ceil(log2 n) - 2^ceil(log2 n) + 1: n=16: 49; n=100: 573; n=1000: 8977. Merge sort is within about 5 to 9 percent of the information-theoretic minimum (8.9 percent at n=16, 9.1 percent at n=100, 5.2 percent at n=1000).
L4.explanation: The bound is genuinely tight, which is why no comparison sort will ever be dramatically better on comparisons. Every real improvement in sorting since has come from reducing data movement and branch misprediction, not comparisons.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague says 'sorting is $\Omega(n\log n)$, so your $O(n)$ {alg} cannot be correct.' Give the two-sentence rebuttal.
L4.answer: The Omega(n log n) bound applies to algorithms whose only primitive on keys is pairwise comparison; it is a property of the comparison decision-tree model. Radix, counting and bucket sort inspect the representation of keys directly, which the word RAM model permits, so they are outside the model the bound was proved in.
L4.explanation: The correct follow-up is always 'in which model?'. A lower bound with no model named is not a claim. This same move explains why van Emde Boas beats log n predecessor search and why hashing beats ordered dictionaries.

L4.prompt_tpl: Stirling's approximation gives log2(n!) is approximately n*log2(n) - n*log2(e). Using this approximation, estimate the comparison-sort lower bound in bits for n = {n} elements, to one decimal place.
L4.answer: Stirling estimate n*log2(n) - n*log2(e). n=50: 210.1 bits. n=300: 2035.8 bits. n=2000: 19046.2 bits.
L4.explanation: Stirling's formula gives the dominant term of log2(n!); the omitted Theta(log n) term is always positive, so this estimate slightly undershoots the exact bound ceil(log2(n!)) - about 0.9 percent low at n=100, proportionally less as n grows.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the word-RAM / cell-probe setting, you need at least ceil(log2(n)) bits just to give n distinct keys unique addresses. For n = {n}, what is ceil(log2(n))?
L4.explanation: This is the minimum word width w a cell-probe structure needs merely to name n items. Every term in the Patrascu-Thorup bound that subtracts log n from w presupposes w is at least this large, or the keys could not even be written down.

L4.prompt_tpl: The cell-probe predecessor bound has a $\log(S/n)$ term in its denominator. If you replace the structure with {example}, using $S \approx 2^w$ cells, what happens to the query time, and does this contradict the bound?

example: a full lookup table indexed by every possible w-bit key
a precomputed table with one answer for every possible query
an array with one slot for every w-bit integer value

L4.answer: It drops toward O(1), because the log(S/n) term in the denominator grows without bound as S grows, driving the whole bound toward zero -- consistent with the bound, not a violation of it.
L4.explanation: The cell-probe bound is a genuine time-space trade-off, not a fixed floor on time alone. A table with one entry per possible key costs S about 2^w cells (one slot per key value, each holding an O(w)-bit predecessor index) and answers in O(1), and the formula predicts exactly this by letting log(S/n) swallow the whole expression as S grows.
options: It drops toward O(1), because the log(S/n) term in the denominator grows without bound as S grows, driving the whole bound toward zero -- consistent with the bound, not a violation of it.
It stays Theta(log_w n) regardless of S, because time and space are independent resources in the cell-probe model.
It becomes undefined, because the cell-probe model does not allow space larger than the number of keys n.

L4.prompt_tpl: Without invoking Stirling's formula, show that n! is at least (n/2)^(n/2) for n >= {n_min} (hint: the n/2 largest factors in the product n*(n-1)*...*1 are each at least n/2), then use that inequality to derive an $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparison-sorting lower bound in two lines.
L4.answer: n! = n*(n-1)*...*1 includes the n/2 factors from n down to n/2+1, each at least n/2, so n! >= (n/2)^(n/2). Taking log2 of both sides: log2(n!) >= (n/2)*log2(n/2) = (n/2)*(log2(n) - 1), which is Omega(n log n). This is a coarser but self-contained route to the same asymptotic bound Stirling gives exactly.
L4.explanation: This is the standard elementary proof of the comparison-sort lower bound taught before Stirling's formula: it throws away half the factors and still gets the right asymptotic order, because a decision tree with n! leaves needs depth at least log2(n!) regardless of which bound on n! you use to estimate it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Van Emde Boas search runs in O(log log u) time, where u = 2^w is the size of the key universe. When the key length w is Theta(log n) - just enough bits to number {n} distinct keys - show that log log u is Theta(log log n), and say why this is not the same structure as Whetstone's 'The van Emde Boas layout' concept.
L4.answer: u = 2^w, so log2(u) = w. If w = Theta(log2 n), then log2(u) = Theta(log2 n), and taking log2 again gives log2(log2(u)) = Theta(log2(log2 n)) = Theta(log log n). So van Emde Boas's O(log log u) collapses to O(log log n) exactly in the natural regime the Patrascu-Thorup bound singles out as its second tight case. This is not the same structure as Whetstone's 'The van Emde Boas layout', which covers the cache-oblivious van Emde Boas layout for external-memory search trees (Theta(log_B n) transfers) - same author, same recursive-halving idea, but a different, unrelated artefact from the O(log log u) predecessor/priority-queue structure derived here, which Whetstone does not currently cover as its own concept.
L4.explanation: This is why the two headline cases of the predecessor bound - Theta(log_w n) and Theta(log log n) - are not arbitrary: the second one is realised by an actual data structure, van Emde Boas, exactly when keys carry no more bits than they need to be distinct.

sections.note: Sorting is the one problem where theory, cache behaviour and branch prediction all argue at once, and you can hear each of them.

L0.body:
def merge(a, b):                 # stable: on a tie, take from the LEFT run
    i = j = 0; out = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if b[j] < a[i]: out.append(b[j]); j += 1     # strict <  keeps stability
        else:           out.append(a[i]); i += 1
    return out + a[i:] + b[j:]

# worst case comparisons: n*ceil(log2(n)) - 2**ceil(log2(n)) + 1  (exact; n*log2(n)-n+1
# only when n is a power of 2; n=1e6 -> 18,951,425, not 18,931,570)
# extra space: n           (in-place merge exists but is slow in practice)
L0.cloze: The merge takes from the left run when keys are {{c1::equal}}, which is what makes mergesort {{c2::stable}}. Its worst case is $n\lceil\log_{{2}} n\rceil - 2^{{\lceil\log_{{2}} n\rceil}} + 1$ comparisons, equal to $n\log_{{2}} n - n + 1$ only when $n$ is a power of two, and it needs {{c3::n}} words of scratch space.

concepts.L1: Split, sort both halves, merge. Its worst case equals its best case to within a constant, it is stable if the merge breaks ties toward the left run, and it reads both inputs sequentially, which makes it the only classical sort that is naturally external and naturally parallel.
concepts.L2: Stability is not a property of mergesort; it is a property of one comparison in the merge. Write `if b[j] <= a[i]` instead of `<` and the sort is still correct, still $n\log n$, and no longer stable. Every stable sort you rely on is one operator away from silently not being one.
concepts.L3: Two consequences follow from the sequential access pattern. First, mergesort is the external sort: with $M$ memory and $B$ block size you make $n/M$ sorted runs, then merge $M/B$ of them at a time, giving $\Theta((n/B)\log_{M/B}(n/B))$ transfers, which is optimal in the external-memory model. Second, the merge tree is a scheduling problem: merging runs of unequal length costs the sum of lengths at each merge, exactly the Huffman objective, so you always merge the two shortest runs first.

L4.prompt_tpl: Mergesort $n = {n}$ elements. How many comparisons in the worst case (exact worst case is $n\lceil\log_{{2}} n\rceil - 2^{{\lceil\log_{{2}} n\rceil}} + 1$), and how does that compare to the information-theoretic minimum $\log_{{2}}(n!)$?
L4.answer: n=1000: exact worst case = 1000*ceil(log2(1000)) - 2^ceil(log2(1000)) + 1 = 1000*10 - 1024 + 1 = 8977 (the n*log2(n)-n+1 shortcut gives 8966.8, off by 10 because 1000 is not a power of 2). Minimum log2(1000!) = 8529.4, an excess of about 5.2 percent. n=1e6: exact worst case = 1e6*20 - 2^20 + 1 = 18,951,425 (the shortcut gives 18,931,569.6). Minimum log2(1e6!) = 18,488,884.8, an excess of about 2.5 percent.
L4.explanation: Mergesort is within a few percent of optimal on comparisons and the gap shrinks with n. Nothing is left on the table there, which is why all subsequent sorting work targets memory traffic, branch misprediction and adaptivity instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team changes their merge from `if b[j] < a[i]` to `if b[j] <= a[i]` while 'simplifying'. All unit tests pass. Later, a report sorted by {k1} then re-sorted by {k2} comes out in the wrong order within groups. Explain.
L4.answer: The change destroyed stability: on equal keys the merge now prefers the right run, so elements that were adjacent-and-ordered in the first sort get swapped in the second. Sort-by-A-then-sort-by-B only yields the composite order (B, then A) if the second sort is stable. Correctness tests on a single key cannot detect this.
L4.explanation: Stability is invisible to any test that checks only sortedness. It needs a test that sorts records with duplicate keys and asserts the original relative order. This is a real class of production bug because the required test is not the obvious one.

L4.prompt_tpl: You merge two sorted runs of length {p} and {q} (worst case: a perfect interleaving of the two). How many comparisons does the merge step make? Answer with the comparison count.
L4.answer: Comparisons = p + q - 1: every element placed except the very last one is preceded by exactly one comparison that decides which run it comes from; once one run empties, the rest of the other is copied with no comparisons at all. p=5, q=8: 12. p=100, q=150: 249. p=1000, q=2500: 3499.
L4.explanation: The merge writes p+q elements total. Each placement but the last needs one comparison to decide the winner; the last is forced once the other run is known to be exhausted. This bound (p+q-1) is what the worst-case mergesort formula sums over every merge in the recursion.

L4.prompt_tpl: Bottom-up mergesort on n = {n} elements does ceil(log2(n)) levels of merging, and every level copies every element exactly once into a fresh output array. How many element copies happen in total across all levels? Answer with the total copy count.
L4.answer: Total copies = n * ceil(log2 n). n=16 (4 levels): 64 copies. n=1000 (10 levels, since 2^9=512 < 1000 <= 2^10=1024): 10,000 copies. n=1,000,000 (20 levels): 20,000,000 copies.
L4.explanation: Comparisons count decisions; copies count memory traffic, and mergesort pays n log n on both, unlike an in-place sort. This is the real cost that introsort and pdqsort avoid by sorting most of the array without ever leaving it, which is why they beat mergesort on cache-resident data despite similar comparison counts.

L4.prompt_tpl: External mergesort: n = {n} elements live on disk and internal memory holds M = {m} elements at a time. The first pass sorts one memory-load at a time and writes each as a run. How many initial sorted runs does that pass produce? Answer with the run count.
L4.answer: Runs = ceil(n / M), one run per memory-sized chunk (the last run may be short). n=10,000,000, M=100,000: 100 runs. n=10,000,000, M=500,000: 20 runs. n=50,000,000, M=100,000: 500 runs.
L4.explanation: This is stage one of the external-sort model in this concept's L3: form n/M runs in memory, then merge M/B of them at a time from disk. The run count here sets how many merge passes the second stage needs before the file is fully sorted.

L4.prompt_tpl: Merging two sorted runs of length {p} and {q} costs at least min(p, q) comparisons (if one whole run precedes the other) and at most p + q - 1 (if they perfectly interleave). What is the gap between the worst and best case, in comparisons?
L4.answer: Gap = (p+q-1) - min(p,q) = max(p,q) - 1. p=7, q=7: 6. p=60, q=15: 59. p=300, q=1: 299. The gap grows with the larger run, not the smaller one, because the best case is set by whichever run is shorter.
L4.explanation: Most treatments of mergesort quote only the worst case p+q-1 and treat merge cost as fixed; it is not. If the two runs are already mutually ordered (all of one below all of the other) the merge degenerates to a single scan of the shorter run, the mechanism behind natural-run optimizations like Timsort.

L4.prompt_tpl: cppreference documents two complexities for the C++ standard library's in-place merge: one when it can allocate extra memory for the merge, one when it cannot. What happens to the comparison count when no extra memory is available?
L4.answer: It rises from linear to O((p+q) log(p+q)) comparisons in the two runs' combined size p+q, though the result is still correct and stable.
L4.explanation: With a scratch buffer, merging two runs of combined size p+q costs at most p+q-1 comparisons, the ordinary bound this concept derives. Remove the buffer and the algorithm falls back to a recursive, rotation-based in-place merge that is still correct and stable but pays in extra comparisons, not in correctness.
options: It stays linear in the two runs' combined size either way, since merging never needed the extra memory for comparisons.
It rises from linear to O((p+q) log(p+q)) comparisons in the two runs' combined size p+q, though the result is still correct and stable.
It becomes unstable, trading correctness of tie order for staying linear in comparisons.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three sorted runs of length {a}, {b}, {c}, with {a} <= {b} <= {c}, must be combined into one run using two pairwise merges. This concept's own L3 states that each merge costs the sum of the two run sizes it combines, exactly the Huffman objective, so the minimum-cost merge order always combines the two currently-shortest runs first. Design that merge order for these three runs and compute the minimum total cost summed over both merges. Answer with the total cost.
L4.answer: Merge the two shortest, a and b, first (cost a+b), producing a run of size a+b; then merge that with c (cost a+b+c). Total = (a+b) + (a+b+c) = 2a+2b+c. a=5,b=50,c=1000: total=1110. a=10,b=80,c=2000: total=2180. a=20,b=120,c=5000: total=5280. Merging a with c (or b with c) first instead would leave a smaller run for the second merge but a larger one folded in twice, and always costs more: for any of the three possible first-merge choices, total cost is 2(a+b+c) minus whichever run is left for last, so leaving the largest run c for last minimizes the total.
L4.explanation: Total cost is 2(a+b+c) minus whichever run is merged last, since that run's size is counted once while the other two are each counted twice (once alone, once inside the combined run). Minimizing total cost therefore means leaving the largest run for last, i.e. always merging the two currently-shortest runs first -- the same greedy rule that makes Huffman coding's prefix-code lengths optimal.

concepts.t: Quicksort: partitioning, pivot choice, and why it wins

L0.cloze: Quicksort does about {{c1::1.386}} times $n\log_{{2}} n$ comparisons, which is {{c2::more}} than mergesort, yet is faster because it is {{c3::in-place}} and touches memory {{c4::sequentially}} from both ends.

concepts.L1: Choose a pivot, partition around it, recurse on both sides. Expected $2n\ln n$ comparisons, which is $1.386\,n\log_{2} n$ - about 39 percent more than mergesort - and it still wins in practice on every count that is not comparisons.
concepts.L2: Quicksort's advantage is not speed of comparison; it is that the partition is two sequential streams converging, needs no auxiliary array, and moves each element about once per level.
concepts.L3: Compute the expected comparison count. If the pivot is the $i$-th smallest, $C(n) = n - 1 + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(C(i-1) + C(n-i))$. Solving gives $C(n) = 2(n+1)H_{n} - 4n \approx 2n\ln n = 1.386\,n\log_{2} n$. So quicksort makes 39 percent more comparisons than mergesort's $n\log_{2} n$ and still beats it, because a comparison is nearly free and a cache miss is not. Pivot choice controls the tail, not the mean: a fixed first-element pivot is $\Theta(n^{2})$ on sorted input, which is the most common real input; median-of-three fixes sorted input but has known adversarial killers; median-of-medians or a random pivot removes the input dependence entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: Quicksort's expected comparisons are $2n\ln n$; mergesort's worst case is $n\log_{{2}} n$. For $n = {n}$, give both, and the ratio. Answer with the ratio of quicksort comparisons to mergesort comparisons.
L4.answer: Ratio is always 2 ln 2 = 1.3863. n=1000: 13,816 vs 9,966. n=100000: 2,302,585 vs 1,660,964. n=1e6: 27,631,021 vs 19,931,569. Quicksort does 38.6 percent more comparisons at every n.
L4.explanation: The ratio is n-independent because both are c*n*ln(n). Quicksort wins anyway on memory traffic and allocation. This is the cleanest available demonstration that comparison count stopped being the right cost metric decades ago.

L4.prompt_tpl: A quicksort uses `pivot = a[lo]` and recurses on both partitions without tail-call elimination. It crashes with a stack overflow on an input of {n} already-sorted elements. Name both defects.
L4.answer: First: a first-element pivot on sorted input produces partitions of size 0 and n-1 every time, so the recursion depth is n and the comparison count is Theta(n^2). Second: recursing on both sides rather than looping on the larger one means the stack depth follows the recursion depth. Fix both - random or median-of-three pivot, and recurse only into the smaller partition - and depth is bounded by log2(n).
L4.explanation: Recursing into the smaller side bounds stack depth at log2(n) even when the partitioning is terrible, because the smaller side is at most half. That is a worst-case guarantee independent of pivot quality, which is why it is not optional.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which pivot rule gives quicksort a worst case that no input can trigger, for a library sorting {n} elements?
options: A pivot chosen with a per-run random seed: the O(n log n) expectation then holds for every input, since the randomness is in the algorithm, not the data.
Median-of-three: it handles sorted and reverse-sorted input, so no input remains adversarial.
The middle element: it is deterministic and cannot be attacked because the attacker does not know n.
L4.answer: A pivot chosen with a per-run random seed: the O(n log n) expectation then holds for every input, since the randomness is in the algorithm, not the data.
L4.explanation: Median-of-three has documented adversarial killers (McIlroy's antiquicksort). A deterministic median-of-medians pivot gives a true worst-case bound but is too slow for the common case - which is why introsort uses a cheap pivot plus a depth-limited fallback instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: Quicksort's own recurrence counts partitioning a subarray of size $m$ as $m-1$ comparisons. If every pivot split its subarray exactly in half (the best case), the recurrence would be $C(n) = 2C(n/2) + (n-1)$ with $C(1) = 0$. For $n = {n}$ (a power of two), compute $C(n)$ exactly. Answer with the number of comparisons.
L4.answer: C(n) = n*log2(n) - n + 1. n=8: 17. n=64: 321. n=1024: 9217. (Unrolling: C(2)=1, C(4)=5, C(8)=17, C(16)=49, C(32)=129, C(64)=321, ..., C(1024)=9217.) This equals mergesort's worst-case comparison count for a power-of-two array (mergesort's actual count is data-dependent, between about n/2 and n-1 per merge level), so the best case erases quicksort's constant-factor disadvantage relative to that worst case.
L4.explanation: Perfectly balanced splits give the same shape of recurrence as a perfectly balanced merge, $C(n)=2C(n/2)+(n-1)$ - an idealization, not a direct substitution into this concept's own average-case formula, which sums over every pivot rank rather than forcing one $n/2$ split. At the best case quicksort's count matches mergesort's worst-case count, so the 1.386 factor is entirely an average-case, not a best-case, phenomenon.

L4.prompt_tpl: The array holds {n} four-byte ints on a machine with 64-byte cache lines (16 ints per line). During one Hoare partition pass, the two cursors together scan every element of the {n}-element range exactly once, never revisiting a line already passed. How many distinct cache lines does that partition pass touch? Answer with the number of cache lines, rounding up.
L4.answer: Cache lines = ceil(n/16). n=1000: 63. n=100000: 6250. n=1000000: 62500. The two cursors partition the same n elements once each, with no overlap, so the pass costs about n/16 lines total, not 2n/16 - a single sequential sweep, which is the real reason quicksort beats mergesort despite doing more comparisons.
L4.explanation: The cursors i and j scan disjoint, non-overlapping ranges that together cover the whole subarray exactly once, so total memory traffic for one partition pass is one linear sweep, not two: ceil(n/16) lines, matching L1's claim that quicksort touches memory sequentially rather than needing a second array.

L4.prompt_tpl: An array of {n} equal elements is partitioned once by the L0 code's Hoare scheme (strict less-than and greater-than tests). What actually happens, and why?
L4.answer: It still splits close to the middle: both cursors stop on the very first test (every element equals the pivot), so i and j each advance one step per outer iteration and meet near the center, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$ overall despite zero distinct keys.
L4.explanation: Hoare's two-pointer scan advances symmetrically on equal keys: `i` and `j` each take exactly one step before the strict test fails, so the split lands near the midpoint every time - unlike a naive Lomuto scheme using `<=`/`>=`, which pushes every equal element to one side and degrades on duplicate-heavy input.
options: It still splits close to the middle: both cursors stop on the very first test (every element equals the pivot), so i and j each advance one step per outer iteration and meet near the center, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$ overall despite zero distinct keys.
It degrades to $\Theta(n^{2})$, because with only one distinct value there is no way to separate elements less than the pivot from elements greater than it.
The loop never terminates, because `a[i] < p` and `a[j] > p` can never be true when every element equals `p`, so i and j never move past their start positions.

L4.prompt_tpl: Median-of-medians pivot selection gives quicksort a provable worst case of $\Theta(n\log n)$ on {n} elements, yet no major standard library sorts with it on every call. Explain the real engineering reason, and name the concept that describes what libraries actually run instead.
L4.answer: Median-of-medians is Theta(n) but with a large constant (grouping into 5s, recursing to find the median of medians, then partitioning), so it is slower on the typical case even though its growth rate is the same order as a cheap heuristic pivot. Real libraries instead run introsort: a cheap pivot (often median-of-three or a ninther) for the common case, falling back to heapsort only once recursion depth exceeds a limit - a worst-case guarantee bought without paying the median-of-medians tax on every call. See: Introsort, pdqsort, and what your standard library actually runs.
L4.explanation: This is the resolution the paragraph above sets up: a pivot rule with a provable worst case exists (median-of-medians) but its constant factor is too large to use unconditionally, so production sorts buy the same guarantee more cheaply with a depth limit and a fallback algorithm, not a smarter pivot.

concepts.t: Introsort, pdqsort, and what your standard library actually runs

L0.cloze: Introsort limits quicksort recursion depth to {{c1::2\log_{{2}} n}} and then falls back to {{c2::heapsort}}, giving an $O(n\log n)$ {{c3::worst case}}. Below about {{c4::16}} elements it stops and lets one final {{c5::insertion sort}} pass finish the job.

concepts.L1: The hybrid every major C++ standard library ships for std::sort, and Rust ships for slice::sort_unstable: quicksort for the common case, a depth counter switching to heapsort on bad partitions, insertion sort for small runs. Rust's default, stable slice::sort is a separate merge-based algorithm, not this hybrid.
concepts.L2: The final insertion sort is run once over the whole array, not per subarray. After introsort stops at subarrays of size 16, no element is more than 16 positions from its final place, so a single insertion pass costs $O(n)$ and avoids the per-call overhead of thousands of tiny sorts.
concepts.L3: pdqsort is the current refinement and it is worth knowing why. It replaces the branchy partition with a branchless one (BlockQuicksort, Edelkamp and Weiss) that buffers per-block comparison outcomes into an offset array and permutes in a second pass, avoiding the branch the CPU cannot learn to predict: each misprediction stalls the pipeline for a dozen-plus cycles, and on random data roughly half the comparisons mispredict, so branchless partitioning measures a 1.5-3x speedup over introsort. It detects already-partitioned input and skips work, giving $O(n)$ on sorted arrays. And when a partition is badly unbalanced it breaks patterns by swapping a few elements deterministically rather than falling straight to heapsort, so it keeps quicksort's constant in more cases.

L4.prompt_tpl: libstdc++ sets the introsort depth limit to $2\lfloor\log_{{2}} n\rfloor$ and stops recursing at subarrays of {thr} elements. For $n = {n}$, what is the depth limit, and how many subarrays remain for the final insertion pass?
L4.answer: n=1000: floor(log2 1000)=9, depth limit 18; about ceil(1000/16)=63 residual runs. n=1e6: floor(log2 1e6)=19, depth limit 38; about 62500 residual runs. The insertion pass is a single sweep over all n, costing O(n + inversions) with inversions bounded by 16 per element.
L4.explanation: The depth limit is 2 log2 n rather than log2 n because good partitions rarely split exactly in half; 2x gives slack for ordinary luck while still catching genuine quadratic behaviour. Hitting the limit is rare enough that heapsort's worse constant does not matter.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does introsort fall back to heapsort rather than to {alt}?
L4.answer: Heapsort is in-place and worst-case O(n log n). Mergesort would need Theta(n) auxiliary memory, which breaks std::sort's contract of sorting in place with O(log n) stack. Median-of-medians gives a worst-case linear pivot but with a constant roughly 3-5x the common case, and it would be paid on every partition rather than only on the rare bad path. Heapsort's bad constant is acceptable precisely because it almost never runs.
L4.explanation: The design principle: pay for the guarantee only when the guarantee is needed. Introsort's fallback is a circuit breaker, not a subroutine, which is why its constant is irrelevant.

L4.prompt_tpl:
libstdc++'s std::sort computes floor(log2 n) for the depth limit as `std::__bit_width(n) - 1`, where `__bit_width` is `bit_width_of_type - countl_zero(n)` -- one hardware count-leading-zeros instruction, not a loop, which is exactly why it is cheap enough to call before any sorting starts. This Python reproduces the same closed-form value:

def lg(n):
    return n.bit_length() - 1

print(2 * lg(n))

What does it print when n = {n}?
L4.answer: bit_length() - 1 is floor(log2 n); the program prints 2*floor(log2 n). n=7: 4. n=300: 16. n=65536: 32 (exact power of two, so bit_length is 17). n=5,000,000: 44.
L4.explanation: libstdc++'s actual `__lg(n)` is `__bit_width(n) - 1`, and `__bit_width` is defined via `__countl_zero` -- a single clz/bsr-family hardware instruction, O(1), not a shift loop. That is why it is cheap to call once before sorting even starts. It is exact at powers of two too: n=65536=2^16 gives bit_length 17, so lg=16.

L4.prompt_tpl: After introsort's recursion stops, no element sits more than {d} positions from where it belongs once the array is fully sorted (the insertion-sort threshold). Insertion sort's worst-case number of comparisons is bounded above by n times the maximum displacement. What is that upper bound for n = {n} elements with maximum displacement {d}?
L4.explanation: n times d is a loose upper bound (true cost is bounded by the actual number of inversions, which is at most n times d), but it shows why capping displacement at a constant (16) rather than letting it scale with n is what keeps the final insertion-sort pass linear instead of quadratic.

L4.prompt_tpl: libstdc++ sets introsort's depth limit to 2 log2 n before falling back to heapsort. If the factor were {factor} instead of 2, what would change about the worst-case guarantee, and what would change about the typical-case constant?
L4.answer: Factor 1 (log2 n): the O(n log n) worst-case guarantee still holds, since heapsort still eventually triggers, but it triggers far more often -- ordinary, non-adversarial recursions routinely run a little deeper than log2 n from partition imbalance alone, so more runs pay heapsort's worse constant for no reason, slowing the common case. Factor 3 (3 log2 n): still O(n log n) asymptotically (any constant multiple of log2 n is O(log n) depth), but the guard now tolerates deeper bad recursion before intervening, so a genuinely adversarial input burns more comparisons before heapsort kicks in -- worse worst-case constant, same class.
L4.explanation: The depth-limit factor never changes the asymptotic class: any constant times log2 n is still O(log n) recursion depth, so the worst case stays $O(n\log n)$ either way. It only trades how often, and how late, introsort pays heapsort's worse constant. 2x is Musser's measured sweet spot.

L4.prompt_tpl: Heapsort, introsort's worst-case fallback, makes about 2 n log2 n comparisons in the worst case (classical heapsort analysis). The information-theoretic lower bound for comparison sorting (see 'Lower bounds: comparison sorting and the cell-probe model') is log2(n!); Stirling's approximation gives log2(n!) is approximately n log2 n minus n log2 e. Using only these leading terms, what multiple of the lower bound is introsort's worst-case comparison count, for n = {n}?
L4.answer: n=2000: log2 n = 10.966, lower bound approximately 19,046, heapsort's count approximately 43,863, ratio approximately 2.30x. n=2,000,000: log2 n = 20.932, lower bound approximately 38,977,747, heapsort's count approximately 83,726,274, ratio approximately 2.15x. The ratio drifts toward 2 as n grows, since both terms share the same leading n log2 n term and the -n log2 e correction shrinks relative to it.
L4.explanation: Heapsort's worst case is about twice the information-theoretic minimum, not comparison-optimal: the factor of 2 comes from the two comparisons per sift-down level (compare the two children, then compare the winner against the parent) that the classical heapsort analysis charges.

L4.prompt_tpl: libstdc++'s std::sort uses a fixed median-of-three pivot plus a deterministic depth limit that falls back to heapsort, instead of {approach} the way randomized quicksort does (see 'Quicksort: partitioning, pivot choice, and why it wins'). Which is the strongest reason to prefer the deterministic guard?

approach: randomizing the pivot on every partition call
drawing one random pivot choice at the start and reusing it

L4.answer: The deterministic depth-limit guard gives a worst-case bound that holds for every input with certainty, including one built by an adversary who knows the algorithm; randomization only makes the bad case unlikely, not impossible, and a poor or predictable source of randomness can still be defeated.
L4.explanation: Randomization converts a certain worst case into an unlikely one; it does not eliminate it, and a library's worst-case guarantee should not depend on RNG quality or a predictable seed. Introsort instead detects that partitioning is going badly and switches strategy only for that instance, the actual goal of Musser's 1997 paper.
options: Randomization is slower because generating random numbers costs more than a few extra comparisons.

The deterministic depth-limit guard gives a worst-case bound that holds for every input with certainty, including one built by an adversary who knows the algorithm; randomization only makes the bad case unlikely, not impossible, and a poor or predictable source of randomness can still be defeated.
Heapsort is faster than quicksort on average, so triggering it more often improves typical performance.

concepts.t: Counting and radix sort: beating n log n by changing the model

L0.body:
# LSD radix, w-bit keys, r-bit digits: ceil(w/r) stable counting passes.
def radix(a, w=32, r=8):
    for shift in range(0, w, r):
        cnt = [0] * (1 << r)
        for x in a: cnt[(x >> shift) & ((1 << r) - 1)] += 1
        for i in range(1, 1 << r): cnt[i] += cnt[i-1]   # prefix sums
        out = [0] * len(a)
        for x in reversed(a):                           # reversed keeps stability
            d = (x >> shift) & ((1 << r) - 1)
            cnt[d] -= 1; out[cnt[d]] = x
        a = out
    return a
# w=32,r=8 -> 4 passes, 256 counters. w=32,r=16 -> 2 passes, 65536 counters.
L0.cloze: LSD radix sort needs {{c1::\lceil w/r \rceil}} passes over the data with $2^{{r}}$ counters per pass, and each pass must be {{c2::stable}} or the previously sorted digits are destroyed. Iterating in {{c3::reverse}} with a decrementing count array is what makes the counting pass stable.

concepts.L1: Counting sort places $n$ keys from a universe of size $k$ in $O(n + k)$ by histogram and prefix sum. Radix sort applies it digit by digit, $\lceil w/r \rceil$ times, for $O(n\,w/r)$ - linear in $n$ for fixed key width, with no comparisons at all.
concepts.L2: It is not free of $\log n$; it is $O(n\log_{2^{r}} u)$ for a universe $u$, and if keys must be distinct then $u \geq n$ and the passes are $\geq \log_{2^{r}} n$.
concepts.L3: This is why $r$ has an optimum well below the word size. At $r = 8$ the count array is 256 entries, 1 KiB, comfortably in L1, and the scatter touches 256 streams - already more than the typical 10-16 line-fill buffers, but tolerable. At $r = 16$ the counts are 65536 entries, 256 KiB, spilling to L2, and the scatter touches 65536 destinations, which thrashes the TLB with 4 KiB pages. Two passes instead of four is a clean asymptotic win and a practical loss. Real implementations use $r$ around 8 to 11, do the histogram passes for all digits in one read of the input, and often switch to MSD radix with a comparison sort at the bottom so that the recursion sorts locally and stays in cache.

L4.prompt_tpl: Sorting $n = {n}$ keys of {w} bits by LSD radix with $r = {r}$: number of passes, counters per pass, and total element-writes, versus quicksort's expected comparisons.
L4.answer: passes = ceil(w/r); writes = n * passes; counters = 2^r. w=32,r=8: 4 passes, 256 counters, 4e6 writes. w=32,r=11: 3 passes, 2048 counters, 3e6 writes. w=64,r=8: 8 passes, 256 counters, 8e6 writes. w=64,r=11: 6 passes, 2048 counters, 6e6 writes. Quicksort at n=1e6 expects 2n ln n = 27.6e6 comparisons.
L4.explanation: Radix moves far less data than quicksort compares, yet the writes are scattered and quicksort's are sequential. On 32-bit keys radix usually wins by 2-3x out of cache; on 64-bit keys with 8 passes the margin often disappears.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LSD radix sort iterates the input {order} in the placement loop and produces correct output for single-digit keys but garbage for multi-digit ones. Why?
L4.answer: With a count array converted to starting offsets, iterating forwards and incrementing is stable; with a count array converted to ending offsets, you must iterate backwards and decrement. Mixing the two conventions makes the pass anti-stable, which reverses the relative order of keys sharing a digit and therefore destroys the ordering established by all previous, less significant, passes. Single digit keys never expose it because there is no previous pass to destroy.
L4.explanation: LSD radix is correct only because every pass is stable; the invariant is that after pass i the array is sorted by the low i digits. A non-stable pass breaks the invariant while still producing something sorted by the current digit, which is exactly the shape of bug that passes a naive test.

L4.prompt_tpl: Counting sort on n = {n} keys drawn from a universe of size k = {k} performs one increment per key to build the histogram, one addition per bucket after the first to prefix-sum it, and one write per key to place it in the output. Using the total 2n + k - 1 for these three passes, how many elementary operations does it perform?
L4.explanation: Counting sort makes n increments to build the histogram, k-1 additions to prefix-sum it in place, and n writes to place every key, for exactly 2n + k - 1 elementary steps: the explicit constant behind the O(n+k) bound, not just its shape.

L4.prompt_tpl: LSD radix sort on keys that are w = {w} bits wide, processed r = {r} bits at a time, needs ceil(w / r) passes over the array, one per digit. How many passes does it take?
L4.explanation: Every group of r bits, including a final partial group, needs its own stable counting pass, so the pass count rounds up. 64-bit keys at r=12 fit only 5 full 12-bit groups (60 bits) plus 4 leftover bits, which still forces a 6th pass.

L4.prompt_tpl: Counting sort and radix sort run in time close to n, or n times w/r, appearing to beat the Omega(n log n) lower bound that every introductory algorithms course states for sorting. Which statement correctly resolves this apparent contradiction?
L4.answer: The Omega(n log n) bound applies only to comparison-based sorts; counting and radix sort read a key's value as an array index instead of comparing keys pairwise, so the bound does not constrain them.
L4.explanation: The comparison-sort lower bound counts only algorithms that decide order by comparing pairs of keys; it says nothing about an algorithm that uses a key's value as a direct array index, which is exactly what counting and radix sort do.
options: The Omega(n log n) bound applies only to comparison-based sorts; counting and radix sort read a key's value as an array index instead of comparing keys pairwise, so the bound does not constrain them.
The bound is stated incorrectly in most textbooks; counting sort actually performs Omega(n log n) comparisons once cache-miss costs are counted.
Counting sort evades the bound the same way randomized quicksort avoids its worst case: by choosing pivots at random so no adversarial input triggers n log n behavior.

L4.prompt_tpl: At w = {w} bits, r = {r1} needs fewer passes over the array than r = {r2}. Real radix sort implementations often use the smaller r anyway. In one or two sentences, explain the hardware reason, comparing the size of the counter table at each r.
L4.answer: At r=16 the counter table has 2^16 = 65536 entries (256 KiB), which spills past L1 and usually L2 cache and scatters writes across far more destination pages, thrashing the TLB. At r=8 the table has 2^8 = 256 entries (1 KiB), which stays resident in L1 and touches a small, cacheable set of destinations. The extra passes r=8 requires move far less total time than the cache and TLB misses r=16 introduces, so the asymptotically worse choice usually runs faster.
L4.explanation: Pass count is what the asymptotic bound O(n w/r) counts, but on real hardware a counter table that fits in L1 and a scatter pattern that fits the TLB usually beats fewer passes over a table that spills out of cache.

L4.prompt_tpl: A counter array of 2^r entries at 4 bytes each must fit within a {cache_kib} KiB cache. What is the largest integer r for which 2^r times 4 bytes is at most {cache_kib} KiB? Answer with that value of r.
L4.answer: r = floor(log2(cache_kib * 1024 / 4)). 32 KiB: floor(log2(8192)) = 13 (2^13*4 = 32768 B = 32 KiB exactly). 256 KiB: floor(log2(65536)) = 16. 1024 KiB: floor(log2(262144)) = 18. 8192 KiB: floor(log2(2097152)) = 21.
L4.explanation: The counter table is 2^r 4-byte entries, so it fits a C-KiB cache exactly when 2^r * 4 <= C * 1024, i.e. r <= log2(C * 256); the largest integer r is the floor of that bound, exactly the point where the next larger r spills the table out of that cache level.

L4.prompt_tpl: The cumulative-count step in counting sort turns a histogram cnt[0..k-1] into prefix sums, so cnt[d] becomes the number of keys with digit value at most d. In one or two sentences, explain why this prefix-sum step is the same cumulative-sum operation as computing rank in a bitvector rank-and-select structure, and name the Whetstone concept where that operation is reused to answer rank queries in O(1) time.
L4.answer: rank1(i) in a bitvector is the count of set bits before position i, an exclusive prefix sum over the bit array; counting sort's cnt[d], after the prefix-sum step, is the count of keys with digit at most d, an inclusive prefix sum over the histogram array (cnt[d] counts one more position than rank1(d) does). Both compute a cumulative sum over a small fixed-size array, differing only in that inclusive/exclusive offset. The reused, O(1)-query version of this idea appears in Bitvectors with rank and select.
L4.explanation: Counting sort computes a rank-like cumulative sum once, in one linear prefix-sum pass, and throws the intermediate values away after placing the keys; a rank/select structure precomputes and stores the same cumulative sums so any rank query later answers in O(1) instead of a linear scan.

concepts.t: Selection: quickselect, median of medians, introselect

L0.body:
quickselect(a, k):            # expected O(n): n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n
    p = partition(a, random_pivot)
    if k == p: return a[k]
    recurse into ONE side only

median_of_medians(a):         # worst-case O(n), constant ~10x
    groups of 5 -> medians -> median of those, recursively
    guarantees pivot rank in [0.3n, 0.7n]
    T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + cn,  and 1/5 + 7/10 = 0.9 < 1  ->  T(n) <= 10cn
L0.cloze: Quickselect recurses into only {{c1::one}} side, so its expected cost telescopes to {{c2::2n}} rather than $n\log n$. Median of medians uses groups of {{c3::5}} to guarantee the pivot's rank lies between $0.3n$ and $0.7n$, and the recurrence closes because $1/5 + 7/10 = {{c4::0.9}} < 1$.

concepts.L1: Finding the $k$-th smallest without sorting. Quickselect recurses into one partition only: expected $2n$ comparisons, $\Theta(n^{2})$ worst case. Median of medians forces $O(n)$ worst case at high constant. Introselect runs quickselect, falling back once recursion depth signals bad pivots.
concepts.L2: Groups of 5 is not arbitrary and groups of 3 do not work. With group size $g$ the recurrence is $T(n) \leq T(n/g) + T(n(1 - \frac{1}{2}\lceil g/2 \rceil / g)) + cn$, and it is linear only when the two fractions sum to less than 1. At $g = 3$ they sum to exactly $1/3 + 2/3 = 1$ and the bound degrades to $\Theta(n\log n)$.
concepts.L3: Check $g = 5$. The median-of-medians is $\geq$ the medians of half the groups, and $\geq 3$ elements in each of those groups, so at least $3n/10$ elements are below it and symmetrically $3n/10$ above. The recursive call therefore runs on at most $7n/10$. The pivot-finding call is on $n/5$. Since $1/5 + 7/10 = 0.9 < 1$, substituting $T(n) \leq an$ gives $an/5 + 7an/10 + cn \leq an$ whenever $a \geq 10c$: linear, with a constant around 10. Quickselect's expected cost is $n + n/2 + n/4 + \ldots = 2n$ under random pivots. So the deterministic algorithm is about five times slower than the randomised one in exchange for removing a tail that occurs with vanishing probability.

L4.prompt_tpl: Expected comparisons for quickselect on $n = {n}$ elements with random pivots, versus fully sorting first. Give both. Answer with the expected number of quickselect comparisons.
L4.answer: Quickselect expects about 2n comparisons (the geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + ...). n=1000: about 2000 vs sorting's 2n ln n = 13,816 (ratio ln(1000) = 6.9x). n=1e6: about 2,000,000 vs 27,631,021 (ratio ln(1e6) = 13.8x). The ratio is exactly ln n, so selection's advantage over sort-then-index grows without bound as n grows -- it is not a fixed multiple.
L4.explanation: The precise expected count for the median is about 3.39n, and about 2n for a random rank; both are Theta(n) with a small constant. The habit of calling sort() to get a median is a log-n factor thrown away, which matters on large arrays and in inner loops.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show why median of medians uses groups of 5 and not groups of {g}, by writing the recurrence and checking whether the fractions sum below 1.
L4.answer: With groups of 3, the median-of-medians beats at least 2 elements in half the groups, so at least 2*(n/3)/2 = n/3 elements are below it and n/3 above, leaving a recursive call on up to 2n/3. Pivot finding costs T(n/3). The fractions are 1/3 + 2/3 = 1 exactly, so the substitution T(n) <= an fails: no constant a works and the solution is Theta(n log n). Groups of 5 give 1/5 + 7/10 = 0.9 < 1 and close.
L4.explanation: Any group size 5 or larger works; 5 minimises the constant among odd sizes because larger groups make the median-of-each-group step more expensive without buying much extra pivot quality. This is the classic worked example of a recurrence whose linearity depends on a strict inequality.

L4.prompt_tpl: Median of medians splits n = {n} elements into groups of 5 (the last group may be smaller). How many groups does it form? Answer with the number of groups.
L4.answer: Groups = ceil(n/5). n=1000: 200 groups. n=100000: 20,000 groups. n=7: 2 groups (one full group of 5, one partial group of 2).
L4.explanation: Group size 5 is fixed by the algorithm; a leftover group smaller than 5 (here, 2 elements) is still processed, usually merged into the recursive median-finding step. The group count sets how many median-of-5 computations run before recursing.

L4.prompt_tpl: An optimal comparison network finds the median of 5 elements in exactly {c} comparisons. For n = {n} elements split into groups of 5 (the last group may be smaller), how many comparisons does median-of-medians spend finding every group's median (ceil(n/5) groups total)? Answer with the total comparison count.
L4.answer: Total = c * ceil(n/5). n=1000: 6*200 = 1200 comparisons (1.2n). n=1e6: 6*200000 = 1,200,000 comparisons (1.2n). n=7: 6*2 = 12 comparisons (ceil(7/5) = 2 groups, the second group has only 2 elements). This single step alone already costs Theta(n) with constant 6/5, before the partition pass or the recursive call on the medians even start.
L4.explanation: The '6' comes from an optimal sorting network for 5 elements (worst case 6 comparisons, not 10, since you only need the median, not a full order). This step is one of the several Theta(n) passes -- median-finding, partitioning, two recursive calls -- that sum to the ~10cn bound.

L4.prompt_tpl: Quickselect always partitions on the FIRST element and always recurses toward the target, with no randomisation. On an already-sorted ascending array of n = {n} elements, searching for the maximum forces every partition to remove exactly one element. How many comparisons does this adversarial input force in total? Answer with the comparison count.
L4.answer: Comparisons = n(n-1)/2, the triangular sum (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1. n=100: 4950. n=10000: 49,995,000. This is Theta(n^2) -- the exact failure mode that a random pivot (quickselect) or a guaranteed-decent pivot (median of medians) exists to avoid.
L4.explanation: First-element pivoting on sorted input is the selection analogue of quicksort's classic worst case: every partition only discards the pivot itself, so the recursion never shrinks by more than one element. This is why production code never uses a fixed pivot rule.

L4.prompt_tpl: Median-of-medians stays linear only when 1/g + 1 - ceil(g/2)/(2g) is below 1 (at exactly 1 it degrades to n log n, as it does at g=3). For group size g = {g}, compute this sum as a decimal.
L4.answer: g=4: 1/4 + 1 - ceil(2)/8 = 1.0 -- degrades to Theta(n log n), the same failure as g=3, even though 4 is even. g=6: 1/6 + 1 - ceil(3)/12 = 0.917 -- stays linear. g=7: 1/7 + 1 - ceil(4)/14 = 0.857 -- stays linear and is the next odd size after 5.
L4.explanation: Parity is not what decides linearity -- g=4 fails and g=6 succeeds. What matters is whether the guaranteed-excluded fraction (roughly (g+1)/(4g)) is large enough that the two recursive fractions sum below 1. g=5 is simply the smallest size that works with the smallest constant.

L4.prompt_tpl: Introselect exists to do for selection what introsort does for sorting: keep the fast algorithm's average speed but cap its worst case at O(n) instead of Theta(n^2). Design it: what should it count during quickselect's recursion, what threshold should trigger a fallback, and which algorithm should it fall back to? Name the trade-off the fallback pays for that guarantee.
L4.answer: Count recursion depth (or consecutive badly-unbalanced partitions). Once depth exceeds a budget like 2*log2(n) -- the same trigger introsort uses -- abandon quickselect's partitioning and switch to a worst-case-linear selector: the classical choice is median-of-medians, which guarantees the target is found in O(n) even from that point on. The trade-off: the fallback pays median-of-medians' roughly 10x-larger constant, but only on the rare inputs that would otherwise have driven quickselect to Theta(n^2) -- exactly the same 'pay for the guarantee only when needed' trade introsort makes by falling back to heapsort.
L4.explanation: This is the same circuit-breaker design as introsort (see 'Introsort, pdqsort, and what your standard library actually runs'): a fast optimistic algorithm with no worst-case guarantee, monitored by a depth counter, backed by a slower algorithm that does have the guarantee. The fallback's bad constant is irrelevant because it almost never runs.

concepts.t: Dynamic arrays: growth factor and amortised append

L0.cloze: Amortised copies per element is $1/(g-1)$: doubling costs {{c1::1}} copy per element, $1.5\times$ growth costs {{c2::2}}. Summing every block ever freed crosses the next request for any $g < 2$, not just $g < \varphi$; the golden ratio instead comes from requiring only the last {{c3::two}} freed blocks to cover the next one, $g^{{2}} \le g + {{c4::1}}$, giving $g \le \varphi = {{c5::1.618}}$.

concepts.L1: A contiguous array plus a size and a capacity, where a full append allocates a larger block, copies, and frees. The growth factor $g$ is the only tuning knob, and it trades copy work $1/(g-1)$ per element against memory slack of up to $(g-1)$ times the live size.
concepts.L2: Growing by a constant, not a factor, is the actual disaster: appending 1024 at a time makes $n$ appends cost $\Theta(n^{2})$ total copies, not $\Theta(n)$.
concepts.L3: Total copies for $n$ appends with factor $g$: capacities are $1, g, g^{2}, \ldots$ up to about $n$, and the copies performed are the sum of the capacities below $n$, a geometric series equal to $n/(g-1)$ to first order. At $g = 2$ that is $n$; at $g = 1.5$ it is $2n$. With constant growth $c$ you resize $n/c$ times and copy $c + 2c + \ldots + n = n^{2}/(2c)$ elements: quadratic. The golden-ratio argument needs a sharper model than summing every block ever freed: that sum alone crosses the next request for any $g < 2$, not just below $\varphi$ (at $g=1.9$, freed $1+1.9+3.61+6.859=13.37$ already exceeds the 5th block, $13.03$). One derivation reproducing $\varphi$: assume only the two most recently freed blocks are still around to coalesce; requiring $g^{k} \leq g^{k-1}+g^{k-2}$ for every $k$ reduces to $g^{2} \leq g+1$, i.e. $g \leq \varphi = 1.618$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Appending $n = {n}$ elements starting from capacity 1 with growth factor {g}: total element copies, number of reallocations, and worst-case memory used relative to the live data.
L4.answer: g=2, n=1000: reallocs = ceil(log2 1000) = 10, copies = 2^10 - 1 = 1023, peak capacity 1024 so up to 2x live memory at the moment of a resize plus the old block still held, i.e. 3x transiently. g=2, n=1e6: 20 reallocs, 1,048,575 copies. g=1.5, n=1000: about 18 reallocs, about 2000 copies, peak slack 50 percent. g=1.5, n=1e6: about 35 reallocs, about 2e6 copies.
L4.explanation: Note the transient 3x: during a resize the old and new blocks are both live, so peak RSS for a doubling vector is three times the live data, not two. That is a common surprise in memory-constrained services and an argument for reserve().

L4.prompt_tpl:
```cpp
for (auto& x : v) if (x == {k}) v.push_back(x * 2);
```
This compiles and usually appears to work. What is wrong?
L4.answer: push_back may reallocate, which invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector - including the range-for's internal begin/end iterators and the reference x. After a reallocation the loop reads freed memory. It 'works' whenever spare capacity happens to absorb the append, which makes it a heisenbug that appears only at particular sizes.
L4.explanation: Iterator invalidation is a correctness consequence of the growth policy, not a performance one. The fixes are reserve() ahead of the loop, collecting into a second vector, or indexing by position and re-reading v.size() each iteration.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C++ vector starts at capacity 1 and doubles capacity on every reallocation. After exactly {n} push_back calls with no reserve(), how many total element copies has the implementation performed? Answer with the number of copies.
L4.answer: Copies = $2^{\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil} - 1$. n=50: ceil(log2 50)=6, copies=$2^{6}-1=63$. n=300: ceil(log2 300)=9, copies=511. n=2000: ceil(log2 2000)=11, copies=2047. n=50000: ceil(log2 50000)=16, copies=65535.
L4.explanation: Each resize copies exactly the current size, and resizes happen at sizes $1, 2, 4, \ldots$, so the total is the geometric sum up to the first power of two at or above $n$: one short of that power of two, always under $n$ itself doubled.

L4.prompt_tpl: That same vector (capacity 1, doubling on every fill, no reserve()) is appended to {n} times. How many reallocations happen in total? Answer with the count of reallocations.
L4.answer: Reallocations = $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$. n=10: 4. n=100: 7. n=5000: 13. n=200000: 18.
L4.explanation: Capacity after $k$ reallocations is $2^{k}$, so the smallest $k$ with $2^{k} \geq n$ is $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$. This is also the exact number of times any single element could in principle have been copied, which bounds the worst-case latency of one unlucky append.

L4.prompt_tpl: A poorly written dynamic array grows by a fixed amount instead of a factor: capacity increases by {c} every time it fills, starting from capacity {c}, with no pre-allocation. After {n} appends, how many total element copies have happened? Answer with the number of copies.
L4.answer: With $m = \lceil n/c \rceil$ capacity levels, total copies $= c \cdot m(m-1)/2$. n=1000, c=10: m=100, copies=49500. n=100000, c=100: m=1000, copies=49950000. n=10000, c=50: m=200, copies=995000. These are quadratic in $n$ for fixed $c$, not linear.
L4.explanation: Copies at each resize are a multiple of $c$ (the sizes at which resizes happen: $c, 2c, 3c, \ldots$), so the total is $c$ times a triangular number in $m = n/c$: quadratic overall. This is exactly the L2 disaster - appending 1024 at a time costs $\Theta(n^{2})$, not $\Theta(n)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Suppose only the two most recently freed blocks (not the whole allocation history) are assumed still available when a vector needs its next, larger block; older freed memory may already have been reused by other allocations. If capacity grows by a fixed factor g each reallocation, write the requirement that those two blocks together can cover the next request, and solve for the largest g for which that holds at every reallocation.
L4.answer: Two reallocations ago the freed block had size $g^{k-2}$, one reallocation ago $g^{k-1}$, and the block now needed is $g^{k}$. Requiring $g^{k-1} + g^{k-2} \geq g^{k}$ and dividing through by $g^{k-2}$ gives $g + 1 \geq g^{2}$, i.e. $g^{2} - g - 1 \leq 0$. The positive root of $g^{2}-g-1=0$ is $g = (1+\sqrt{5})/2 \approx 1.618$, the golden ratio $\varphi$: for $g \leq \varphi$ the two most recently freed blocks always cover the next request; for $g > \varphi$ they never do.
L4.explanation: This is the mechanism that actually produces the 1.618 figure quoted for fbvector. Summing the ENTIRE freed history instead (as the doubling identity $1+2+\cdots+2^{k-1}=2^{k}-1$ suggests) crosses the next request for any $g<2$, not just $g<\varphi$; it is the stricter two-block-only model that singles out the golden ratio specifically.

L4.prompt_tpl: An open-addressing hash table doubles its underlying array whenever the load factor crosses a threshold, exactly like a dynamic array doubling its capacity. Explain why the 1/(g-1) amortised-copies-per-element argument transfers directly to hash table resizing, and name the one extra thing that has to happen to every entry during a hash table resize that a plain array resize does not need.
L4.answer: The argument transfers unchanged because both structures pay for a resize by copying every live element into one new, larger contiguous block, and it is the multiplicative (not additive) growth that keeps total copies over $n$ operations at $O(n)$ rather than $O(n^{2})$ - the proof is identical, only the payload being moved differs. What a hash table resize does extra: every entry must be placed at a new slot determined by its hash modulo the new table size, so it is not just copied but relocated - a vector element keeps the same relative position after a resize, but a hashed element's slot is a function of the capacity itself and generally changes.
L4.explanation: See Hash tables: chaining versus open addressing for the full treatment. CPython's dict resize reinserts every key using its cached hash rather than recomputing it, exactly to avoid paying for hash() a second time on top of the copy - the same amortised-doubling argument, with one extra cost layered on for the relocation.

concepts.t: Hash tables: chaining versus open addressing

L0.body:
chaining        buckets[h] -> node -> node -> NULL
                load factor alpha may exceed 1; one pointer chase per probe
                delete is trivial; memory is 1 allocation per entry

open addressing buckets are the entries; probe until an empty slot
                alpha < 1 strictly; linear probing expected probes:
                   successful   (1 + 1/(1-alpha))/2
                   unsuccessful (1 + 1/(1-alpha)^2)/2
                alpha=0.75 ->  2.50 /   8.50
                alpha=0.90 ->  5.50 /  50.50
                alpha=0.95 -> 10.50 / 200.50   <- the cliff
L0.cloze: Linear probing costs about $(1 + 1/(1-\alpha)^{{2}})/2$ probes for an {{c1::unsuccessful}} lookup, which is {{c2::8.5}} at $\alpha = 0.75$ and {{c3::200.5}} at $\alpha = 0.95$. Deletion in open addressing cannot simply blank a slot; it needs a {{c4::tombstone}} or backward-shift.

concepts.L1: Two ways to resolve collisions. Chaining stores a list per bucket and tolerates load factors above 1. Open addressing stores entries in the bucket array itself and probes for a free slot, which keeps everything in cache lines but degrades sharply as the table fills.
concepts.L2: The cost of open addressing is not linear in load factor, it is quadratic in $1/(1-\alpha)$ for unsuccessful lookups - and unsuccessful lookups are the common case in a set membership test or an insert.
concepts.L3: Knuth's linear-probing analysis under uniform hashing gives successful probes $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \frac{1}{1-\alpha})$ and unsuccessful $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \frac{1}{(1-\alpha)^{2}})$: at $\alpha = 0.9$ that is 5.5 and 50.5. Chaining at the same $\alpha = 0.9$ has expected chain length $\alpha$: a successful search examines about $1+\alpha/2 \approx 1.45$ nodes, an unsuccessful one walks the whole chain, about $\alpha \approx 0.9$ nodes - a miss is cheap in chaining, the opposite of open addressing, where a miss is always the expensive case. Chaining's figures stay linear past $\alpha=1$; open addressing's unsuccessful cost is quadratic in $1/(1-\alpha)$ and undefined there. Yet open addressing usually wins up to moderate load: its probes are consecutive words in one or two cache lines, chaining's are dependent pointer chases into unrelated allocations, each paying its own allocator header.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table is at load factor $\alpha = {a}$. Give expected probes for a successful and an unsuccessful lookup, and say which of the two matters more for an insert-heavy workload. Answer with the expected probes for a successful lookup.
L4.answer: successful = (1 + 1/(1-a))/2; unsuccessful = (1 + 1/(1-a)^2)/2. a=0.5: 1.50 / 2.50. a=0.75: 2.50 / 8.50. a=0.9: 5.50 / 50.50. a=0.95: 10.50 / 200.50. Inserts are unsuccessful lookups by definition (you probe until you find a free slot), so the quadratic branch is the one that governs insert cost.
L4.explanation: This is why resize thresholds cluster at 0.5 to 0.875 and why 'just fill it up' is wrong. Note that these numbers assume uniform hashing; a weak hash makes them optimistic, and Robin Hood or quadratic probing changes the variance but not the mean.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are storing {n} entries of {sz} bytes each, with frequent deletion and lookups that mostly miss. Chaining or open addressing?
L4.answer: sz=8: open addressing, kept at alpha <= 0.75. Eight-byte entries pack 8 per cache line so a probe run is nearly free, and the resize copy is cheap. Handle deletion with backward-shift rather than tombstones so misses do not degrade. sz=256: chaining, or open addressing on a table of (hash, pointer) pairs with the payload out of line. Moving 256-byte entries on every probe-run shift and every resize dominates, and misses that mostly miss are exactly what tombstones make worse.
L4.explanation: The general rule is to keep the probed array small and dense. Swiss tables do this explicitly with a separate one-byte-per-slot control array, so a miss usually reads only control bytes and never touches an entry at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table is at load factor $\alpha = {a}$. Give the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful lookup (equivalently, an insert).
L4.explanation: This is the branch that governs insert cost, since an insert probes exactly like a failed lookup. It is why open-addressing resize thresholds sit well below 1: at alpha=0.9 an insert costs 50 probes on average.

L4.prompt_tpl: A chaining hash table stores {n} keys across {m} buckets with a well-distributed hash function. What is the expected number of entries in each bucket, i.e. the load factor $\alpha$?
L4.answer: alpha = n/m. n=4000,m=1000: 4.0. n=9000,m=6000: 1.5. n=18000,m=1000: 18.0 - all fine for chaining, since a bucket is a list with no capacity limit, unlike open addressing where alpha must stay below 1.
L4.explanation: Chaining has no ceiling on alpha: it just means longer lists per bucket. This is the structural reason chaining tolerates skewed or high-volume workloads that would deadlock open addressing.

L4.prompt_tpl: You choose to resize an open-addressing table whenever an unsuccessful lookup would cost more than {k} expected probes. Using $(1 + 1/(1-\alpha)^2)/2 = k$, what load factor $\alpha$ triggers the resize?
L4.explanation: Real resize thresholds (0.5 to 0.9 depending on implementation) are exactly a choice of tolerable k made this way, not a folklore number: pick the worst probe count you will accept and solve for alpha. This is the calculation behind the concrete thresholds used by the Robin Hood and Swiss-table schemes covered next.

L4.prompt_tpl: An open-addressing table's delete routine writes table slot {s} back to the same EMPTY marker used for a slot that was never filled, instead of a tombstone. Keys A, B, C all hashed to slot {s} and were inserted in that order via linear probing; B is then deleted this way. What happens to a later lookup for C, and why?
L4.answer: Lookup for C starts at slot s, finds A (not a match, keep probing), reaches B's old slot, and now reads EMPTY - the standard probe loop stops at the first EMPTY it sees, so it reports C as absent even though C still sits one slot further along. Marking a deleted slot the same as a never-used slot silently breaks every lookup that used to probe through it. The fix is a distinct tombstone marker (lookup keeps probing through it, insert may reuse it) or backward-shift deletion, which slides later entries in the run back so a plain EMPTY becomes safe again.
L4.explanation: This is one of the most common production open-addressing bugs, because insert-only and lookup-only test suites never exercise it - it only appears once delete and a probe-run lookup interact, exactly the scenario the L0 line about tombstones is warning about.

L4.prompt_tpl: An open-addressing table using linear probing is never resized, and inserts push the load factor to $\alpha = {a}$, at or above 1. Describe mechanically what happens on the next insert attempt, and say why chaining never hits the same wall at the same $\alpha$.
L4.answer: Every slot is occupied (or, past alpha=1, there simply are not enough slots to place a new key at all), so the probe sequence for a new key visits every slot in the table without ever finding EMPTY: an unmodified insert loop runs forever, or a bounds-checked one aborts once it has probed the full table. This is a correctness failure, not a slowdown. Chaining never reaches this wall at the same alpha because a bucket is a list with no capacity limit - at alpha=1.2 each bucket just holds slightly more than one node on average, and insert is still O(1) expected.
L4.explanation: This is the concrete reason open-addressing resize thresholds are hard-coded well under 1.0 (typically 0.5 to 0.9): crossing alpha=1 is not degraded performance, it is an insert that can no longer succeed.
