L0.body:
Lay a complete binary tree of height h in memory by RECURSION, not by level:
  split at height h/2 -> one top subtree of height h/2
                      -> 2^(h/2) bottom subtrees of height h/2
  store the top subtree contiguously, then each bottom subtree contiguously, recursively

  BFS (level) layout   : Theta(log2 n - log2 B)   transfers    n=2^30, B=64 -> 24
  vEB (recursive) layout: Theta(log_B n)          transfers    n=2^30, B=64 ->  5
  and the algorithm never mentions B. Cache-oblivious: optimal at EVERY level at once.
L0.cloze: The van Emde Boas layout splits a tree of height $h$ into a top subtree of height {{c1::h/2}} and $2^{{h/2}}$ bottom subtrees, storing each {{c2::contiguously}} and recursing. A search then costs $\Theta({{c3::\log_{{B}} n}})$ transfers without the code ever knowing {{c4::B}}.

concepts.L1: A recursive memory layout for a static search tree. Split the tree at half its height, store the top piece contiguously, then each bottom piece contiguously, recursively. Searching costs $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ block transfers for every block size $B$ simultaneously, with $B$ appearing nowhere in the code.
concepts.L2: This is not the van Emde Boas priority queue, which is a different structure with $O(\log\log u)$ operations. Named after, not authored by: the priority queue is van Emde Boas's 1970s construction; this cache-oblivious layout is a later technique (Prokop, 1999) using the same halving idea. Unrelated artefact.
concepts.L3: The analysis is a one-line trick. Consider the recursion level at which subtrees first fit in a block: those subtrees have between $\sqrt{B}$ and $B$ nodes, so their height is at least $\frac{1}{2}\log_{2} B$. A root-to-leaf path of length $\log_{2} n$ crosses at most $\log_{2} n / (\frac{1}{2}\log_{2} B) = 2\log_{B} n$ such subtrees, and each is contiguous so it costs at most two transfers. Total: $O(\log_{B} n)$, matching the B-tree bound. The point is that the argument holds for every $B$ at once, so the same array is optimal in L1, in L2, in RAM against page size, and on disk - no tuning, no re-layout per machine.

L4.prompt_tpl: A static search tree over $n = 2^{{{e}}}$ keys, block holding $B = {B}$ keys. Give block transfers for binary search on a sorted array, an Eytzinger/BFS layout, and a van Emde Boas layout.
L4.answer: Sorted array binary search and BFS layout both cost about log2(n) - log2(B); vEB costs about log2(n)/log2(B). e=30,B=8: 27 vs 27 vs 10. e=30,B=64: 24 vs 24 vs 5. e=20,B=8: 17 vs 17 vs 6.7. e=20,B=64: 14 vs 14 vs 3.3. e=40,B=8: 37 vs 37 vs 13.3. e=40,B=64: 34 vs 34 vs 6.7.
L4.explanation: The gap widens with B, which is the whole point: additive savings versus divisive savings. In practice the BFS layout still wins for arrays under a few MB because its address arithmetic is one shift and the hardware prefetcher can speculate both children; vEB wins once the array leaves last-level cache.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is a cache-oblivious layout preferable to a B-tree tuned for {b} bytes, when both achieve $\Theta(\log_B n)$?
L4.answer: Because the memory hierarchy has several levels with different block sizes, and a B-tree tuned to one of them is suboptimal at the others. A node sized to a 4096-byte page reads 64 cache lines per node visit while a binary search inside it touches about 8, wasting L1 and L2 bandwidth; a node sized to a 64-byte line has fanout 8 and pays far too many page reads on disk. The vEB layout is simultaneously optimal at every level, and it needs no re-tuning when the hardware changes.
L4.explanation: The honest counterweight: constants. A tuned B-tree usually beats the cache-oblivious structure on the level it was tuned for, so cache-obliviousness wins when the workload spans levels, when the hardware is unknown, or when nobody will ever tune it - which describes most software.

L4.prompt_tpl: A van Emde Boas layout stores n = {n} keys with block size B = {B} keys per block. The model's search cost is $\log_{B} n$, equal to $\ln n / \ln B$. Compute this number for these values, to two decimal places.
L4.explanation: This is the $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ bound as an actual number, not a restated big-O. Moving B from 64 to 4096 (64x bigger blocks) only cuts the count by half, because the cost divides by $\log_{2} B$, not by B: bigger blocks buy logarithmically diminishing returns.

L4.prompt_tpl: A complete binary tree of height h = {h} (so n = 2^h keys) is stored two ways: a BFS/level layout costs about $\log_2 n - \log_2 B$ block transfers per search, while a van Emde Boas layout costs about $\log_2 n / \log_2 B$. For block size B = {B} keys, compute the ratio of the BFS layout's transfer count to the vEB layout's transfer count (BFS divided by vEB), to two decimal places.
L4.explanation: BFS's saving from bigger blocks is additive (log2 B fewer transfers); vEB's is divisive (transfers divided by log2 B). The BFS/vEB ratio keeps growing as B grows, which is exactly why vEB pulls ahead once the tree outgrows cache: bigger blocks help vEB far more than they help BFS.

L4.prompt_tpl: A van Emde Boas layout is built for n = {n} keys with block size B = {B} keys, so n is far smaller than B. The formula gives $\log_{B} n$ transfers, a number less than 1. What is the real minimum number of block transfers a search needs here, and why does that not contradict the $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ claim?
L4.answer: At least 1, always -- once n <= B the whole tree already fits in a single contiguous block, so the recursion bottoms out at O(1) transfers regardless of what the fraction log_B(n) evaluates to (0.33 for n=10,B=1024; 0.55 for n=100,B=4096). The precise bound in the literature is $O(1+\log_{B} n)$; $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ on its own is only tight once n grows past B, and this concept states it loosely for the regime where that holds.
L4.explanation: The '+1' is not pedantry: without it the formula would predict a search costing a fraction of a transfer, which is meaningless. $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ is a statement about growth as n passes B many times over, not a formula valid at every n.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive why a root-to-leaf path in a van Emde Boas layout crosses at most $2\log_{B} n$ recursively-contiguous subtrees, each costing O(1) transfers: identify the height at which a subtree first has between $\sqrt{B}$ and B nodes, and use it to bound the number of such subtrees on a path of length $\log_2 n$. Then check your bound numerically for n = {n} keys and B = {B}.
L4.answer: A subtree first has between sqrt(B) and B nodes at the recursion level where its height first drops to at most log2(B): since height halves every recursive step, the level just before that had height > log2(B) and the level at or after has height >= (1/2)log2(B), so a subtree crossed at this level has size at least 2^((1/2)log2 B) = sqrt(B). A root-to-leaf path has length log2(n); each subtree crossed consumes at least (1/2)log2(B) of that length, so the path crosses at most log2(n) / ((1/2)log2(B)) = 2 log2(n)/log2(B) = 2 log_B(n) such subtrees, each contiguous and so at most 2 transfers. Numerically: n=1,000,000, B=8: 13.29; n=1,000,000, B=64: 6.64; n=1,000,000,000, B=8: 19.93; n=1,000,000,000, B=64: 9.97.
L4.explanation: This is the entire proof in one inequality: because it never refers to a specific B, the same layout is simultaneously near-optimal for every block size, which is the definition of cache-oblivious and the reason no per-machine tuning is needed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Fenwick trees, covered elsewhere in this domain, get O(log n) updates purely from index arithmetic on lowbit(i), with no block size anywhere in the bound. Contrast that bound's model with the van Emde Boas layout's $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ for B = {B} and n = {n}: which cost model is each one stated in, and why does making blocks bigger shrink one bound but leave the other unchanged?
L4.answer: Fenwick's O(log n) is a comparison/word-RAM operation count: it counts arithmetic and array-access steps, and B never enters the accounting because the model does not group memory into blocks. The van Emde Boas bound $\Theta(\log_{B} n)$ is an external-memory (I/O) model count: it counts block transfers, and B is a parameter of that model, not of the algorithm. Growing B (a bigger cache line or page) shrinks $\log_{B} n$ because the model literally charges less per transfer when each one carries more keys; it does nothing to lowbit(i), which never counted transfers to begin with. The two bounds are not competing answers to the same question -- they are answers to different questions.
L4.explanation: The recurring trap in this domain: a complexity claim is meaningless without naming its model. Two structures with 'the same' log n behaviour can be optimizing completely different resources, and only one of them cares how big your cache line is.

L0.cloze: $\mathrm{{ rank }}_{{1}}(i)$ counts the {{c1::ones}} before position $i$; $\mathrm{{ select }}_{{1}}(k)$ returns the position of the $k$-th one. A practical constant-time rank uses a {{c2::two-level}} index plus one {{c3::POPCNT}}, costing about {{c4::25}} percent extra space over the raw bits.

concepts.L1: Two constant-time primitives on a bit array: rank counts the set bits before a position, select finds the position of the $k$-th set bit. With $o(n)$ extra bits, both are $O(1)$, and together they are the substrate that every succinct structure is built on.
concepts.L2: Rank and select are not symmetric in difficulty. Rank answers a prefix-sum query at a known index: fixed loads plus one popcount (about 3 cycles alone), so it is latency-bound by those loads, not the popcount itself, once the index misses cache.
concepts.L3: The point of succinctness is a precise claim: store $n$ bits in $n + o(n)$ bits total while answering queries in $O(1)$, where the $o(n)$ is genuinely sublinear rather than a constant factor. Jacobson's original rank index used $O(n\log\log n/\log n)$ extra bits, which is $o(n)$ but with a bad constant. Vigna's rank9 design stores the 512-bit superblock's 64-bit absolute counter and its seven 9-bit sub-counters (63 bits, padded to 64) as two adjacent 64-bit words next to the data, so a rank query touches one or two cache lines instead of three scattered arrays, at 25 percent overhead - and the cache behaviour matters far more than 12.5 versus 25 percent.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bitvector of $n = {n}$ bits carries a two-level rank index: one 64-bit absolute counter per {sb}-bit superblock, plus its relative sub-counters packed into however many 64-bit words they need. Give the raw size, the index size, and the overhead percentage.
L4.answer: n=1e9 bits = 125 MB raw. sb=512: ceil(1e9/512)=1,953,125 superblocks; each needs a 64-bit absolute counter plus seven 9-bit sub-counters (max value 448) packed into one more 64-bit word (63 of 64 bits used) = 128 bits index; total index = 2.5e8 bits = 31.25 MB, overhead 25 percent. sb=1024: ceil(1e9/1024)=976,563 superblocks; now 15 sub-counters need 10 bits each (max value 960) = 150 bits, which needs 3 packed 64-bit words (only 78 percent full) instead of 1; each superblock costs 64+192=256 bits; total index is again about 2.5e8 bits = 31.25 MB, overhead still 25 percent. 512 is the largest power-of-two superblock whose sub-counters exactly fill one packed word (63/64 bits used); bigger superblocks need more packed words, not fewer.
L4.explanation: The absolute counter is a fixed 64 bits regardless of superblock size, but the packed sub-counters need more bits as superblocks grow, and eventually spill into extra 64-bit words. 512 is the largest superblock whose sub-counters still pack into exactly one such word, which is why it is the standard choice.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is $\mathrm{{ select }}_{{1}}$ harder to make constant-time than $\mathrm{{ rank }}_{{1}}$, given a bitvector of {n} bits?
L4.answer: Rank is a prefix sum evaluated at a known index: precompute cumulative counts at fixed positions, add a stored partial, and popcount the remainder of one word. Every step is a direct lookup. Select asks the inverse question - find the index where the cumulative count first reaches k - which is a search, and the answer's position is not determined by k in any indexable way because it depends on the data's density. Constant-time select needs a hierarchy of sampled answers with different structures for dense and sparse regions (Clark's construction); practical libraries sample every 8192nd one and binary-search within, then do a broadword select inside the word.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry is worth internalising because it recurs: prefix aggregates are cheap and their inverses are searches. It is the same reason a Fenwick tree does prefix sums trivially and 'find the smallest prefix with sum >= k' needs a descent.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bitvector holds {n} bits, indexed with Vigna's rank9 layout: one 64-bit absolute counter plus seven 9-bit relative sub-counters (packed into a second 64-bit word) per 512-bit superblock. How many index bits does this cost in total? Answer with the number of index bits.
L4.answer: n=1,000,000: ceil(1000000/512)=1954 superblocks * 128 bits = 250,112 bits (31,264 bytes). n=8,000,000,000: 15,625,000 superblocks * 128 = 2,000,000,000 bits = 250,000,000 bytes (250 MB), exactly 25 percent of the 1,000,000,000-byte raw bitvector. n=4,294,967,296 (2^32): 8,388,608 superblocks * 128 = 1,073,741,824 bits = 2^30 bits, exactly 25 percent of 2^32 raw bits.
L4.explanation: Each 512-bit superblock costs a fixed 128 index bits (64-bit absolute counter plus seven 9-bit sub-counters padded to 64 bits) regardless of n, so total index size is always 25 percent of the raw bitvector - the constant this concept's L3 states.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the rank1 code, for a query at position i the three terms are super[i >> 9] = {s}, sub[i >> 6] = {sb}, and popcount(bits[i >> 6] & mask) = {p}. What does rank1(i) return?
L4.answer: rank1(i) is just the sum of the three terms: 1000+12+3=1015; 50000+63+40=50103; 0+5+0=5.
L4.explanation: rank1 is nothing but this three-term sum: the code has already done the hard part by precomputing the index, so the query itself is one addition chain, which is why it answers in O(1) once the index is resident in cache.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bitvector has exactly {n} bits, not necessarily a multiple of 512. The implementation still allocates ceil(n / 512) superblocks of raw storage. How many raw bits of padding does the final, partial superblock waste?
L4.answer: n=1000: ceil(1000/512)=2, 2*512-1000=24 bits wasted. n=5000: ceil=10, 10*512-5000=120 bits. n=100000: ceil=196, 196*512-100000=352 bits. n=4096: ceil=8 (exact multiple), 8*512-4096=0 - no padding when n is already a multiple of 512.
L4.explanation: Padding is the standard off-by-boundary edge case for any block-structured index: it is exactly 0 when n is a multiple of the superblock size, and otherwise ranges up to 511 bits, which is why real code must special-case the last partial superblock.

L4.prompt_tpl: Generalise the packing trick from the sb=512-versus-sb=1024 case above: a superblock of {sb} bits is split into sb/64 blocks of 64 bits, giving (sb/64 - 1) stored relative sub-counters, each needing the minimum bit-width to represent values up to ((sb/64) - 1) * 64. Derive the total index bits per superblock: the 64-bit absolute counter plus however many whole 64-bit words the packed sub-counters require. What is the total index-bits-per-superblock for sb={sb}?
L4.answer: sb=256: 4 blocks, 3 sub-counters, max value 192, w=ceil(log2(193))=8 bits, 3*8=24 packed bits needs ceil(24/64)=1 word: total=64+64=128 bits. sb=512: 8 blocks, 7 sub-counters, max 448, w=9 bits, 7*9=63 packed bits needs 1 word: total=64+64=128 bits (the standard case). sb=1024: 16 blocks, 15 sub-counters, max 960, w=10 bits, 15*10=150 packed bits needs ceil(150/64)=3 words: total=64+192=256 bits - overhead does not shrink as sb grows, the same non-monotonicity found by hand above. sb=2048: 32 blocks, 31 sub-counters, max 1984, w=11 bits, 31*11=341 packed bits needs ceil(341/64)=6 words: total=64+384=448 bits.
L4.explanation: 512 is not an arbitrary choice: it is the largest power-of-two superblock whose packed sub-counters still fit in exactly one 64-bit word, so total index cost stays at 128 bits. Past 512 the word count jumps faster than the counter count shrinks, so overhead never drops below 25 percent - the same effect the sb=512-vs-1024 exercise found by direct computation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Some practical rank9-style implementations interleave each superblock's 512 data bits together with its 128 index bits into one contiguous 640-bit (80-byte) block, trading a separate index array (as in this concept's L0 pseudocode) for better cache locality. Assuming that interleaved layout, how many whole superblocks fit inside one {page}-byte memory page?
L4.answer: page=4096: floor(4096/80)=51 superblocks (51*80=4080 bytes used, 16 bytes left over), covering 51*512=26,112 raw bits per page. page=16384 (a typical huge page): floor(16384/80)=204 superblocks, covering 204*512=104,448 raw bits per page.
L4.explanation: This is the word-RAM model meeting the external-memory model: once the bitvector outgrows cache, what matters is how many superblocks - not how many bits - fit per page, since a rank query on cold data faults in whole pages, not individual bits.

L0.body:
Monotone sequence of n values from a universe of size u. Split each value's bits:
  low  l = floor(log2(u/n)) bits, verbatim into an n*l bit array
  high the rest, in UNARY into a bitvector of n + u/2^l bits (2n to 3n)

  total = n*l + n + u/2^l bits, <= n*(l+3), ~0.5 bits/elem above the information bound

  n = 1e6 postings from u = 2^32 :  l = 12, total = 12e6+1e6+2^20 = 14.05e6 bits = 1.76 MB
                       raw 32-bit:  4.00 MB          gzip of deltas: variable, no random access
  access(i) = (select1(high, i) - i) << l | low[i]     <- O(1), no decompression
L0.cloze: Elias-Fano stores the low {{c1::\lfloor\log_{{2}}(u/n)\rfloor}} bits of each value verbatim and the high bits in {{c2::unary}}, costing at most $n(3 + \lfloor\log_{{2}}(u/n)\rfloor)$ bits total (exactly $nl+n+u/2^{{l}}$). Random access is $O(1)$ via {{c3::select}} on the high-bits vector, with no {{c4::decompression}} step.

concepts.L1: A compressed sorted-integer representation supporting $O(1)$ random access. Low bits verbatim, high bits in unary, total at most $n(3+\lfloor\log_{2}(u/n)\rfloor)$ bits - within about two bits/element of the information-theoretic optimum. `nextGEQ` (successor) is $O(1+\log(u/n))$, not $O(1)$.
concepts.L2: It is not a compression scheme you decompress. `access(i)` is a select on the high-bits vector plus a shift plus a load, so you read element $i$ of a compressed list without touching elements $0$ to $i-1$. That is the property varint, delta-plus-gzip and Frame-of-Reference all lack, and it is why inverted indexes moved to it.
concepts.L3: The information-theoretic minimum for a sorted sequence of $n$ distinct values from a universe $u$ is $\log_{2}\binom{u}{n} \approx n\log_{2}(u/n) + n\log_{2} e$ bits. With $l = \lfloor\log_{2}(u/n)\rfloor$, Elias-Fano spends $nl + n + u/2^{l}$ bits. Writing $u/n = t\cdot 2^{l}$ with $t \in [1,2)$, the gap over the optimum is $1 + t - \log_{2} t - \log_{2} e$ bits per element, tight between about $0.47$ (at $t = 1/\ln 2$) and $0.56$ (at the endpoints) - well inside the folklore "2 bits" bound. Take $n = 10^{6}$ ids from $u = 2^{32}$: $l = \lfloor\log_{2}(2^{32}/10^{6})\rfloor = 12$, a high-bits vector of $10^{6}$ ones and $2^{32}/2^{12} = 2^{20}$ zeros. Total $14.05 \times 10^{6}$ bits $\approx 1.76$ MB against 4 MB raw.

L4.prompt_tpl: Encode a sorted list of $n = {n}$ values drawn from a universe $u = 2^{{{e}}}$ with Elias-Fano. Give $l$, the bits per element, the total size in MB, and the ratio against a raw fixed-width array.
L4.answer: l = floor(log2(u/n)); total bits = n*l + n + u/2^l (not simply n*(l+2), since u/2^l ranges up to just under 2n). n=1e6, e=32: u/n=4295, l=12, total=14.05e6 bits=1.76 MB, vs 4 MB raw (32-bit): 2.28x smaller. n=1e6, e=40: u/n=1.1e6, l=20, total=22.05e6 bits=2.76 MB vs 5 MB (40-bit rounded to 5 bytes): 1.81x. n=1e8, e=32: u/n=42.9, l=5, total=734.2e6 bits=91.78 MB vs 400 MB: 4.36x. n=1e8, e=40: u/n=11000, l=13, total=1534.2e6 bits=191.78 MB vs 500 MB: 2.61x.
L4.explanation: The denser the sequence relative to its universe, the better Elias-Fano does - it spends log2(u/n) bits, so a dense list costs almost nothing. That is exactly the regime of an inverted index's common terms, which is why it wins there and not on sparse random ids.

L4.prompt_tpl: A search engine stores posting lists and needs to intersect two lists of {a} and {b} postings by skipping. Elias-Fano, delta-plus-varint, or Roaring?
L4.answer: b=1 thousand: Elias-Fano or Roaring. The intersection should be driven by the short list, doing 1000 successor searches into the long one; that needs O(1) random access or skipping, which delta-plus-varint cannot provide without a separate skip list because decoding is inherently sequential. b=900 thousand: both lists are dense and similar in size, so a merge is right and Roaring's bitmap containers make the intersection a word-wise AND - far faster than either compressed-sequence scheme.
L4.explanation: The decision is driven by access pattern, not by compression ratio: sequential merge favours Roaring's bitmaps, skewed skipping favours Elias-Fano's constant-time successor. Delta-plus-varint is the smallest for pure sequential scans and the worst for everything else.

L4.prompt_tpl: A sorted list of n = {n} distinct values is drawn from a universe of size u = 2^{e}. Using l = floor(log2(u/n)), how many bits does the low-bits array (n values times l bits) use in total? Answer with the number of bits.
L4.explanation: l = floor(log2(u/n)) low bits per element, so the low-bits array alone is n*l bits - it grows with n and with how many low bits each value keeps, independent of the high-bits (unary) array computed separately.

L4.prompt_tpl: Same setup: n = {n} values from a universe u = 2^{e}, with l = floor(log2(u/n)). The high-bits bitvector has n ones and u/2^l zeros, written in unary. How many bits does it use in total? Answer with the number of bits.
L4.answer: high bits = n + u/2^l. n=500000, e=24: u/2^l=524,288, total=1,024,288 bits. n=500000, e=34: u/2^l=524,288 again (same relative position within its power-of-two bracket), total=1,024,288 bits. n=2000000, e=24: u/2^l=2,097,152, total=4,097,152 bits. n=2000000, e=34: u/2^l=2,097,152, total=4,097,152 bits.
L4.explanation: The high-bits array is never exactly 2n: it is n + u/2^l, and because 2^l <= u/n < 2^(l+1), u/2^l lands anywhere in [n, 2n), so the array is between 2n and 3n bits - closer to 2n only when u/n sits just under the next power of two.

L4.prompt_tpl: Special case: the universe is exactly u = k times n, where k = {k} is a power of two and n = {n}. Then l = log2(k) exactly. How many bits does the high-bits (unary) bitvector then use?
L4.answer: u/2^l = n exactly here (since u/n = k = 2^l exactly), so the high array has n ones and n zeros: 2n bits. n=10000: 20,000 bits. n=1,000,000: 2,000,000 bits. This exact-2n bound only holds when u/n is precisely a power of two; in general it is anywhere between 2n and 3n.
L4.explanation: This is the one case where the folklore 'high-bits array is 2n bits' is exactly true rather than an approximation - when u/n is an exact power of two there is no rounding slack left in l, so u/2^l collapses to exactly n and the array is exactly 2n bits.

L4.prompt_tpl: A posting list of {n} entries is Elias-Fano encoded. access(i) costs O(1) via one select on the high bits. Does nextGEQ(v), the successor query used to skip while intersecting posting lists, cost the same O(1) in the worst case?
L4.answer: No - nextGEQ needs a select plus a bounded search within the high-bits run it lands on, costing O(1 + log(u/n)).
L4.explanation: access(i) is O(1) because select lands exactly on the right unary run. nextGEQ first selects to the right high-bits region, then must scan or binary-search within it for the smallest value >= v, which costs O(1+log(u/n)) - not free, though independent of n once in the right neighbourhood.
options: Yes - nextGEQ is also a single select on the high bits, so it is O(1) just like access(i).
No - nextGEQ needs a select plus a bounded search within the high-bits run it lands on, costing O(1 + log(u/n)).
No - nextGEQ has no shortcut at all and requires a full O(log n) binary search over the whole encoded list.

L4.prompt_tpl: Take n = {n} values drawn from a universe u = 2^{e}, with l = floor(log2(u/n)). Writing u/n = t * 2^l for some t in [1,2), Elias-Fano's total size is n*(l+1+t) bits. Compare this to the information-theoretic optimum, n*log2(u/n) + n*log2(e) bits. What is the tight range of the gap, in bits per element, as t ranges over [1,2)? Give the two endpoint values (the specific n and u only set the scale; the gap range itself does not depend on them).
L4.answer: Total $= n(l+1+t)$ bits. Optimum $\approx n\log_{2}(u/n) + n\log_{2} e = n(l + \log_{2} t + \log_{2} e)$ bits, since $u/n = t\cdot 2^{l}$ gives $\log_{2}(u/n) = l + \log_{2} t$. Gap per element $= (l+1+t) - (l+\log_{2} t + \log_{2} e) = 1 + t - \log_{2} t - \log_{2} e$. This is smallest at $t = 1/\ln 2 \approx 1.4427$, giving about $0.471$ bits, and largest at the endpoints $t=1$ and $t\to 2$, giving $2-\log_{2} e \approx 0.557$ bits. So the true gap sits in about $[0.47, 0.56]$ bits per element - tighter than the folklore 'within 2 bits' bound, which is a safe but loose worst case.
L4.explanation: Elias-Fano's real overhead over the information-theoretic bound is not a loose 2 bits: calculus over the free parameter t (how far u/n sits above 2^l) pins the gap to a narrow 0.47-0.56 bit window, connecting this concept to Bitvectors with rank and select, whose O(1) select is what makes the whole scheme work.

L0.body:
Sequence S over alphabet of size sigma. Recursively split the alphabet in half.

  root:  one bitvector, bit i = 0 if S[i] is in the lower half of the alphabet, else 1
         left child holds the subsequence of lower-half symbols, right child the rest
  depth: log2(sigma). total bits: n * log2(sigma) + o(n log sigma)  -- same as the raw text

  access(i)        = log2(sigma) rank operations, walking down
  rank_c(i)        = log2(sigma) rank operations   <- count occurrences of c in S[0..i)
  select_c(k)      = log2(sigma) select operations, walking up
L0.cloze: A wavelet tree splits the {{c1::alphabet}} in half at each level, storing one bitvector per node, for a total depth of {{c2::\log_{{2}} \sigma}}. It answers $\mathrm{{ rank }}_{{ c }}$ and $\mathrm{{select}}_{{c}}$ in $O(\log\sigma)$ by walking {{c3::down}} and {{c4::up}}, in space equal to the sequence itself.

concepts.L1: A hierarchy of bitvectors that generalises rank and select from bits to an arbitrary alphabet. Each level splits the alphabet in half and records which half each remaining symbol fell into, giving $O(\log\sigma)$ access, rank and select in $n\log\sigma + o(n\log\sigma)$ bits - the size of the sequence itself.
concepts.L2: It replaces the sequence rather than indexing it, which is the property that matters: you store the wavelet tree instead of the text, not alongside it.
concepts.L3: Trace $\mathrm{rank}_{c}(i)$. At the root, if $c$ is in the lower alphabet half, the count of lower-half symbols before position $i$ is $i - \mathrm{rank}_{1}(i)$, so recurse into the left child at position $i - \mathrm{rank}_{1}(i)$; otherwise recurse right at $\mathrm{rank}_{1}(i)$. After $\log_{2}\sigma$ steps the alphabet has narrowed to $c$ alone and the position is the answer. Every step is one rank on a bitvector, which is $O(1)$, so the whole query is $O(\log\sigma)$ - for DNA ($\sigma = 4$) that is two steps, for byte text ($\sigma = 256$) eight.

L4.prompt_tpl: A wavelet tree over a sequence of $n = {n}$ symbols from an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$. Give the depth, the total bitvector bits before rank overhead, and the number of rank operations for one $\mathrm{{ rank }}_{{ c }}$ query.
L4.answer: depth = ceil(log2(sigma)); bits = n * log2(sigma); rank ops = depth. sig=4: depth 2, n=3e9 -> 6e9 bits = 750 MB raw, 2 rank ops. sig=256: depth 8, n=3e9 -> 2.4e10 bits = 3 GB raw, 8 rank ops. n=1e9, sig=4: 2e9 bits = 250 MB raw. n=1e9, sig=256: 8e9 bits = 1 GB raw. With Vigna's practical rank9 index (the two-level design used in 'Bitvectors with rank and select'), each level costs about 25 percent extra, not 12.5: totals become 937.5 MB, 3.75 GB, 312.5 MB and 1.25 GB respectively.
L4.explanation: The human genome at 3 gigabases over a 4-letter alphabet costs 750 MB of raw wavelet-tree bits and about 937.5 MB once a real 25 percent rank index is added per level - close to the raw 2-bit-packed sequence's size, yet it answers substring queries the raw sequence cannot. That is what 'succinct' buys: query capability at nearly no space premium.

L4.prompt_tpl: Trace $\mathrm{{ rank }}_{{ c }}(i)$ down one level of a wavelet tree, for a symbol $c$ in the {half} half of the alphabet. State the new position.
L4.answer: Lower half: c's occurrences are exactly the positions where the root bitvector is 0, so the number of them before i is i - rank1(i), and the recursion continues in the left child at position i - rank1(i) = rank0(i). Upper half: they are the 1 positions, so continue in the right child at position rank1(i). After log2(sigma) such steps the alphabet range is the single symbol c and the current position is rank_c(i).
L4.explanation: Each level costs exactly one rank on a bitvector, and the position mapping is the only bookkeeping. That is the entire algorithm - which is why the wavelet tree is usually described as 'rank and select, lifted from bits to symbols'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A wavelet tree is built over an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$, not necessarily a power of two. How many levels deep is the tree? Answer with the depth as an integer.
L4.answer: depth = ceil(log2(sigma)). sigma=5: ceil(log2(5))=ceil(2.32)=3. sigma=20: ceil(log2(20))=ceil(4.32)=5. sigma=26: ceil(log2(26))=ceil(4.70)=5. sigma=1000: ceil(log2(1000))=ceil(9.97)=10.
L4.explanation: Depth must be an integer, so any alphabet size that is not a power of two still pays for the next power of two up: sigma=5 (DNA plus an ambiguity code) costs the same 3 levels as sigma=8, and the unused leaf positions are simply never reached.

L4.prompt_tpl: A wavelet tree over $n = {n}$ symbols from an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$ stores exactly one bit per symbol at every level, before any rank or select index is added. How many raw bits does that cost in total? Answer with the number of bits.
L4.answer: raw bits = n * depth = n * ceil(log2(sigma)). n=1e9, sigma=20: depth=5, bits=5e9. n=1e9, sigma=70: depth=7, bits=7e9. n=5e7, sigma=20: depth=5, bits=2.5e8. n=5e7, sigma=70: depth=7, bits=3.5e8.
L4.explanation: Every one of the n symbols contributes exactly one bit to exactly one bitvector at each of the depth levels, so the total is n times depth whether you sum level by level or symbol by symbol - the same n*log(sigma) bound this concept's L1 states.

L4.prompt_tpl: A wavelet tree is built over an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$. What does the tree degenerate into, and why?
L4.answer: sigma=1: depth = ceil(log2(1)) = 0, so the tree has no levels and no bitvectors - every symbol already equals the one possible symbol c, so rank_c(i) = i and select_c(k) = k with no structure needed. sigma=2: depth = ceil(log2(2)) = 1, so the tree is a single node holding one bitvector over the whole sequence, which is exactly a plain bitvector with rank and select - not merely similar to one, it IS one.
L4.explanation: Both boundary alphabet sizes are useful sanity checks: sigma=1 forces depth to zero, and sigma=2 collapses the whole recursive structure to its own base case - confirming that Bitvectors with rank and select is the sigma=2 special case of a wavelet tree, not just an analogous idea.

L4.prompt_tpl: English text is normally stored as 8-bit bytes per character, but a wavelet tree only needs enough bits per level to cover the real alphabet. For an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$, what percentage of the 8-bit baseline does the wavelet tree's per-symbol bit cost (its depth) save? Answer with a percentage from 0 to 100.
L4.answer: depth = ceil(log2(sigma)) bits per symbol, versus a fixed 8. sigma=26 (lowercase letters): depth=5, saving (8-5)/8 = 37.5 percent. sigma=62 (alphanumeric): depth=6, saving 25 percent. sigma=95 (printable ASCII): depth=7, saving 12.5 percent.
L4.explanation: This is the estimate a wavelet tree actually delivers on ordinary text: not compression in the gzip sense, but paying only for the bits the real alphabet needs instead of the fixed 8-bit width every character is normally stored in.

L4.prompt_tpl: Bitvectors with rank and select lays out its practical rank index as one 64-bit cumulative counter plus 64 more bits of packed sub-counters per {sb}-bit superblock. A wavelet tree needs one such index on every level's bitvector. Derive the index's overhead as a fraction of the raw bits it indexes, then use it to find the tree's total size including that overhead for $n = {n}$ symbols from an alphabet of size $\sigma = {sig}$. Answer with the number of bits.
L4.answer: overhead fraction = (64 + 64) / sb = 128 / sb bits of index per sb bits of raw data (not a memorised '25 percent'). sb=512: overhead = 128/512 = 0.25. sb=1024: overhead = 128/1024 = 0.125 - twice the superblock, half the relative index cost, matching Bitvectors' own sb=512 vs sb=1024 comparison. total bits = n * depth * (1 + overhead), depth = ceil(log2(sigma)). sb=512: n=2e9,sig=16 -> depth=4, raw=8e9, total=1.0e10 bits (1.25 GB); n=2e9,sig=200 -> depth=8, raw=1.6e10, total=2.0e10 bits (2.5 GB); n=5e8,sig=16 -> depth=4, raw=2e9, total=2.5e9 bits (312.5 MB); n=5e8,sig=200 -> depth=8, raw=4e9, total=5.0e9 bits (625 MB). sb=1024: n=2e9,sig=16 -> total=9.0e9 bits (1.125 GB); n=2e9,sig=200 -> total=1.8e10 bits (2.25 GB); n=5e8,sig=16 -> total=2.25e9 bits (281.25 MB); n=5e8,sig=200 -> total=4.5e9 bits (562.5 MB).
L4.explanation: 25 percent is not a constant to memorise - it falls out of the layout: two 64-bit words of index per 512-bit superblock is 128/512. Doubling the superblock to 1024 bits halves that fraction to 12.5 percent at the cost of a longer in-word scan, the same space-versus-scan trade Bitvectors with rank and select makes, now paid once per wavelet-tree level instead of once.

L4.prompt_tpl: A balanced wavelet tree over $\sigma = 256$ symbols costs 8 rank operations to access any symbol, no matter how common it is. Suppose one symbol occurs {frac} of all positions. Name a wavelet tree variant that would make that common symbol cheaper to access than a rare one, and the classic coding algorithm it borrows its shape from.
L4.answer: Shape the tree by symbol frequency instead of by alphabet midpoint, using Huffman's algorithm: the most frequent symbol gets the shortest root-to-leaf path (as short as depth 1), rare symbols sit deeper. This is the Huffman-shaped wavelet tree (Grossi, Gupta and Vitter, 2003): its expected access cost is $O(H_{0}(S) + 1)$ rank operations, where $H_{0}$ is the sequence's zero-order empirical entropy, instead of the fixed $O(\log\sigma)$ a balanced split always pays; its total space is $nH_{0}(S) + o(n\log\sigma)$ bits, matching zero-order entropy compression rather than the raw $n\log\sigma$ bound this concept's L1 states for the balanced case.
L4.explanation: This is the same trade Huffman and arithmetic coding make against a fixed-width byte code, applied to a data structure instead of a byte stream: spend fewer bits, and here fewer rank operations, on what is common, more on what is rare, so average cost tracks the source's entropy rather than the raw alphabet size.

L0.body:
Split a 32-bit universe into 2^16 chunks of 2^16 values. Each chunk gets a container
chosen by its OWN cardinality:

  array container   cardinality <= 4096   sorted uint16[]      2 bytes/value
  bitmap container  cardinality >  4096   uint64[1024]         8192 bytes, flat
  run container     few long runs         (start, length)[]    4 bytes/run

  4096 * 2 bytes == 8192 bytes == 2^16 bits. The threshold is exactly the break-even.

  AND(array, bitmap)  = probe the bitmap per array element   -> O(|array|)
  AND(bitmap, bitmap) = 1024 word ANDs, SIMD, no branches
L0.cloze: Roaring partitions a 32-bit universe into $2^{{16}}$ chunks and picks a container per chunk: an {{c1::array}} of 16-bit values up to cardinality {{c2::4096}}, a {{c3::bitmap}} above that, and a {{c4::run}} container for long consecutive stretches. The 4096 threshold is exactly where $4096 \times 2$ bytes equals $2^{{16}}$ bits.

concepts.L1: A compressed bitmap that partitions the universe into $2^{16}$-value chunks and chooses a container type per chunk by density: sorted 16-bit array when sparse, uncompressed bitmap when dense, run-length pairs when clustered. Set operations dispatch on the pair of container types.
concepts.L2: It beats run-length schemes like WAH and Concise by keeping random access, not by compressing better. WAH must decode from the start to test one bit; Roaring binary-searches the chunk index, then does one word test in a bitmap container, or a bounded binary search (at most $\log_2(4096)=12$ steps) in an array container.
concepts.L3: The 4096 threshold is not tuned, it is derived: an array container stores each value in 2 bytes, so 4096 values cost 8192 bytes, and a bitmap container over $2^{16}$ values costs $2^{16}/8 = 8192$ bytes flat. Below the threshold the array is smaller; above it, the bitmap. Because the choice is per chunk, one bitmap can hold dense regions as flat words and sparse tails as small arrays, which is what real data looks like. The operation matrix then lets each pair use its best algorithm: bitmap-AND-bitmap is 1024 vectorisable word ANDs with no branches; array-AND-bitmap probes the bitmap once per array element and is $O(\text{smaller})$; array-AND-array is a galloping merge.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Roaring bitmap holds {k} values spread uniformly over the full 32-bit universe. How many chunks are occupied, what container type does each get, and what is the total size?
L4.answer: There are 65536 chunks of 65536 values each. k=1e5 uniform: about 1.53 values per chunk, so essentially all 65536 chunks are occupied with tiny arrays; total is about 1e5*2 bytes of values plus 65536 container headers and index entries, roughly 200 KB of data and a comparable amount of overhead - Roaring is poor on ultra-sparse uniform data. k=1e8: about 1526 values per chunk, still below 4096, so array containers throughout: 1e8*2 = 200 MB. A flat 2^32-bit bitmap would be 512 MB regardless.
L4.explanation: Uniform-random data is Roaring's worst case, and it is worth knowing that: the structure wins on clustered data, which is what document ids, timestamps and sorted keys actually are. At k=1e8 uniform the array containers are still smaller than a flat bitmap, but only by 2.6x.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a search index whose document ids run from 0 to about 16.7 million (2^24), intersect a rare term's posting list of {a} values with a common term's posting list of {b} values, both scattered uniformly over that id range. Which Roaring container pairing does the work, and what is the cost?
L4.answer: Both posting lists sit in the same 2^24 id range, which splits into 256 chunks (2^24 / 2^16). b=10 million: 10,000,000/256 is about 39063 values per chunk, far above the 4096 array/bitmap crossover, so essentially all 256 of b's chunks are bitmap containers; a's 1000 values average about 3.9 per chunk, so a's chunks stay arrays. The pairing is array-AND-bitmap: walk a's roughly 256 occupied chunks and, for each of a's array elements, test one bit in the matching bitmap - about 1000 bit tests total, set by a's size, not b's. b=1 thousand: both posting lists average about 3.9 values per chunk, so both are array containers, and the work is a merge over the two sorted chunk directories plus, within matching chunks, a small array merge - about 2000 element comparisons, O(a+b).
L4.explanation: The asymmetric case is the important one: intersection cost is driven by the smaller operand, not the larger, once one side is dense enough to become a bitmap container. That is what makes Roaring the right structure for search-engine posting lists, where a rare term must be intersected against a common one over the same id range.

L4.prompt_tpl: A single Roaring chunk (2^16 possible values) has cardinality {n}. Roaring always stores it in whichever of the array (2 bytes per value) or bitmap (flat 8192 bytes) representation is smaller. How many bytes does this chunk's container use?
L4.answer: Container bytes = min(2*n, 8192). n=500: 1000 bytes (array). n=4096: 8192 bytes (array and bitmap tie exactly, so the <=4096 rule keeps it an array). n=5000: 8192 bytes (bitmap, since the array would need 10000 bytes). n=60000: 8192 bytes (bitmap).
L4.explanation: This is the whole design in one formula: Roaring never pays more than min(array cost, bitmap cost) per chunk. The exact tie at n=4096 is why that specific cardinality is the documented threshold.

L4.prompt_tpl: A run container stores {r} (start, length) runs at 4 bytes per run. How many bytes does this run container use, regardless of how many individual values the runs cover in total?
L4.answer: Bytes = 4*r. r=10: 40 bytes. r=50: 200 bytes. r=200: 800 bytes. r=1000: 4000 bytes.
L4.explanation: Run container cost depends only on the number of runs, never on cardinality -- a chunk with 60000 values in 3 runs costs 12 bytes, cheaper than either an array or a bitmap container for the same chunk.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Roaring bitmap indexes values from a full 32-bit universe. A value v = {v} needs a chunk key (which of the 65536 chunks it falls in). Answer with the chunk key, computed as v divided by 65536 and rounded down.
L4.answer: chunk key = floor(v / 65536). v=70000: chunk 1. v=5: chunk 0. v=4294967295 (the largest 32-bit value): chunk 65535, the last one. v=3000000000: chunk 45776.
L4.explanation: The chunk key is just the top 16 bits of the 32-bit value; the low 16 bits (v mod 65536) are the position that container stores. This split is why Roaring never needs more than 65536 containers.

L4.prompt_tpl: A chunk has cardinality 60000 (well above the 4096 array/bitmap threshold), but its 60000 values happen to form only {c} runs of consecutive integers. A run container costs 4 bytes per run; a bitmap container for this chunk always costs 8192 bytes flat. Which container is actually smaller here, and by how many bytes?
L4.answer: Run bytes = 4*c. c=3: 12 bytes, run wins by 8180 bytes. c=100: 400 bytes, run wins by 7792 bytes. c=2048: 8192 bytes, an exact tie with the bitmap. c=5000: 20000 bytes, the bitmap now wins by 11808 bytes -- past 2048 runs, flattening to a bitmap is cheaper even though the array/bitmap cardinality rule alone would never have chosen array over bitmap here (60000 is far past 4096 either way).
L4.explanation: The 4096 cardinality threshold from L0 governs only the array-versus-bitmap choice; Roaring actually picks the minimum of three container costs, and a highly clustered dense chunk can beat both via the run container, regardless of cardinality.

L4.prompt_tpl: Real Roaring uses 2-byte array entries, so each chunk holds 2^16 positions and the array/bitmap crossover cardinality is 4096, where array bytes (n times 2) equal bitmap bytes (2^16 divided by 8). Suppose a hypothetical variant instead used {w}-byte array entries, so each chunk held 2^(8*w) positions. Derive the new crossover cardinality n-star where array bytes (w times n) equal bitmap bytes (2^(8*w) divided by 8), and give n-star for this w.
L4.answer: Setting w*n = 2^(8w)/8 gives n-star = 2^(8w)/(8w). w=1 byte: chunk holds 2^8=256 positions, bitmap=32 bytes, n-star=32. w=2 bytes (real Roaring): chunk holds 2^16=65536 positions, bitmap=8192 bytes, n-star=4096 -- the actual documented threshold falls straight out of the formula. w=4 bytes: chunk would hold the entire 2^32 address space as one chunk, bitmap=536870912 bytes, n-star=134217728.
L4.explanation: The 4096 threshold is not a tuned magic number: it is the unique fixed point of the general formula 2^(8w)/(8w) at w=2. This generalizes the same cost-equality argument the concept's own L3 uses for the real 2-byte case.

concepts.t: Graph representations: adjacency list, CSR, and locality

L0.cloze: CSR stores a graph as an {{c1::offset}} array of length $V+1$ and a {{c2::neighbour}} array of length $E$, so a vertex's adjacency list is a {{c3::contiguous}} range. A `vector<vector<int>>` costs a separate {{c4::allocation}} and header per vertex and scatters the edges across the heap.

concepts.L1: Three representations with wildly different constants. An adjacency matrix costs $V^{2}$ bits and is only right for small dense graphs. A vector-of-vectors costs a heap allocation and header per vertex.
concepts.L2: The representation, not the algorithm, is usually what decides whether a graph computation fits in memory and runs at bandwidth.
concepts.L3: Count bytes for a graph with $V = 10^{8}$ and $E = 10^{9}$, a realistic social or web graph. CSR: $4(V+1)$ bytes of offsets plus $4E$ bytes of neighbours, 400 MB plus 4 GB, and both arrays are read sequentially when iterating vertices in order. `vector<vector<int>>`: 24 bytes of header per vertex is 2.4 GB before a single edge, each inner vector is a separate allocation with up to 100 percent capacity slack, and the edge data is scattered so every vertex visit is a cache miss to an unpredictable address. The adjacency matrix at $V^{2}$ bits is $1.25$ petabytes and is not a candidate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A graph has $V = {V}$ vertices and $E = {E}$ edges. Give the memory for CSR with 32-bit indices, for a `vector<vector<int32_t>>` (24-byte header, no slack), and for a bit-packed adjacency matrix.
L4.answer: CSR = 4(V+1) + 4E. V=1e6,E=1e7: 4 MB + 40 MB = 44 MB. V=1e8,E=1e9: 400 MB + 4 GB = 4.4 GB. vector-of-vectors = 24V + 4E: 24 MB + 40 MB = 64 MB; 2.4 GB + 4 GB = 6.4 GB (and that ignores allocator overhead and capacity slack, which typically add 50-100 percent). Matrix = V^2/8 bytes: 125 GB; 1.25 PB.
L4.explanation: The header cost alone makes vector-of-vectors 45 percent larger at V=1e8, and the real figure with allocator overhead is closer to double. The matrix is disqualified at any realistic V; it is only correct for dense graphs of a few thousand vertices, where its O(1) edge test earns its keep.

L4.prompt_tpl: Building the transpose of a CSR graph with $V = {V}$ vertices takes $O(V + E)$ and no comparisons. Describe the algorithm.
L4.answer: It is a counting sort on destination vertex. Pass one: for every entry in the neighbour array, increment count[dst]. Pass two: prefix-sum the counts into the transposed offset array. Pass three: walk the original graph again, and for each edge (u,v) write u into new_neighbour[cursor[v]++]. Three linear passes, no sort, no allocation beyond the two output arrays.
L4.explanation: The transpose is needed by Kosaraju's SCC algorithm, by reverse BFS in bidirectional search, and by PageRank's pull formulation. That it costs one linear pass rather than a sort is a direct consequence of the representation, and it is the kind of thing an adjacency-list-of-lists makes needlessly awkward.

L4.prompt_tpl: CSR offsets for a graph show offset[v] = {a} and offset[v + 1] = {b}. What is the out-degree of v?
L4.answer: Out-degree = offset[v+1] - offset[v]. a=100,b=2500: 2400. a=500,b=4000: 3500. a=2000,b=9000: 7000. Always exactly 2 reads (offset[v] and offset[v+1]), independent of V or E: the degree is O(1) to compute because it never touches the neighbour array. Answer with the out-degree.
L4.explanation: This is the whole point of storing offsets rather than lengths: any vertex's degree, or its neighbour range, comes from two array reads regardless of graph size. A vector<vector<int32_t>>[v].size() gives the same fact but through a pointer chase to a separately allocated block, which is where the cache miss comes from.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CSR graph has E = {E} directed edges and 32-bit (4-byte) neighbour entries. How many bytes does the neighbour array alone occupy?
L4.answer: bytes = 4E. E=5,000: 20,000 bytes. E=2,000,000: 8,000,000 bytes. E=500,000,000: 2,000,000,000 bytes. The offset array (4(V+1) bytes) is separate and, for any graph with average degree above 1, far smaller than this array.
L4.explanation: The neighbour array is one flat run of E entries -- every directed edge contributes exactly one 4-byte slot, contiguous in memory, which is what makes a sequential scan over it cache-friendly compared to chasing separately allocated per-vertex vectors.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague builds CSR for a graph with $V = {V}$ vertices as `int32_t offset[V];` (not V + 1), fills it with a prefix sum of per-vertex degree counts so offset[v] holds the start index for vertex v, then runs `for (int v = 0; v < V; v++) for (int i = offset[v]; i < offset[v + 1]; i++) visit(neighbour[i]);`. What is wrong, and what happens for the last vertex?
L4.answer: The array is one element short: offset[V] is never allocated, so the read offset[v + 1] on the final iteration (v = V - 1) reads offset[V], which is out of bounds. This is undefined behaviour because it is a read past the end of the array -- independent of VLA vs fixed-size vs heap-allocated storage; in practice, on most implementations, it reads whatever bits happen to sit at that address (here, likely adjacent stack memory), but the standard guarantees nothing, so the last vertex's neighbour range can end at a garbage index instead of at E, either truncating or overrunning its adjacency list. The fix is offset[V + 1], with offset[V] set to E as the end sentinel.
L4.explanation: This is the concrete failure mode of the V-vs-V+1 sizing error: every vertex except the last still works, because their offset[v+1] is a real, written entry, so the bug only shows up on the boundary case and can pass small tests while corrupting production runs on the last vertex of every graph.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CSR graph has an isolated vertex v with offset[v] = {a} and offset[v + 1] also equal to {a}. How many times does the loop body run for v? If the same graph were instead built as `vector<vector<int32_t>>` and v's inner vector was default-constructed and never pushed to, how many bytes has that inner vector allocated on the heap?
L4.answer: Zero times: offset[v] == offset[v+1], so the loop condition i < offset[v+1] is false on the first check and the body never runs. Zero heap bytes: a default-constructed std::vector holds three null pointers (begin, end, end-of-storage) and allocates nothing until the first insertion, so an isolated vertex costs only the 24-byte in-place header already counted in the outer array, no separate allocation.
L4.explanation: Both representations handle the empty-adjacency case correctly and for the same underlying reason: neither one materialises anything for a range of length zero. Where they differ is the non-empty case, where CSR's range is a slice of one shared array and vector-of-vectors pays a real allocation per non-empty vertex.

L4.prompt_tpl: Ignoring the offset array's $+1$, a CSR graph with $V = {V}$ vertices, 32-bit indices and average out-degree $\bar d$ uses $32V(1 + \bar d)$ bits; a bit-packed adjacency matrix uses $V^2$ bits. Derive the average out-degree $\bar d^*$ at which the two are equal.
L4.answer: Setting 32V(1+d) = V^2 and dividing by 32V (V > 0) gives 1 + d = V/32, so d* = V/32 - 1. V=3200: d*=99. V=320,000: d*=9,999. V=32,000,000: d*=999,999. Below d*, CSR uses fewer bits than the matrix; above it, the matrix is smaller. Answer with d*.
L4.explanation: The break-even degree grows linearly with V, so for any graph large enough that the matrix's $V^{2}$ bits matter at all (V in the millions, as in L3's worked example), the average degree would have to reach hundreds of thousands before the matrix wins on memory alone -- far past any real sparse graph. This is the arithmetic behind L3's claim that the matrix is 'never a candidate' at that scale.

L0.body:
Kahn's algorithm: queue of in-degree-0 vertices; emit, decrement successors, repeat.
  if fewer than V vertices are emitted, the remaining ones are on or downstream of a cycle.
  -> topological sort IS cycle detection. Same pass, no extra work.

# Once vertices are in topological order, shortest paths are ONE linear pass:
for u in topo_order:
    for (v, w) in adj[u]:
        dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w)      # O(V + E). Negative weights fine.

# Longest path in a DAG: same loop with max. NP-hard on general graphs, linear here.
L0.cloze: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly emits a vertex of in-degree {{c1::0}}; if fewer than $V$ vertices are emitted, the rest are on or downstream of a {{c2::cycle}}. Relaxing edges in topological order gives shortest paths in $O({{c3::V+E}})$ and tolerates {{c4::negative}} weights, which Dijkstra does not.

concepts.L1: A linear ordering of a DAG's vertices in which every edge points forward. Kahn's algorithm produces it by repeatedly emitting an in-degree-zero vertex, and fails exactly when a cycle exists - so topological sorting and cycle detection are one algorithm, not two.
concepts.L2: Once you have the order, the hard graph problems collapse. Single-source shortest paths on a DAG is one linear relaxation pass, handles negative weights that break Dijkstra, and needs no priority queue. Longest path, which is NP-hard on general graphs, is the same loop with max.
concepts.L3: The correctness argument for DAG relaxation is one sentence: when the loop reaches $u$, every edge into $u$ has already been relaxed, because every predecessor precedes $u$ in topological order, so `dist[u]` is final before it is used. Dijkstra lacks this guarantee and must instead argue that the minimum unsettled distance can never decrease - an argument a negative edge destroys. This is where build systems, spreadsheet recalculation, dataflow scheduling and autograd tape replay all live: make, Bazel, the dask task graph and PyTorch's backward pass are topological orders with a linear pass over them. Kahn's algorithm also yields the critical path by relaxing with max instead of min.

L4.prompt_tpl: A build graph has {V} targets and {E} dependency edges. Give the cost of a topological sort, of computing the critical path length, and of detecting a cycle.
L4.answer: All three are O(V + E) = 450,000 operations, and they are the same pass: Kahn's algorithm emits vertices in order, relaxing with max as it goes gives the critical path, and if the emitted count is less than V the unemitted vertices are exactly those on or downstream of a cycle. There is no reason to run three passes.
L4.explanation: That the cycle report names the vertices still holding non-zero in-degree is the practically useful part: a build tool can print the actual dependency loop rather than 'cycle detected'. Recovering the specific cycle needs one DFS restricted to those vertices.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need single-source shortest paths on a graph with {n} vertices where some edge weights are negative. The graph is a DAG. Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, or DAG relaxation?
options: DAG relaxation: topological sort then one linear pass, O(V+E), correct with negative weights because every predecessor is finalised before the vertex is used.
Dijkstra with a binary heap: O((V+E) log V) and negative weights only affect the constant.
Bellman-Ford: O(VE), the only algorithm that is correct with negative weights.
L4.answer: DAG relaxation: topological sort then one linear pass, O(V+E), correct with negative weights because every predecessor is finalised before the vertex is used.
L4.explanation: Dijkstra's invariant - the minimum unsettled tentative distance is final - breaks under a negative edge, giving wrong answers, not just extra cost. Bellman-Ford is $O(VE)$; even for a sparse DAG with $E \approx V$ that is about $V^{2} = 10^{12}$ operations at $V=10^{6}$, roughly $5\times10^{5}$ times the $O(V+E)\approx 2\times10^{6}$ DAG pass.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DAG has four vertices 0,1,2,3 with edges 0 to 1 (weight {a}), 0 to 2 (weight {b}), 1 to 3 (weight 4), and 2 to 3 (weight 2). Using topological order 0,1,2,3 and relaxing with min starting from dist[0] = 0, what is dist[3] after the pass? Answer with the number.
L4.answer: dist[1] = a (only predecessor is 0), dist[2] = b, and dist[3] = min(dist[1]+4, dist[2]+2) because 1 and 2 both precede 3 and both incoming edges are relaxed before dist[3] is read. For (a,b) = (4,1): min(8,3) = 3. For (a,b) = (10,6): min(14,8) = 8.
L4.explanation: The only way to get this wrong is to relax out of order, e.g. computing dist[3] before dist[2] is final. Topological order guarantees every predecessor of 3 (here, 1 and 2) is already finalised, so a single min over its incoming edges is correct and final on the first touch.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kahn's algorithm runs on a graph with {V} vertices, of which {c} are on or downstream of a cycle and so never reach in-degree 0. How many vertices does the algorithm emit before its queue goes empty?
L4.answer: Every vertex not on or downstream of a cycle eventually reaches in-degree 0 and gets emitted; every vertex that is one of the c cycle-touched vertices never does. Emitted count = V - c. For (V,c) = (12,2): 10 emitted. For (V,c) = (50,7): 43 emitted.
L4.explanation: This is the practical payoff of Kahn's algorithm doubling as a cycle detector: the count alone tells you whether a cycle exists (emitted < V), and the specific vertices left in the in-degree array tell you which ones to report to the user.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DAG has several different valid topological orders (some vertices are unordered relative to each other). You run DAG relaxation once using order A and once using a different valid order B. Do the resulting dist[] arrays differ?
L4.answer: No: the correctness argument only needs every predecessor to precede its successors, which holds for every valid topological order, so both runs finalise the same dist[] values.
L4.explanation: Shortest-path distances are a property of the graph and weights, not of the algorithm's traversal order. The topological-order requirement is only strong enough to guarantee each dist[] value is read after it is final; any order meeting that bar gives the same, unique shortest-path values.
options: No: the correctness argument only needs every predecessor to precede its successors, which holds for every valid topological order, so both runs finalise the same dist[] values.
Yes: you must use the lexicographically smallest topological order, otherwise some distances stay at infinity.
Yes: relaxing in a different order changes which edge is examined first at a tie, so the two arrays can disagree on vertices with two equal-length shortest paths.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 5-vertex DAG has edges 0 to 1 (weight p), 0 to 2 (weight q), 1 to 3 (weight 4), 2 to 3 (weight 6), 1 to 4 (weight 9), and 3 to 4 (weight 3), for any p, q > 0. Relaxing with max in topological order from dist[0] = 0 gives dist[4] = max(p, q) + 9. Which statement correctly explains, for every positive p and q, which path into vertex 4 is critical?
L4.answer: The path 0-1-3-4 (through vertex 3, cost p+4+3 = p+7) can never be critical: it is always strictly beaten by the direct edge 0-1-4 (cost p+9) using the same prefix p, since 7 < 9. The real competition is between the direct path 0-1-4 (cost p+9) and the path 0-2-3-4 (cost q+6+3 = q+9): the direct path is critical when p is at least q, and the path through vertices 2 and 3 is critical when q exceeds p.
L4.explanation: dist[3] = max(p+4, q+6) and dist[4] = max(dist[1]+9, dist[3]+3) = max(p+9, max(p+7, q+9)). Because p+9 > p+7 for every p, the p+7 branch is dead on arrival and dist[4] collapses to max(p+9, q+9) = max(p,q)+9 - but that surviving q+9 term still routes through vertex 3, just from vertex 2 instead of vertex 1. Spotting which sub-path is structurally dominated (true for all p,q) versus which one genuinely competes is exactly what a scheduler's critical-path pass has to get right; plugging in numbers alone would not reveal that vertex 3 is only sometimes irrelevant.
options: The path 0-1-3-4 (through vertex 3, cost p+4+3 = p+7) can never be critical: it is always strictly beaten by the direct edge 0-1-4 (cost p+9) using the same prefix p, since 7 < 9. The real competition is between the direct path 0-1-4 (cost p+9) and the path 0-2-3-4 (cost q+6+3 = q+9): the direct path is critical when p is at least q, and the path through vertices 2 and 3 is critical when q exceeds p.
Vertex 3 is on every critical path, because it is the only vertex with two incoming edges and relaxing with max always favours vertices with more predecessors.

The direct edge 0-1-4 (cost p+9) is critical for every positive p and q, since 9 is the largest single edge weight in the graph and dist[4] is dominated by whichever edge has the largest individual weight.

L4.prompt_tpl: DAG relaxation is a special case of dynamic programming: the DAG is the dependency graph of subproblems, and topological order is a valid memoisation order. State what plays the role of the DP table, the transition, and the base case here, using dist[], adj[] and the source vertex. Then say why a recurrence whose subproblem-dependency graph has a cycle (unlike a DAG) cannot be evaluated this way at all.
L4.answer: DP table: dist[]. Transition: dist[v] = min over (u,v) in edges of dist[u] + w(u,v), i.e. the same relaxation as the L0 loop. Base case: dist[source] = 0, everything else starts at infinity. A cyclic dependency graph has no topological order, so there is no evaluation sequence in which every subproblem's inputs are already solved before it is - the recurrence has to be solved as a system (e.g. Bellman-Ford's repeated relaxation, or Gaussian elimination for the stationary distribution of a Markov chain) rather than computed once, in order.
L4.explanation: Naming the correspondence explicitly is what makes 'Dynamic programming, structurally' generalise: every DAG-shaped recurrence, not just shortest paths, can be evaluated with one topological pass and no recursion or memo table bookkeeping at all.

concepts.t: Strongly connected components: Tarjan's one-pass algorithm

L0.cloze: Tarjan's algorithm tracks `index` (DFS discovery time) and `low` (the smallest index reachable). A vertex is an SCC {{c1::root}} exactly when `low == index`, and the SCC is the stack segment above it. A cross edge updates `low` only if the target is still {{c2::on the stack}}. Contracting each SCC yields the {{c3::condensation}}, which is always a {{c4::DAG}}.

concepts.L1: A maximal set of vertices mutually reachable from each other. Tarjan finds all of them in a single depth-first search using a discovery index and a low-link value, in $O(V+E)$. Kosaraju needs two passes and the transpose; Tarjan needs one pass and no extra graph.
concepts.L2: The `on_stack` test is the whole correctness argument and the place implementations go wrong. A back or cross edge to a vertex already assigned to a finished SCC must not lower `low`, because that component is closed; only edges into vertices still on the stack - still candidates for the current component - may.
concepts.L3: The value of SCCs is the condensation. Contract every SCC to a single node and the resulting graph is acyclic, by construction: any cycle among components would make them mutually reachable and therefore one component. That converts an arbitrary directed graph into a DAG, at which point topological order, DAG relaxation and dynamic programming over the order all become available. Concretely: 2-SAT is solved by building the implication graph, computing SCCs, and reporting unsatisfiable exactly when some variable and its negation share a component - linear time for a problem that looks NP-hard.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directed graph has $V = {V}$, $E = {E}$. Give the cost of Tarjan's SCC algorithm and of Kosaraju's, counting edge traversals and any extra memory.
L4.answer: Tarjan: one DFS, V + E = 1.1e8 traversals, extra memory index/low/on_stack per vertex (about 9V bytes = 90 MB) plus an explicit stack. Kosaraju: build the transpose (another O(V+E) counting sort and a second 4E-byte neighbour array, 400 MB at 32-bit indices), then two DFS passes, so about 2(V+E) = 2.2e8 traversals plus the transpose build. Roughly 3x the work and 400 MB more memory.
L4.explanation: Both are O(V+E); the constants and the memory are the decision. Kosaraju is easier to explain and to get right, which is why it appears in courses; Tarjan is what ships. Note that a recursive Tarjan will overflow the stack on a 1e7-vertex graph and must be written iteratively.

L4.prompt_tpl: An implementation updates `v.low = min(v.low, w.low)` for {edge} edges as well as tree edges. What breaks?
L4.answer: Using w.low (rather than w.index) for a non-tree edge, or using it for an edge into an already-completed component, propagates a low-link value out of a closed SCC and merges distinct components. The correct rule is: tree edge -> min with w.low; edge to a vertex still on the stack -> min with w.index; edge to a vertex not on the stack -> ignore entirely. The bug produces too few, too large components and is invisible on any graph whose SCCs happen to be singletons.
L4.explanation: The failure is silent and data-dependent: acyclic test graphs pass, and the first graph with two adjacent non-trivial components is wrong. A property test - every reported component must be mutually reachable, and the condensation must be acyclic - catches it immediately.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directed graph has {V} vertices and {E} edges, stored as an adjacency list. Tarjan's algorithm makes one DFS pass over it, using an explicit stack of vertices still under consideration. Across the whole run, how many times is a vertex pushed onto that stack?
L4.answer: Exactly V, independent of E: each vertex is pushed the instant it is first discovered (when its index is assigned) and popped exactly once, when its SCC closes. For V = 50, 2000, 250000 that is 50, 2000, 250000 pushes respectively; E only changes how many neighbour checks happen while vertices sit on the stack, not how many times they are pushed.
L4.explanation: on_stack is set true on first visit and never re-pushed afterwards; the DFS assigns .index to each vertex exactly once, so total pushes equal V regardless of edge count or graph shape. Pushing a vertex twice would corrupt the on_stack invariant the whole low-link correctness argument depends on.

L4.prompt_tpl: In Tarjan's algorithm, right after vertex v's whole adjacency list has been scanned and any recursive calls on its neighbours have returned, which test correctly identifies v as the root of a just-completed SCC?
L4.answer: v.low == v.index
L4.explanation: low only drops below index when some vertex in v's subtree has a back or cross edge into a strictly earlier, still-open component. If that never happens, v's own index is the smallest index reachable from v, so v cannot be absorbed into an ancestor's component - it roots its own, and the stack unwinds down to v.
options: v.low == v.index
v.low < v.index
v.on_stack == false

L4.prompt_tpl: Tarjan's algorithm runs on a directed graph with {V} vertices and {E} edges, stored as an adjacency list with $O(1)$ array indexing (the word-RAM model that the $O(V+E)$ bound assumes). Counting only edge-list reads, not the $O(V)$ push/pop bookkeeping, how many edge slots does the single DFS examine in total?
L4.answer: Exactly E: every directed edge (u, w) sits once in u's adjacency list and the DFS reads it exactly once while scanning u's neighbours - whether it turns out to be a tree, back, or cross edge - then moves on. For E = 2500, 150000, 12000000 that is 2500, 150000, 12000000 reads.
L4.explanation: The word-RAM model is what licenses calling each adjacency-list step O(1): indexing an array and comparing two indices are single machine-word operations. Replace it with a disk-resident or pointer-chased list (an external-memory model) and each edge read costs a cache or page miss instead, so O(V+E) no longer measures wall-clock time.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 2-SAT instance has {n} boolean variables and {m} clauses, each of the form (a or b). Its implication graph has one vertex per literal ($2n$ vertices total) and, for every clause, two directed edges: not-a to b, and not-b to a. Tarjan's algorithm computes the SCCs of this implication graph in one DFS to decide satisfiability. How many directed edges does the implication graph have in total?
L4.answer: 2m: each of the m clauses contributes exactly two implication edges, independent of n (n only fixes the vertex count 2n). For m = 6, 20, 900 that is 12, 40, 1800 edges.
L4.explanation: This reduction is why 2-SAT, unlike 3-SAT, is solvable in linear time: build the O(n+m)-size implication graph, run Tarjan's algorithm once, and the instance is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable x and its negation not-x land in the same SCC, because that means x implies not-x and not-x implies x, so no truth value for x is consistent.

L4.prompt_tpl: The L0 trace recurses via `dfs(w)` inside the neighbour loop, so one DFS-tree edge followed costs one call-stack frame that stays live until that whole subtree finishes. For a directed graph that is a single path v1 -> v2 -> ... -> v{V} (V = {V}), derive the maximum depth the call stack reaches, then explain why this makes recursive Tarjan unsafe on a graph with V around 1e7 on a typical machine, and describe the rewrite (an explicit heap-allocated stack of (vertex, resume-position) pairs, replacing each recursive call with a push and each return with a pop) that removes the problem without changing which edges the algorithm classifies as tree, back, or cross.
L4.answer: On the path graph, dfs(v1) calls dfs(v2) before it can finish, which calls dfs(v3), and so on: no call returns until the deepest vertex vV is reached, so the recursion depth equals V - here 1000, 200000, or 10000000 frames deep. Each frame holds v's local state (index, low, the adjacency-list iterator position) and is typically tens to a few hundred bytes, while a thread's call stack is usually a few MB by default (for example 8 MB on a typical Linux main thread) - so a few tens of thousands of live frames is already enough to exhaust it, and V = 1e7 overflows it many times over, crashing the process (a segfault, or a RecursionError once Python's own recursion-depth guard trips first). Rewriting the DFS to keep its own stack of (vertex, resume-position) pairs on the heap moves that same per-vertex state off the call stack: 'entering dfs(w)' becomes 'push w', and 'returning from dfs(w)' becomes 'pop w and continue its caller's loop from where it left off'. The heap has no fixed few-MB ceiling, so V = 1e7 frames of state fit fine, and because the explicit stack processes vertices in exactly the order the recursive version would have called and returned from them, every edge is still classified tree, back, or cross identically - only where the pending-vertex state lives has changed, not the algorithm.
L4.explanation: This is the gap between the O(V+E) bound and a working implementation: the bound says nothing about call-stack depth, and a graph shaped like a long path (or a long chain of forward edges) drives recursion depth to V, not to the tree height of a balanced structure. Production Tarjan implementations are iterative for exactly this reason - the existing Kosaraju-vs-Tarjan compute template's explanation flags the same V = 1e7 failure case.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that contracting every SCC of a directed graph to a single vertex produces a graph with no directed cycles. Structure it as a proof by contradiction, and say precisely what a cycle among contracted components would force about the original graph.
L4.answer: Suppose the condensation had a cycle through distinct components C1 -> C2 -> ... -> Ck -> C1. Each arrow Ci -> Ci+1 means some vertex of Ci has an edge into some vertex of Ci+1, so every vertex of Ci+1 is reachable from every vertex of Ci; following the cycle around, every Ci is reachable from every Cj among these components. Then any two vertices drawn from different Ci's are mutually reachable, so by definition they lie in the same SCC - contradicting the assumption that C1, ..., Ck were distinct maximal SCCs. So no such cycle exists: the condensation is a DAG.
L4.explanation: This is the fact Tarjan's algorithm sets up for everything downstream: once SCCs are contracted, topological order, DAG relaxation and DP over that order all apply safely, because acyclicity is guaranteed by construction rather than assumed. It is also why the 2-SAT implication graph, once contracted, can be topologically ordered to read off a satisfying assignment directly.

prereqs: Topological order and DAG relaxation
Graph representations: adjacency list, CSR, and locality
