concepts.t: Minimum spanning trees: the cut and cycle properties

L0.body:
CUT property: for any partition of V into (S, V-S), the lightest edge crossing
the cut is in SOME MST. (with distinct weights, in EVERY MST)
CYCLE property: for any cycle, the strictly heaviest edge is in NO MST (tied -> may be in one)

Kruskal: sort edges, add if it joins two components (union-find)  O(E log E)
  = CUT property on accepted edges, CYCLE property on rejected ones
Prim: grow one tree, take the lightest edge leaving it  O(E log V) with a heap
  = repeatedly applying the CUT property
Boruvka: each component picks its lightest outgoing edge, contract. PARALLEL
L0.cloze: The {{c1::cut}} property says the lightest edge across any partition belongs to some MST; the {{c2::cycle}} property says the strictly heaviest edge on any cycle belongs to none (a tie for heaviest can survive). Kruskal accepts each edge by the {{c3::cut}} property and rejects the rest by the cycle property; Prim applies the cut property with the cut fixed at the growing tree, and {{c4::Boruvka}} applies it to every component at once, which is what makes it parallel.

concepts.L1: Two exchange arguments generate every MST algorithm. The cut property: for any partition of the vertices, the lightest crossing edge is in some MST. The cycle property: on any cycle, the heaviest edge is in none. Kruskal, Prim and Boruvka are three schedules for applying them.
concepts.L2: Learning three algorithms is the wrong decomposition; there are two theorems and three orders in which to apply them. The practical consequence is Boruvka: every component chooses its lightest outgoing edge independently, so a round is embarrassingly parallel, which is why distributed and GPU implementations are Boruvka-based.
concepts.L3: The cut property's proof is a two-line exchange. Suppose $e$ is the lightest edge crossing cut $(S, V \setminus S)$ and some MST $T$ omits it. Adding $e$ to $T$ creates exactly one cycle, which must cross the cut an even number of times, so it contains another crossing edge $f$ with $w(f) \geq w(e)$. Swap them: $T - f + e$ is still spanning, still a tree, and no heavier. Hence some MST contains $e$. The cycle property is the mirror image. Every algorithm is now a corollary. Kruskal considers edges in increasing weight and rejects one exactly when it closes a cycle in which it is heaviest - and its cost is dominated by the $O(E\log E)$ sort, not by the $O(E\alpha(V))$ union-find.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kruskal on $V = {V}$, $E = {E}$: give the cost of the sort and of the union-find work, and say which dominates. Then give Boruvka's round count.
L4.answer: Sort: E log2 E = 1e7 * 23.25 = 2.3e8 comparison units. Union-find: E * alpha(V) with alpha <= 4, about 4e7 unit operations. The sort dominates by roughly 6x. Boruvka: at most log2(V) = 20 rounds, each O(E), so about 2e8 edge visits - comparable to the sort but fully parallelisable across components within a round.
L4.explanation: Because the sort dominates, the real Kruskal optimisation is to avoid sorting all E edges: use a heap and stop once V-1 edges are accepted, or radix sort integer weights. Boruvka's appeal is not its sequential cost but that each round is a parallel reduction.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove the cycle property: on any cycle $C$, an edge $f$ of strictly maximum weight is in no MST. Assume weights are {w}.
L4.answer: Suppose some MST T contains f. Removing f splits T into two components, S and V-S, and f crosses that cut. The cycle C also crosses the cut, and since a cycle crosses any cut an even number of times, C contains another crossing edge g != f. By assumption w(g) < w(f). Then T - f + g is spanning, connected and strictly lighter, contradicting minimality. Hence no MST contains f.
L4.explanation: This is the same exchange argument as the cut property, run in the other direction, and it is exactly what Kruskal's rejection test implements: an edge that closes a cycle among already-accepted (lighter) edges is the heaviest on that cycle, so it is safely discarded.

L4.prompt_tpl: A graph has $n = {n}$ vertices. Kruskal's algorithm scans edges in increasing weight order and accepts an edge whenever it joins two different components. Which property directly justifies that an accepted edge belongs to some MST?
L4.answer: The cut property: it is the lightest edge crossing the cut between the two components it joins.
L4.explanation: Kruskal's accept step is the cut property (CLRS Cor. 23.2): the edge is a light edge for the cut separating its two current components, so it is safe. The cycle property explains Kruskal's rejections instead -- a rejected edge is exactly the heaviest edge on the cycle it would close.
options: The cut property: it is the lightest edge crossing the cut between the two components it joins.
The cycle property: it is the heaviest edge on some cycle in the graph.
None: Kruskal's correctness needs a fresh global argument for each graph, with no single reusable property.

L4.prompt_tpl: To run Kruskal's sort step on $E = {E}$ edges, a comparison sort costs about E log2(E) comparisons. Compute that count for this E, and answer with the number of comparisons.
L4.answer: E log2(E): E=1000 gives about 9,966 comparisons; E=100,000 gives about 1,660,964; E=5,000,000 gives about 111,267,483.
L4.explanation: This is the idealized comparison count for sorting E items, the same bound used in the concept's L3 to argue the sort dominates Kruskal's union-find work, which costs only about E times the (near-constant) inverse-Ackermann factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: Boruvka's algorithm on a graph with $V = {V}$ vertices needs at most ceil(log2(V)) rounds, since each round at least halves the number of surviving components. Compute that maximum round count for this V.
L4.answer: ceil(log2(V)): V=16 gives 4 rounds; V=1000 gives 10 rounds; V=1,000,000 gives 20 rounds.
L4.explanation: Each round contracts every surviving component with at least one other, so the component count is multiplied by at most one half; starting from V components, ceil(log2(V)) halvings reach a single component.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 3-cycle (triangle) has all three edge weights equal to {w}. The cycle property is often stated loosely as 'the heaviest edge on a cycle is in no MST.' Does that unqualified statement correctly predict what happens to this triangle's edges? Explain what the property actually requires.
L4.answer: No, the unqualified statement fails here. The cycle property needs the heaviest edge to be strictly heaviest (unique on the cycle). With all three weights tied, dropping any single edge leaves a 2-edge spanning tree of the same total weight, so all three possible spanning trees are MSTs and every edge of the triangle is in some MST -- none is excluded. The correct statement: a strictly-heaviest edge on a cycle is in no MST; a tied-heaviest edge carries no such guarantee.
L4.explanation: The exchange proof breaks under ties: swapping the 'heaviest' edge for another cycle edge of the same weight does not strictly decrease total weight, so the contradiction that excludes it never arises. This is the same distinct-weights caveat the cut property already carries in this concept's L0.

L4.prompt_tpl: Boruvka's algorithm runs at most ceil(log2(V)) rounds, and each round costs O(E) (every surviving edge is inspected once to find its component's lightest outgoing edge). Derive the total O(E log V) work bound from these two facts, and explain why this round structure is what makes Boruvka, rather than Kruskal or Prim, the natural base for {context}.

context: a GPU implementation that must expose fine-grained parallel work
a distributed protocol like Gallager-Humblet-Spira, where components are on different machines

L4.answer: Total work = sum over rounds of O(E) = O(E) times the number of rounds = O(E) times O(log V) = O(E log V), since the number of components starts at V and is at most halved each round, so at most ceil(log2(V)) rounds remain before one component is left. Kruskal is inherently sequential in its union-find merges (each processed one edge at a time in sorted order) and Prim in its heap extractions (one vertex at a time); a Boruvka round instead lets every surviving component search for its lightest outgoing edge independently of the others, so the O(E) work within a round has no cross-component data dependency and can be split across processors or machines with only an end-of-round synchronization.
L4.explanation: The bound is a geometric series in the number of components, not in E, which is why it stays O(E log V) even though later rounds touch far fewer live edges than E; the same log V also bounds Prim's heap depth, but Boruvka earns it through parallel rounds instead of a sequential priority queue.

concepts.t: Graph algorithms in the forms actually needed

L0.body:
BFS            unweighted shortest path, O(V+E)      | 0-1 BFS: deque, O(V+E)
Dijkstra       non-negative weights, O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap
Bellman-Ford   negative weights, O(VE); detects a negative cycle on pass V
DAG relaxation topological order, O(V+E), negatives fine
Floyd-Warshall all pairs, O(V^3), 3 nested loops, k OUTERMOST
A*             Dijkstra + h(v); admissible h (never overestimates) -> optimal
               consistent h (h(u) <= w(u,v) + h(v)) -> no reopening
Tarjan         SCCs, articulation points, bridges - all one DFS with low-links
L0.cloze: In Floyd-Warshall the {{c1::k}} loop must be outermost. A heuristic that never overestimates is {{c2::admissible}} and makes A* optimal; a stronger heuristic satisfying $h(u) \leq w(u,v) + h(v)$ is {{c3::consistent}} and additionally prevents {{c4::reopening}} closed nodes.

concepts.L1: BFS/DFS, topological sort and cycle detection, Dijkstra with a binary heap, Bellman-Ford for negative edges, Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs, A* with an admissible heuristic, Tarjan for SCCs and articulation points.
concepts.L2: Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap is asymptotically better and slower in practice — a good concrete example of constants dominating. Also, Dijkstra fails on negative edges, and the reason (the greedy invariant breaks) is worth being able to state.
concepts.L3: Dijkstra's greedy invariant is the thing to be able to state: when a vertex is removed from the priority queue, its tentative distance is final, because every remaining path to it must leave the settled set through some frontier vertex whose tentative distance is already at least as large, and all remaining edges are non-negative. A single negative edge destroys the argument - a later, longer-looking path can become shorter - which is why Dijkstra is not merely inefficient on negative weights but wrong.

L4.prompt_tpl: Floyd-Warshall is written with the loops ordered `for i: for j: for k:` on a graph with {V} vertices. Some pairs come out with distances that are too large. Why?
L4.answer: The invariant requires that after the k-th outer iteration, dist[i][j] is the shortest path using only intermediate vertices from {1..k}. With k innermost, dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] may not yet have been relaxed through earlier intermediates when they are read, so paths that need two or more intermediates in a particular order are missed. The result is an upper bound that is sometimes correct - which is why small test graphs pass.
L4.explanation: This is the classic Floyd-Warshall bug and it is a statement about the dynamic programming order, not about loops. The DP is over the set of allowed intermediates; k indexes the DP layer, so it must be the outer dimension. i and j may be swapped freely.

L4.prompt_tpl: A road-network router over {V} nodes must answer point-to-point queries in milliseconds. Dijkstra, bidirectional Dijkstra, or A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic?
L4.answer: All three, layered - and none alone is fast enough at 2e7 nodes. Plain Dijkstra settles a disc around the source and touches millions of nodes. Bidirectional Dijkstra searches two smaller discs and cuts the settled count by roughly the square root of the area, typically 2-5x. A* with straight-line distance is admissible (it never overestimates a road distance) and consistent, so it needs no reopening, and it elongates the search toward the target for another few times. Production routers go further with contraction hierarchies or hub labelling, which precompute shortcuts and answer queries in microseconds.
L4.explanation: Naming admissibility versus consistency is the discriminating detail: admissible guarantees optimality but may require reopening closed nodes; consistent (triangle inequality on h) guarantees each node is settled once, which is what makes A* as cheap per node as Dijkstra.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directed graph has {V} vertices and {E} edges, possibly with negative weights but no negative cycle reachable from the source. Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge once per pass and runs a {V}-th pass purely to confirm no negative cycle exists. In the worst case, how many total edge relaxations does it perform across all passes? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: Total relaxations = V * E: each of the V passes (V-1 to guarantee correctness once no negative cycle exists, plus one more to detect one if it does) scans every edge once. V=5, E=8: 5*8=40. V=50, E=120: 50*120=6000. V=1000, E=3000: 1000*3000=3,000,000. This is the O(VE) bound written out exactly, not just asymptotically.
L4.explanation: Each of the V passes scans all E edges once, so total work is exactly V*E. The V-th pass is not extra safety margin: if any edge still relaxes on it, a negative cycle is reachable from the source and Bellman-Ford reports failure instead of distances.

L4.prompt_tpl: Floyd-Warshall runs three nested loops, each ranging independently over all {V} vertices, with k outermost. How many total (i, j, k) index combinations does the innermost loop body execute? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: The body runs once per (i, j, k) triple and each index ranges independently over all V vertices, so the count is V^3. V=4: 4^3=64. V=10: 10^3=1000. V=200: 200^3=8,000,000. This is the source of the O(V^3) time bound; the DP order rule (k outermost) fixes correctness, not this count.
L4.explanation: V^3 falls straight out of three independent loops of length V. Getting the k-outermost order right (tested elsewhere on this concept) is what makes the V^3 iterations compute the correct answer, not what reduces their number.

L4.prompt_tpl: Dijkstra on a graph with {V} vertices and {E} edges uses a binary heap: one extract-min per vertex and one decrease-key (or insert) per edge, each costing about log2({V}) comparisons. Estimate the total number of heap-comparison operations. Answer with that estimate.
L4.answer: Total heap-comparison work is about (V+E) * log2(V): V+E total heap operations (V extract-mins plus E decrease-keys), each paying about log2(V) comparisons in a binary heap. V=16, E=30: 46*log2(16)=46*4=184. V=1024, E=5000: 6024*10=60,240. V=1,000,000, E=3,000,000: 4,000,000*log2(1,000,000) is approximately 79,726,274. This is just the arithmetic behind the stated O((V+E) log V) bound.
L4.explanation: This multiplies out the O((V+E) log V) bound literally: V extract-mins plus E decrease-keys, each about log2(V) comparisons in a binary heap. It is an estimate (a real heap's constant factors vary), which is why the tolerance is loose.

L4.prompt_tpl: A* is run on a weighted graph with {V} vertices using a heuristic that overestimates the true remaining distance to the goal by as much as {slack} for some nodes, while remaining admissible and consistent everywhere else. The search settles a node and returns a path {slack} longer than optimal. Which property did the heuristic lose, and why does that specific failure follow from overestimation rather than underestimation?
L4.answer: The heuristic lost admissibility: $h(v)$ exceeds the true remaining distance for some $v$. A* settles nodes greedily by $f = g + h$; if $h$ overestimates near the goal, a node on the true shortest path can show a higher $f$ than a node on a longer path whose $h$ happens to be accurate, so the longer path gets expanded and settled first and is never reconsidered. Underestimation alone (losing only consistency while keeping admissibility, i.e. $h(u) > w(u,v) + h(v)$ for some edge) cannot cause this: it can force reopening of already-closed nodes, which costs extra work, but $g + h$ still never exceeds the true optimal cost along the real shortest path, so A* still eventually returns it.
L4.explanation: Admissible ($h$ never overestimates) is what guarantees optimality; consistent is the stronger triangle-inequality condition that additionally guarantees each node is settled exactly once. Losing admissibility breaks correctness outright; losing only consistency costs efficiency (reopening), not correctness.

L4.prompt_tpl: Define dist_k[i][j] as the length of the shortest path from i to j using only intermediate vertices numbered 1 through k, on a graph with {V} vertices. Write the recurrence for dist_k[i][j] in terms of dist_(k-1) terms, and explain why Floyd-Warshall is safe to overwrite a single 2D array in place across all k rather than keeping V separate layers.
L4.answer: $\text{dist}_{k}[i][j] = \min(\text{dist}_{k-1}[i][j],\ \text{dist}_{k-1}[i][k] + \text{dist}_{k-1}[k][j])$: either the best path avoiding vertex k, or a path that passes through k exactly once (passing through it twice cannot help when there is no negative cycle). In-place overwriting is safe because during iteration k the only cells read to update dist[i][j] are dist[i][k] and dist[k][j], and neither changes during iteration k: applying the recurrence to dist[i][k] itself gives $\min(\text{dist}[i][k], \text{dist}[i][k] + \text{dist}[k][k])$, which collapses back to dist[i][k] because dist[k][k] is at least 0 with no negative cycles. So row k and column k are fixed points of this iteration's update, and one shared array reproduces the two-array recurrence exactly. This is dynamic programming over the set of allowed intermediates, the same layered-state shape as 'Dynamic programming, structurally'.
L4.explanation: The recurrence is the whole correctness proof; the in-place argument is the practical reason the textbook O(V^3) time bound needs only O(V^2) space. Forward connection: this is the same define-state / write-the-transition / argue-safety pattern as general DP.

concepts.t: Bipartite matching and the augmenting-path bound

L0.body:
Berge's theorem: a matching M is maximum  <=>  no augmenting path exists.
  augmenting path = starts and ends at UNMATCHED vertices, alternates unmatched/matched
  flip it (XOR with M) and |M| increases by exactly 1

  naive: find one augmenting path per augmentation      O(V*E)
  Hopcroft-Karp: find a MAXIMAL SET of shortest vertex-disjoint augmenting paths per phase
                 shortest-path length strictly increases each phase
                 at most 2*sqrt(V) phases, each O(E)   ->  O(E*sqrt(V))
  V=1e4, E=1e5:  naive 1e9   vs   Hopcroft-Karp 1e7
L0.cloze: Berge's theorem: a matching is maximum exactly when no {{c1::augmenting}} path exists. Hopcroft-Karp augments along a maximal set of {{c2::vertex-disjoint shortest}} paths per phase, and because the shortest augmenting-path length strictly {{c3::increases}} each phase, at most ${{c4::2\sqrt{{V}}}}$ phases are needed, giving $O(E\sqrt{{V}})$.

concepts.L1: Matching pairs up vertices with no shared endpoints. Berge's theorem reduces maximality to the absence of augmenting paths, so every algorithm is a search strategy for them. Hopcroft-Karp batches shortest augmenting paths into phases and runs in $O(E\sqrt{V})$.
concepts.L2: The $\sqrt{V}$ is not a heuristic bound, it is a counting argument: after $\sqrt{V}$ phases the shortest augmenting path has length at least $\sqrt{V}$, and vertex-disjoint paths of that length can number at most $V/\sqrt{V} = \sqrt{V}$, so at most $\sqrt{V}$ augmentations remain. Two bounds of $\sqrt{V}$ meeting in the middle.
concepts.L3: Bipartite matching is where a large class of assignment problems lands after a change of variable, and recognising the reduction is the skill. Scheduling jobs to machines with eligibility constraints, assigning shards to nodes, and register allocation on an interval graph are all matchings. Hall's theorem: a matching saturating side $L$ exists exactly when every subset $S \subseteq L$ has $|N(S)| \geq |S|$; this saturating matching is a perfect matching only when $|L| = |R|$ too, since then saturating one side saturates the other. Failure names the bottleneck set $S$ directly. Dinic's algorithm on a unit-capacity bipartite graph reduces exactly to Hopcroft-Karp: the same algorithm under two names.

L4.prompt_tpl: Maximum bipartite matching on a graph with $V = {V}$ vertices and $E = {E}$ edges. Compare the naive augmenting-path algorithm with Hopcroft-Karp.
L4.answer: Naive: O(V*E). V=1e4,E=1e5 -> 1e9. V=1e6,E=1e7 -> 1e13. Hopcroft-Karp: O(E*sqrt(V)). V=1e4,E=1e5 -> 1e5*100 = 1e7. V=1e6,E=1e7 -> 1e7*1000 = 1e10. The speedup is sqrt(V): 100x at V=1e4, 1000x at V=1e6.
L4.explanation: At V=1e6 the naive algorithm is 1e13 operations - hours - and Hopcroft-Karp is 1e10, seconds to a minute. The gap is exactly sqrt(V), and it comes entirely from batching augmentations into phases rather than from any change to how a single path is found.

L4.prompt_tpl: A scheduler must assign {j} jobs to machines, each job eligible for a subset of machines, each machine taking one job. Show this is bipartite matching, and say what Hall's condition tells you when no full assignment exists.
L4.answer: Jobs on the left, machines on the right, an edge for each eligibility. A full assignment is a matching saturating the job side. Hall's condition says one exists iff every subset S of jobs has |N(S)| >= |S| - at least as many eligible machines as jobs in the subset. When it fails, the violating set S is a certificate: those |S| jobs collectively can only run on |N(S)| < |S| machines, which names the exact bottleneck to report or to fix by adding eligibility.
L4.explanation: The certificate is the operationally valuable part. 'No feasible schedule' is useless to an operator; 'these 12 jobs can only run on these 9 GPUs' is actionable. Hopcroft-Karp produces the violating set as a by-product of its final failed BFS layer.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bipartite graph has V = {V} vertices in total. Hopcroft-Karp runs in O(E times sqrt(V)) and the naive one-augmenting-path-per-iteration algorithm runs in O(V times E). Since both bounds scale the same way in E, by what integer factor is Hopcroft-Karp faster, independent of E?
L4.answer: The E factor cancels: (V*E)/(E*sqrt(V)) = V/sqrt(V) = sqrt(V). V=2500 -> 50x. V=40000 -> 200x. V=1000000 -> 1000x.
L4.explanation: Both bounds are linear in E, so it cancels out of the ratio and the speedup depends only on V. That is not a coincidence: sqrt(V) is exactly the same quantity that bounds the number of phases in Hopcroft-Karp's own phase analysis.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bipartite graph has {nL} vertices on the left and {nR} vertices on the right. What is the largest possible size of any matching, i.e. the maximum number of augmentations the naive one-path-per-iteration algorithm could ever need to perform on this graph?
L4.answer: A matching can use each vertex at most once, so its size is bounded by the smaller side. nL=1200,nR=900 -> 900. nL=1200,nR=50000 -> 1200. nL=50000,nR=900 -> 900. nL=50000,nR=50000 -> 50000.
L4.explanation: Every augmentation grows the matching by exactly one edge, and a matching can never use more than min(|L|,|R|) edges since each vertex is matched at most once. So this number is also the worst-case count of augmentations the naive algorithm performs before it must stop.

L4.prompt_tpl: Hopcroft-Karp needs at most 2 times sqrt(V) phases on a bipartite graph with V = {V} total vertices. What is the largest whole number of phases this bound permits?
L4.answer: V=10000 -> sqrt(V)=100, 2*100=200 phases. V=90000 -> sqrt(V)=300, 2*300=600 phases. V=123456 -> sqrt(V) is about 351.36, 2*sqrt(V) is about 702.73, rounded up to 703 phases.
L4.explanation: The bound 2*sqrt(V) is not always an integer, so the algorithm needs the ceiling of it as an actual phase count. V=123456 is not a perfect square, which is why its bound rounds up from 702.7 phases to 703: a fractional phase does not exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run the standard bipartite augmenting-path search (as in Kuhn's algorithm or Hopcroft-Karp) on a general, non-bipartite graph instead. What actually goes wrong?
L4.answer: Berge's theorem still holds, but odd-length cycles (blossoms) can trap a plain BFS/DFS search, so finding augmenting paths needs blossom contraction, as in Edmonds' algorithm.
L4.explanation: Berge's theorem (a matching is maximum iff no augmenting path exists) holds for every graph, bipartite or not. What breaks is only the search: in a general graph an odd cycle can make a plain walk miss a real augmenting path, which is why Edmonds' blossom algorithm contracts odd cycles before searching.
options: Nothing changes: Berge's theorem holds for all graphs, so the same simple BFS/DFS search for augmenting paths still finds a maximum matching.
Berge's theorem still holds, but odd-length cycles (blossoms) can trap a plain BFS/DFS search, so finding augmenting paths needs blossom contraction, as in Edmonds' algorithm.
Augmenting paths no longer exist once the graph is not bipartite, so no algorithm can enlarge a non-maximum matching.

L4.prompt_tpl: You reduce a bipartite matching instance to a flow network: a source s with a capacity-1 edge to every left vertex, a sink t with a capacity-1 edge from every right vertex, and the original bipartite edges at capacity 1. All capacities are integers. Explain, without just asserting the two numbers are equal, why the value of the maximum s-to-t flow in this network must equal the size of the maximum matching in the original bipartite graph. Your explanation should use the integrality of max flow and how a unit-capacity flow decomposes into paths.
L4.answer: Because every capacity is an integer (all are 1), the max-flow max-integrality theorem guarantees an integral maximum flow exists. An integral flow of value F on this network decomposes into F edge-disjoint unit paths of the form s -> left -> right -> t (no other shape is possible, since every left vertex has in-degree 1 from s and every right vertex has out-degree 1 to t, so flow cannot split or merge at either side). Each such path's middle edge is a distinct bipartite edge using a distinct left vertex and a distinct right vertex, so the F paths correspond exactly to a matching of size F. Conversely any matching of size k gives k such disjoint paths, i.e. a flow of value k, so the maximum flow value and the maximum matching size cannot differ in either direction: they are equal.
L4.explanation: The equality is not a coincidence to memorise but forced by two directions: (1) any integral flow of value F decomposes into F disjoint s-left-right-t paths because degree-1 bottlenecks at s and t rule out any other path shape, and each path is one matched edge, so max flow <= max matching is impossible to violate; (2) any matching of size k is itself k disjoint paths, i.e. a flow of value k, so max matching <= max flow. Together they pin the two values to be identical.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague argues: 'Hopcroft-Karp finds a maximal set of vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths every phase, and a graph with V = {V} vertices can have at most {V} pairwise vertex-disjoint augmenting paths, so the algorithm could need up to {V} phases - no better than the naive algorithm.' Find the bug in this reasoning.
L4.answer: The bug is the disjoint-path count: paths get longer every phase, and a set of vertex-disjoint paths each of length at least L can use at most V/L vertices total, so it has at most V/L paths, not V. Once the shortest path length reaches sqrt(V) (after at most sqrt(V) phases), only V/sqrt(V) = sqrt(V) disjoint paths remain, and each later phase does at least one augmentation, so at most sqrt(V) more phases finish the matching. Total: O(sqrt(V)), not O(V).
L4.explanation: The colleague ignores path length. 'At most V disjoint paths' only holds for length-1 paths; Hopcroft-Karp's argument is that the shortest augmenting path strictly lengthens every phase, shrinking the disjoint-path budget from V toward sqrt(V), and it is that shrinking budget that produces the O(sqrt(V)) phase bound.

L0.body:
max-flow min-cut: max flow value == min cut capacity. Always. (LP duality)

Ford-Fulkerson  augment along any path in the residual graph   O(E * maxflow)
Edmonds-Karp    augment along the SHORTEST path (BFS)          O(V * E^2)
Dinic           BFS level graph, then blocking flow by DFS     O(V^2 * E)
                unit capacities: O(E * sqrt(E)); bipartite: O(E * sqrt(V))

residual edge: forward capacity c-f, and a BACK edge of capacity f (this is what lets
               the algorithm undo an earlier bad routing decision)
L0.cloze:
Max flow equals min cut, always. Sending $f$ units along $u \to v$ creates a
{{c1::residual back edge}} $v \to u$ of capacity $f$, which is what lets a later path
{{c2::undo}} an earlier routing choice. Edmonds-Karp augments along the
{{c3::shortest}} residual path; Dinic uses a {{c4::level graph}} and blocking flows,
and on unit-capacity bipartite graphs runs in $O(E\sqrt{{V}})$.

concepts.L1: Ford-Fulkerson, Edmonds-Karp, Dinic. Max-flow min-cut duality. Bipartite matching reduces to max flow; so do a surprising number of assignment and scheduling problems.
concepts.L2: The skill isn't the algorithm, it's recognizing a flow problem in disguise. Project selection, image segmentation, and baseball elimination all reduce to min cut.
concepts.L3: The back edge is what makes the whole thing work and is the detail people omit. Sending $f$ units along $u \to v$ creates a residual edge $v \to u$ of capacity $f$; a later augmenting path may use it, which cancels part of the earlier routing. Without it the algorithm is a greedy that gets stuck at a locally maximal flow. The duality is what makes flow a modelling language: at termination, the vertices reachable from the source in the residual graph form one side of a cut whose capacity equals the flow, and that cut is the answer to a completely different-looking question.

L4.prompt_tpl: Bipartite matching on $V = {V}$, $E = {E}$ with unit capacities, solved as max flow. Give Dinic's bound here and compare it to its general bound.
L4.answer: General Dinic is O(V^2 E): V=1e4,E=1e5 -> 1e13; V=1e6,E=1e7 -> 1e19, hopeless. With unit capacities on a bipartite graph, Dinic reduces to O(E sqrt(V)): 1e5*100 = 1e7, and 1e7*1000 = 1e10. Same algorithm, and the special structure buys eight to nine orders of magnitude.
L4.explanation: Dinic on unit-capacity bipartite graphs IS Hopcroft-Karp - the level graph is the BFS layering and the blocking flow is the maximal set of vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths. Knowing that the general bound does not apply to your instance is the difference between 'intractable' and 'a second'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Model this as a min cut: {problem} Describe the network.

problem: select a profit-maximising subset of projects where some projects require others
segment an image into foreground and background given per-pixel priors and a smoothness penalty

L4.answer: Projects: source -> project with capacity = profit for profitable projects; cost -> sink with capacity = cost of each required resource; project -> its prerequisites with infinite capacity so a cut can never sever a dependency. Max profit = total positive profit minus min cut; the source side of the cut is the chosen set. Image: each pixel is a vertex; source -> pixel with capacity = foreground likelihood, pixel -> sink with capacity = background likelihood, and pixel-to-neighbour edges with capacity = smoothness penalty. The min cut is the segmentation boundary.
L4.explanation: The recurring pattern is that infinite-capacity edges encode hard constraints (a cut may never cross them) and finite ones encode costs. Once you see that, 'find a partition minimising total penalty subject to implications' reads as min cut on sight, which is the skill the preserved note names.

L4.prompt_tpl: An edge from u to v has capacity {c} and currently carries flow {f} units. After sending this flow, what is the residual capacity of the forward edge u to v in the residual graph?
L4.answer: Residual forward capacity = c - f. c=80,f=5 -> 75. c=150,f=20 -> 130. c=600,f=45 -> 555. The f units already sent do not vanish from the accounting: they reappear as a separate back edge v to u with capacity f, which is a different quantity from this forward residual.
L4.explanation: The residual graph splits one capacitated edge into two: a forward edge with whatever capacity is left (c minus f) and a backward edge with capacity equal to the flow already sent (f). Confusing the two, or forgetting the back edge exists at all, is the most common bug in a from-scratch max-flow implementation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cut (S, T) in a flow network has exactly three edges crossing from S to T, with capacities {a}, {b}, and {c} (no edges cross from T back to S). If this is a minimum cut, what is the value of the maximum flow, by the max-flow min-cut theorem?
L4.answer: Cut capacity sums only the edges crossing S to T, so capacity = a+b+c, and the theorem says max flow equals this exactly. a=6,b=9,c=3 -> 18. a=18,b=27,c=12 -> 57. a=44,b=61,c=95 -> 200.
L4.explanation: This reads the theorem directly rather than merely bounding with it: the max flow does not just fail to exceed the min cut, it equals it exactly, because at termination the source's reachable set in the residual graph is a cut that the flow already saturates edge for edge.

L4.prompt_tpl: A flow network with integer capacities has {E} edges and a maximum flow value of {F}. Using the O(E * maxflow) worst-case bound for Ford-Fulkerson, estimate the number of primitive operations in the worst case.
L4.explanation: The bound is pseudo-polynomial: it scales with the numeric value of the max flow, not with its number of digits, so huge capacities force billions of augmentations even when V and E stay small. That gap is exactly why Edmonds-Karp and Dinic, whose bounds depend only on V and E, replaced plain Ford-Fulkerson.

L4.prompt_tpl: A student implements Ford-Fulkerson by repeatedly finding any s-t path with positive residual capacity and augmenting along it, with no rule for which path to pick. A colleague claims this can fail to terminate at all if some capacities are irrational, even though it always terminates with integer or rational capacities. Is the colleague right, and why does an irrational capacity change anything?
L4.answer: The colleague is right. With integer (or rational) capacities every augmentation raises the flow by at least one unit (or one multiple of the common denominator), so the strictly increasing, bounded-above sequence of flow values must be finite. With irrational capacities and an adversarial choice of augmenting paths, no such lower bound on the increase exists: Ford and Fulkerson's own example (10 vertices, 48 edges) augments forever, and the flow values converge to a limit that need not even equal the true maximum flow. Zwick (1995) found the smallest such network: 6 vertices, 8 edges.
L4.explanation: Path choice matters more than it looks. Edmonds-Karp and Dinic both terminate in polynomially many phases regardless of whether capacities are rational, because their bound is a counting argument on path lengths, not on the capacities being well-behaved numbers. Plain Ford-Fulkerson has no such argument, so an adversary choosing the path each round can stall it forever.

L4.prompt_tpl: A from-scratch max-flow implementation omits the back (reverse) residual edges to save code. On a graph with edges s to a (capacity 1), s to b (capacity 1), a to b (capacity 1), a to t (capacity 1), and b to t (capacity 1), a depth-first search happens to pick the path s, a, b, t first and saturates it. What flow value does the buggy implementation report, and what is the true maximum flow?
L4.answer: The buggy version reports 1: after s-a-b-t saturates all three of those edges, the only forward edges left are s-b and a-t, and no all-forward path from s to t remains (b has no unsaturated forward edge left, and there is no original edge from b to a). The true maximum flow is 2: with back edges, s, b, then the back edge b to a, then a, t is a valid augmenting path (residual capacity 1 on each hop), adding a second unit; and the cut {s} versus the rest has capacity 1+1=2, certifying 2 as optimal.
L4.explanation: This is the L3 fact made concrete: the back edge exists specifically so a later path can cancel part of an earlier bad choice. An implementation that omits it does not crash or run slow, it silently returns a valid-looking but wrong, too-small flow - the worst kind of bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: A max-flow implementation stores capacities in a single adjacency matrix `cap[u][v]` indexed only by node pair, instead of one entry per edge. The input graph has two separate parallel edges from u to v (both can carry flow at the same time), with capacities {c1} and {c2}, and the code does `cap[u][v] = c` once for each edge in input order. What is the true combined capacity from u to v that a correct per-edge residual-graph implementation should support?
L4.answer: True combined capacity = c1 + c2, since the two parallel edges are distinct and both can be saturated simultaneously. c1=4,c2=7 -> 11. c1=15,c2=9 -> 24. c1=6,c2=25 -> 31. The matrix-indexed version instead has the second `cap[u][v] = c` assignment silently overwrite the first, so it only ever sees one edge's capacity, never their sum.
L4.explanation: This is the classic what-breaks-if for a from-scratch implementation: representing the graph by node-pair (a matrix or a dict keyed on (u,v)) quietly collapses parallel edges, understating the true capacity and, in the worst case, the true max flow. A per-edge or adjacency-list representation with explicit edge objects does not have this failure mode.

L0.body:
# The four questions, in order. Answer them in words before writing code.
#  1. STATE      what does dp[...] MEAN? A sentence, not a shape.
#  2. TRANSITION what choices lead into this state, and what do they cost?
#  3. ORDER      in what order are all dependencies of a state already computed?
#  4. BASE       which states are known outright?

# edit distance: dp[i][j] = min ops to turn A[0..i) into B[0..j)
dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j] + 1,            # delete A[i-1]
               dp[i][j-1] + 1,            # insert B[j-1]
               dp[i-1][j-1] + (A[i-1] != B[j-1]))
L0.cloze: State first: `dp[i][j]` must have a meaning stated as a {{c1::sentence}}, not a shape. The remaining questions are the {{c2::transition}}, the {{c3::order}} in which dependencies are already computed, and the {{c4::base}} cases. Edit distance keeps one row, so its space is $O(\min(n,m))$.

concepts.L1: Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems. The design questions are the state definition and the transition. Space optimization by keeping only the needed frontier. Bitmask DP for subset states, digit DP for numeric constraints.
concepts.L2: The reliable way to get unstuck is to define the state precisely in words before writing anything. Most failed DP attempts are underspecified states, not wrong recurrences.
concepts.L3: The reason 'define the state in words' works is that it forces the two properties the method requires. Optimal substructure means the optimum for a state is composed from optima of smaller states - which you can only check once you can say what a state is. Overlapping subproblems means the same state is reached by many paths, which is what makes memoisation pay; if states never repeat, you have a search, not a DP. Almost every failed attempt has an underspecified state: `dp[i]` meaning 'the best answer up to $i$' is not a definition, because it does not say whether element $i$ is used, and the transition then cannot be written.

L4.prompt_tpl: A candidate defines `dp[i]` as 'the longest increasing subsequence in the first $i$ elements' and cannot write a transition for an array of {n} elements. Fix the state definition and give the transition.
L4.answer: The state is underspecified: knowing the best length in a prefix says nothing about what value the subsequence ends on, so you cannot decide whether element i may extend it. Redefine: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ENDING EXACTLY at index i. Then dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j < i with a[j] < a[i]), or 1 if none, and the answer is max over all i. O(n^2), or O(n log n) with the patience-sorting tails array.
L4.explanation: The added clause 'ending exactly at i' is the whole fix, and it is a sentence, not code. This is the single most common DP failure and it is diagnosable before any code is written: if you cannot state the transition, the state is wrong.

L4.prompt_tpl: Edit distance between strings of length {n} and {m}. Give time, the naive space, the optimised space, and the space needed to also recover the alignment.
L4.answer: Time O(nm): 1e6, 5e6, 1e8, 5e8 cell updates. Naive space O(nm) at 4 bytes: 4 MB, 20 MB, 400 MB, 2 GB. Row-optimised space O(min(n,m)) : 4 KB, 4 KB, 4 KB, 20 KB. Recovering the alignment naively needs the full table; Hirschberg's algorithm recovers it in O(nm) time (about 2x the cell updates) and O(min(n,m)) space.
L4.explanation: The 2 GB case is why Hirschberg exists: the value is cheap to compute in linear space, and it is the traceback that appears to force the quadratic table. Divide-and-conquer on the middle column removes it at the cost of one constant factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: 0/1 knapsack with {n} items and capacity {w}: the state dp[i][c] is defined for every item-prefix i from 0 to {n} and every capacity c from 0 to {w}, one entry per (i, c) pair, each filled from two already-computed entries. How many (i, c) states does the table hold in total?
L4.answer: States = (n+1)(w+1), since i ranges over n+1 values (0..n items considered) and c over w+1 values (0..w capacity). n=10,w=20: 11*21=231. n=50,w=100: 51*101=5151. n=200,w=500: 201*501=100701. Each state does O(1) work, so total time is O(nw); a 1-D rolling array (iterating c from w down to the item's weight) drops space from O(nw) to O(w).
L4.explanation: The +1s are easy to drop under time pressure: i must include the 'zero items considered' base case and c must include capacity 0, so the grid is (n+1) by (w+1), not n by w. This state-counting habit generalises to every DP: count states before estimating time.

L4.prompt_tpl: Matrix chain multiplication over {n} matrices uses state dp[i][j], the minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j, defined for every 1 $\leq$ i $\leq$ j $\leq$ n. How many distinct (i, j) states are there?
L4.answer: States = n(n+1)/2, the count of pairs with i<=j out of n items (a triangular number). n=5: 15. n=20: 210. n=100: 5050. Each state tries O(j-i) split points k, so total time is O(n^3) and space (one entry per state) is O(n^2).
L4.explanation: Counting (i,j) with i<=j is the same triangular-number count as counting edges in a complete graph plus self-loops: n(n+1)/2, not n^2. Getting the state count right is what lets you predict the O(n^3) time before writing any code.

L4.prompt_tpl: Held-Karp dynamic programming for the traveling salesman problem over {n} cities uses state dp[mask][j], the cheapest path visiting exactly the cities in the subset mask and ending at city j, for every subset mask of the n cities and every city j in mask. Counting states as 2^n subsets times n choices of j (an over-count, since j must lie in mask, but fine for the order of magnitude), how many states are there?
L4.answer: States ~= 2^n * n. n=10: 1024*10=10240. n=15: 32768*15=491520. n=20: 1048576*20=20971520. Each state tries up to n next cities, so time is O(2^n n^2) and space O(2^n n) words -- why Held-Karp beats brute force (n!) but is still only usable up to about n=20 on a laptop.
L4.explanation: This is bitmask DP: the state packs a whole subset into one integer, mask, so 'which cities are visited' becomes an array index instead of a set data structure. The same trick handles any small-n subset-based state.

L4.prompt_tpl: The 1-D space-optimised 0/1 knapsack update is dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wt] + val) for one item of weight wt and value val, with an outer loop over all {n} items and an inner loop over the capacities c. Which direction must the inner c loop run for this to still compute the 0/1 (each item used at most once) answer, and what does the DP silently compute instead if you get the direction backwards?
L4.answer: The inner loop must run c from the capacity down to wt (descending), not ascending. Descending order guarantees dp[c - wt] read during item i's pass still holds the value from before item i was considered, so the update can add item i at most once. Running c ascending lets dp[c - wt] already include item i (it was updated earlier in the same pass), so the same item can be folded in again and again -- the recurrence silently becomes the unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies per item), not 0/1.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common 0/1-knapsack space-optimisation bug: the code looks identical either direction, runs without error, and returns a plausible but wrong (too-large) answer. It is exactly the DP 'order' question from the four-questions checklist -- direction of the loop is part of the order, not an implementation detail.

L4.prompt_tpl: Coin change (unlimited copies of each denomination) for minimum number of coins uses dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1) over coins c, for amount {amt} with a denomination set that includes a 1-value coin. Which loop nesting computes the correct minimum coin count: coin as the outer loop with amount inner, amount as the outer loop with coin inner, or does it not matter which one is outer for this objective?
L4.answer: Either loop order gives the correct minimum, because unlimited reuse is what the recurrence wants either way.
L4.explanation: Unlike 0/1 knapsack, unbounded reuse is exactly what the recurrence wants, so it does not matter whether a coin gets reused within the same outer pass or a later one -- dp[a-c] is always allowed to already include c. Loop order only matters here if you are counting distinct combinations (not permutations), where coin-outer is required to avoid double-counting orderings.
options: Coin must be the outer loop; amount as the outer loop gives a wrong (too-small) minimum.
Amount must be the outer loop and coin the inner loop only; the other order overcounts reuse.
Either loop order gives the correct minimum, because unlimited reuse is what the recurrence wants either way.

L4.prompt_tpl: Every DP recurrence with an explicit order of computation is exactly a shortest/longest-path computation on a DAG: one node per state, one edge per transition weighted by that transition's cost, and the DP's 'order' step is precisely a topological order of that DAG (see Topological order and DAG relaxation). For the edit-distance recurrence dp[i][j] on strings of length {n} and {m}, name the DAG's nodes, its edges (with weights), its unique source node, and the node whose value is the final answer.
L4.answer: Nodes: one per state (i, j) with 0 <= i <= n, 0 <= j <= m -- an (n+1) by (m+1) grid. Edges (weight 1 unless noted): (i-1,j) -> (i,j) weight 1 (delete), (i,j-1) -> (i,j) weight 1 (insert), (i-1,j-1) -> (i,j) weight 0 or 1 (match or substitute). Source: (0,0), the only node with no incoming edges. Answer node: (n,m), the far corner, reachable only after every state it depends on has been settled. This is the same DAG shape as knapsack and interval DP with a different edge set -- see Three DP state shapes: knapsack, LIS, and interval for the other two.
L4.explanation: Seeing DP as 'shortest path on the DAG of states' is what makes the order question mechanical instead of a guess: any topological order of that DAG is a legal computation order, and the four-questions checklist (state, transition, order, base) is just naming the DAG's nodes, edges, a valid topological sort, and its sources.

concepts.t: Three DP state shapes: knapsack, LIS, and interval

L0.body:
# 1. VALUE-INDEXED (0/1 knapsack): dp[w] = best value with capacity w
for item in items:
    for w in range(W, item.wt - 1, -1):  # DESCENDING = 0/1; ASCENDING = unbounded
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - item.wt] + item.val)

# 2. POSITION-INDEXED (LIS): tails[k] = smallest tail of a length-(k+1) increasing subseq
#    tails sorted -> binary search -> O(n log n)

# 3. INTERVAL (matrix chain, optimal BST): dp[i][j] over split k, O(n^3)
#    dp[i][j] = min over i<=k<j of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost
#    BST: cost = w(i,j), same for every k. Chain: cost = p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j], DEPENDS on k
L0.cloze: In 0/1 knapsack the capacity loop must run {{c1::descending}} so each item is used once; running it ascending gives the {{c2::unbounded}} knapsack. LIS in $O(n\log n)$ keeps a sorted `tails` array where `tails[k]` is the {{c3::smallest}} tail of any increasing subsequence of length $k+1$. Interval DP iterates over a {{c4::split point}} $k$, whose cost depends on $k$ for matrix chain but not for optimal BST, and is $O(n^{{3}})$.

concepts.L1: Three recurring DP skeletons. Value-indexed (knapsack): state is a resource budget, items consumed in an outer loop; loop direction decides reuse. Position-indexed (LIS): state is a prefix, the answer accumulates left to right. Interval: state is a subrange $[i,j]$, built from a split point $k$.
concepts.L2: The knapsack loop direction is the sharpest example of a DP where the order is the algorithm. Descending over capacity means `dp[w - wt]` still holds the value from before this item was considered, so the item is used at most once; ascending means it holds a value that may already include this item, so the item may be reused.
concepts.L3: 0/1 knapsack is $O(nW)$: polynomial in the numeric value of $W$, exponential in the bits needed to write $W$ down - pseudo-polynomial, why knapsack is NP-hard yet routine at realistic capacities. LIS's $O(n^{2})$ form asks 'best subsequence ending at $i$'; the $O(n\log n)$ form asks 'for each achievable length, the smallest possible tail', which is monotone and binary-searchable - a factor of about $n/\log n$ fewer comparisons, not merely a $\log$ factor. Interval DP tries every split $k$ for every $(i,j)$: $O(n^{2})$ states times $O(n)$ splits gives $O(n^{3})$ - the same split-at-a-point cost shape as in Divide and conquer as a cost recurrence, just summed over every subrange instead of one.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 0/1 knapsack with capacity {W} loops `for w in range(item.wt, W+1)` and reports values that are too high. What problem is it actually solving?
L4.answer: The unbounded knapsack, where each item may be taken any number of times. Ascending order means dp[w - wt] may already have been updated with the current item during this same item's pass, so the item is reused. Descending order guarantees dp[w - wt] still reflects the state before this item, enforcing at most one copy. The fix is one word: range(W, item.wt - 1, -1).
L4.explanation: Both loops are correct algorithms for different problems, which is why the bug produces plausible output rather than a crash. A test with one item whose weight is at most W/2 and high value exposes it immediately: 0/1 must take it once, unbounded takes it floor(W/wt) times.

L4.prompt_tpl: 0/1 knapsack with $n = {n}$ items and capacity $W = {W}$. Give the time and space, and explain in one line why this does not contradict knapsack being NP-hard.
L4.answer: Time O(nW): 1e6 and 1e9 cell updates. Space O(W) with the rolling one-dimensional array: 4 KB and 4 MB at 4 bytes per entry. It does not contradict NP-hardness because O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial: W is written in log2(W) bits, so the running time is exponential in the input size. W=1e6 needs 20 bits; a W of 2^60 would be written in 60 bits and be entirely infeasible.
L4.explanation: Pseudo-polynomial is the precise word and it is worth using. It explains why knapsack, subset-sum and partition are solved daily in practice while remaining NP-hard, and it is the same observation that makes counting sort linear.

L4.prompt_tpl: Patience-sorting LIS runs one binary search per element over the sorted tails array, whose length never exceeds n. Modeling each binary search as costing ceil(log2(n)) comparisons in the worst case, estimate the total number of comparisons across all n elements for n = {n}. Answer with the total comparison count.
L4.explanation: This is the real comparison count behind 'O(n log n)', not a restatement of the bound. Binary search over an array of size up to k needs at most ceil(log2(k+1)) comparisons; capping k at n overestimates slightly but shows what the log factor actually costs in comparisons, not just an exponent.

L4.prompt_tpl: Matrix-chain / optimal-BST interval DP has states dp[i][j] for 1 <= i < j <= n and tries every split k with i <= k < j. For n = {n}, how many total (state, split) pairs does the algorithm examine -- i.e. how many times is the min(...) recurrence evaluated? Answer with that count.
L4.explanation: Group states by d = j-i: there are n-d states with that gap, each trying d splits, so the total is sum over d=1..n-1 of d*(n-d), which telescopes to (n^3-n)/6 -- the real constant behind O(n^3), and the exact figure the closed-form dp[i][j] recurrence has to iterate.

L4.prompt_tpl: Interval DP with dp[i][j] = min over i<=k<j of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost, evaluated over every state with the full split range tried at each: what is the tight worst-case time complexity in the comparison model, for n = {n} items?
L4.explanation: O(n^2) states times up to O(n) split points tried at each gives O(n^3) in the comparison / word-RAM model, where each candidate split costs O(1) once dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j] are already computed -- the same shape as the exact (n^3-n)/6 count this concept's other template derives.
options: O(n log n)

L4.prompt_tpl: Two variants of the tails-array LIS step differ only in the binary-search bound (Python's bisect module). Both run this update for each x in a: `i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)` for STRICT (strictly increasing) or `i = bisect.bisect_right(tails, x)` for NON-DECREASING (equal values allowed), then: `if i == len(tails):` on its own line, `    tails.append(x)` indented under it, then `else:` on its own line, `    tails[i] = x` indented under that. For a = [5] * {n} (n equal values), give len(tails) under STRICT and under NON-DECREASING as two numbers separated by a comma.
L4.answer: STRICT stays at length 1: bisect_left(tails, 5) returns 0 every time (tails[0]=5 is already >= 5), so it keeps overwriting tails[0]. NON-DECREASING grows by one every time: bisect_right(tails, 5) returns len(tails) every time (5 is never strictly greater than an existing 5), so it always appends. n=5 -> 1,5. n=50 -> 1,50.
L4.explanation: bisect_left finds the first slot not smaller than x and overwrites it, which forbids a run of equal values from ever extending the sequence. bisect_right finds the first slot strictly greater than x, so a run of ties keeps landing past all of them and appending -- one bound switch changes 'strictly increasing' into 'non-decreasing'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Interval DP (dp[i][j] = min over i<=k<j of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost) is O(n^3): O(n^2) states times O(n) split points examined at each. For a cost function satisfying the quadrangle inequality, Knuth's optimization proves the optimal split opt(i,j) is monotone: opt(i,j-1) <= opt(i,j) <= opt(i+1,j). In 2-3 sentences, explain why restricting each state's k-search to the range [opt(i,j-1), opt(i+1,j)] instead of the full [i,j) cuts the total work from O(n^3) to O(n^2).
L4.answer: Process states in order of increasing interval length. Each state's search window has width opt(i+1,j) - opt(i,j-1) + 1, and along a fixed diagonal these windows only advance, never retreat, so their widths cannot cover more than O(n) total positions per diagonal instead of O(n) positions per single state; with n diagonals the grand total is O(n^2) instead of O(n^3).
L4.explanation: This is the same amortized argument as a monotone two-pointer sweep: a search window that only grows where the previous state's window left off cannot, summed across a whole diagonal, exceed O(n) total steps, even though any single window can itself be as wide as O(n).

L4.prompt_tpl: Rod cutting: a rod of length {n} is cut into any number of integer-length pieces (a length may repeat), and price[i] is the value of one length-i piece. Which of this concept's three DP shapes does the loop-order lesson from 0/1 knapsack transfer to (value-indexed, position-indexed, or interval), should the loop over remaining length run ascending or descending, and what is the recurrence for dp[L], the best value from a length-L rod?
L4.answer: Value-indexed: the state is a length budget, just like knapsack's capacity. A cut length may be reused any number of times, so this is the unbounded case, and the loop over remaining length runs ascending -- the opposite of 0/1 knapsack's descending rule. Recurrence: dp[0] = 0, dp[L] = max over 1<=i<=L of price[i] + dp[L-i].
L4.explanation: Rod cutting is unbounded knapsack under a different name: 'capacity' becomes 'remaining rod length' and 'items' become 'cut lengths'. Getting the loop direction right here is the same test as the loop-direction bug template on this concept, except ascending is now correct, because reuse is intended, not a bug.

L0.body:
KMP failure function: f[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is
                      also a suffix. Built in O(m); search never backs up in the text.
Z-algorithm       : z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of S and S[i..]. O(n).
Rabin-Karp        : h(s[i+1..i+m]) = (h - s[i]*B^(m-1))*B + s[i+m]   mod a large prime
                    rolling: O(1) per shift. Verify on hash match - hashes collide.
suffix array + LCP: sort all n suffixes; Kasai builds LCP in O(n) from SA and its inverse
Aho-Corasick      : trie of all patterns + failure links = a DFA. O(n + m + z).
L0.cloze: The KMP failure function `f[i]` is the length of the longest proper {{c1::prefix}} of the pattern that is also a {{c2::suffix}} of `P[0..i]`, and it is what lets the search never {{c3::back up}} in the text. A Rabin-Karp hash match must always be {{c4::verified}}, because hashes collide.

concepts.L1: KMP failure function, Z-algorithm, Rabin-Karp rolling hash, suffix arrays with LCP, Aho-Corasick for multi-pattern matching.
concepts.L2: Aho-Corasick is what powers real intrusion detection and content filtering at scale. Rolling hashes underpin rsync and content-defined chunking in deduplication systems — the practical applications are more interesting than the puzzle ones.
concepts.L3: Rolling hashes are the piece with the largest reach outside puzzles, and the mechanism is worth holding precisely. A polynomial hash over a window supports removing the leaving character and adding the entering one in $O(1)$, so a hash of every window of length $m$ over an $n$-byte stream costs $O(n)$ total. rsync uses exactly this: the receiver sends weak rolling checksums of its fixed blocks, the sender rolls a hash across its own file byte by byte and, on a weak match, checks a strong hash - which finds shifted content that a block-aligned comparison would miss entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rabin-Karp over a stream of $n = {n}$ bytes with a window of $m = {m}$ bytes and a 63-bit modulus. Give the number of hash updates, the expected number of spurious matches against one pattern, and the cost of verification.
L4.answer: Hash updates: n - m + 1, about 1e9 - two multiplies and two adds each. Expected spurious matches against a single pattern: (n-m+1)/2^63 = 1e9/9.22e18 = 1.1e-10, effectively never. Verification on a match costs O(m) byte comparisons: 64 or 4096. With a 32-bit modulus instead, expected spurious matches would be 1e9/4.29e9 = 0.23 per scan - still small, but no longer negligible if you scan many files.
L4.explanation: The modulus width is the design decision: it converts an O(nm) worst case into an expected O(n + occurrences*m). A 32-bit rolling hash is fine for rsync, where a weak match is followed by a strong hash anyway, and wrong for a security scanner where a missed verification is a vulnerability.

L4.prompt_tpl: Content-defined chunking cuts a boundary where a rolling hash has {b} low bits zero. Give the average chunk size, and explain why this beats fixed-size chunking when a byte is inserted at the start of a file.
L4.answer: Average chunk size is 2^b bytes: 8192 bytes at b=13, 65536 at b=16 (geometric distribution, so a minimum and maximum size are usually enforced too). Fixed-size chunking aligns boundaries to offsets, so inserting one byte shifts every subsequent boundary and every chunk hash changes - the whole file is re-uploaded. Content-defined boundaries depend only on the surrounding bytes, so after the insertion the boundary positions re-synchronise within one chunk and every subsequent chunk is unchanged and already stored.
L4.explanation: This is the single idea behind every modern deduplicating backup system, and it is a rolling hash plus a threshold. The min/max size clamps matter in practice because the geometric distribution produces both 1-byte and megabyte chunks otherwise.

L4.prompt_tpl: KMP failure function over pattern P = {p} (f[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix of P[0..i]). Give f[m-1], the array's last entry, where m = len(P).
L4.answer: aabaabaab -> f[m-1] = 6, m = 9. The pattern is 'aab' repeated three times, and m - f[m-1] = 3 is that repeating period. ababab -> f[m-1] = 4, m = 6. m - f[m-1] = 2, the period 'ab'.
L4.explanation: The last entry of the failure function is the length of P's longest proper border; m minus it gives P's smallest period whenever that period divides m. KMP reuses this same array to skip ahead on a mismatch instead of restarting the search from scratch.

L4.prompt_tpl: Z-algorithm over S = {s} (z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of S and S[i..]). Give the largest z[i] over i from 1 to len(S)-1 (i.e. excluding the trivial z[0]).
L4.answer: aabcaabxaaaz -> max is z[4] = 3: S[4..] = aabxaaaz shares the prefix aab with S. abcabcabc -> max is z[3] = 6: S[3..] = abcabc matches the first 6 characters of S exactly, since S is abc repeated three times.
L4.explanation: A large z[i] for i >= 1 marks a proper substring that repeats as a prefix elsewhere in S. This is the mirror image of the KMP failure function: KMP looks for prefix-suffix overlap from the end of a growing match, Z looks for prefix overlap from every start.

L4.prompt_tpl: Case: {case}. Two implementations search text T for pattern P with the Z-algorithm, checking whether z[i] equals len(P) at the index where T begins. One builds S by concatenating P and T with no separator; the other inserts a unique separator character between them. Give z at the text-start index for each version and say which one wrongly fails to report the real match at the very start of T.
L4.answer: P=aa,T=aaa: no-separator S is `aaaaa`, text starts at index m=2, z[2]=3; 3 does not equal m=2, so the equality test misses a real match. With a separator, S is `aa` + separator + `aaa`, text starts at index m+1=3, z[3]=2, which equals m=2, so the test correctly reports it. P=ab,T=aba: no-separator z at index 2 is 3 (test fails, m=2); with separator, z at index 3 is 2 (test succeeds). P=aaa,T=aaaa: no-separator z at index 3 is 4 (test fails, m=3); with separator, z at index 4 is 3 (test succeeds). Without a separator a repetitive text can extend the match past len(P), so a strict equality check silently drops a real occurrence; the separator caps z at exactly len(P), which is why it is standard practice rather than tidiness.
L4.explanation: The separator is not cosmetic: a periodic text can make the Z-value overshoot len(P), and the usual implementation, which tests equality against len(P), then misses a genuine match. Capping with a separator that appears in neither string is the standard, safer idiom.

L4.prompt_tpl: KMP's failure-function construction runs an outer loop over i from 1 to m-1; on each iteration it may run an inner while loop that sets k = f[k-1] repeatedly before testing p[i] against p[k]. For a pattern of length m = {m}, use the potential $\Phi = k$ to bound the total number of inner-loop reductions across the whole construction, and give the resulting total number of character comparisons.
L4.answer: k increases by at most 1 per outer iteration (only when p[i] equals p[k]), so across all m-1 outer iterations k rises by at most m-1 in total. Each inner-loop step sets k to f[k-1], and f[k-1] is always strictly less than k (a proper border of a length-(k-1) prefix has length at most k-1), so every inner step strictly decreases k by at least 1. Since k starts at 0 and never goes negative, the total number of decreases across the whole run cannot exceed the total number of increases, which is at most m-1. m=9: at most 8 outer increases and at most 8 inner reductions, so at most 16 character comparisons total, still $O(m)$. m=20: at most 19 increases and 19 reductions, at most 38 comparisons, still $O(m)$.
L4.explanation: This is the same shape as the amortized argument in The potential method: k never goes negative, so total decreases cannot exceed total increases, giving O(m) total work despite an inner loop that looks like it could run for up to m steps on a single outer iteration.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must search a text of n = {n} characters for k = {k} fixed patterns of about 20 characters each. Running KMP once per pattern costs about O(n) per pattern after a cheap preprocessing step; Aho-Corasick costs one O(n) scan after building an automaton from all k patterns. Give the total scan comparisons for each approach and say which you would choose and why.
L4.answer: n=1e9. k=5: repeated KMP needs about k*n = 5e9 character comparisons across the five scans; Aho-Corasick needs about n plus the total pattern length, 1e9 + 100, roughly 5x fewer. k=200: repeated KMP needs about 200*1e9 = 2e11 comparisons; Aho-Corasick still needs about 1e9 + 4000, roughly 200x fewer. Aho-Corasick's scan cost is independent of k because the failure-link automaton lets one pass handle every pattern at once; running KMP k times pays the full n-length scan k separate times. Choose Aho-Corasick whenever k > 1 and the patterns are known in advance; plain KMP is the right choice only for a single pattern, or when the pattern set changes on every query and building the automaton each time would dominate.
L4.explanation: The comparison count scales with k for repeated KMP because each pass rescans the whole text; Aho-Corasick's failure-link automaton merges all k patterns into one DFA so scan cost never depends on k. This is why production multi-pattern matchers such as Snort's signature engine use Aho-Corasick rather than one matcher per rule.

L0.body:
SA[k] = starting index of the k-th smallest suffix of S.   |SA| = n integers.
LCP[k] = length of the longest common prefix of S[SA[k-1]..] and S[SA[k]..]

  banana ->  SA: 5 a, 3 ana, 1 anana, 0 banana, 4 na, 2 nana
             LCP:  -   1      3        0        0    2

  construction: SA-IS in O(n) time, O(n) space
  Kasai:        LCP in O(n) from SA + its inverse (uses h[i] >= h[i-1] - 1)
  search P:     binary search, O(m log n); with LCP, O(m + log n)

  memory: 4n bytes (SA) + 4n (LCP) vs ~20n bytes for a suffix TREE. 3 Gbp genome:
          24 GB with SA+LCP, 60 GB as a tree.
L0.cloze: A suffix array stores the {{c1::starting indices}} of all suffixes in sorted order in $4n$ bytes, against roughly {{c2::20n}} for a suffix tree. {{c3::Kasai}}'s algorithm builds the LCP array in $O(n)$, and with LCP a pattern search drops from $O(m\log n)$ to $O(m + {{c4::\log n}})$.

concepts.L1: The sorted array of all suffix start positions, plus an array of longest common prefixes between adjacent entries. Together they answer substring search, repeat finding and longest-common-substring queries, in about two-fifths of the memory a suffix tree needs.
concepts.L2: The suffix array replaced the suffix tree for engineering reasons, not asymptotic ones: both support the same queries in comparable time, but a suffix tree stores nodes, child pointers and edge labels at roughly 20 bytes per character, while a suffix array is one 32-bit integer.
concepts.L3: Kasai's algorithm is the elegant part and the reason LCP is affordable. Process suffixes in text order rather than sorted order and maintain $h$, the LCP of the current suffix with its predecessor in the sorted array. The key observation is that when you move from suffix $i$ to suffix $i+1$ you drop one leading character, so $h$ can fall by at most one: $h_{i+1} \geq h_{i} - 1$. Therefore $h$ decreases at most $n$ times overall and increases at most $n$ times, and the total character comparisons are $O(n)$ despite the naive bound being $O(n^{2})$. It is an amortised argument with $h$ as the potential.

L4.prompt_tpl: A suffix array over a text of $n = {n}$ characters with 32-bit indices. Give the memory for SA, SA+LCP, and an equivalent suffix tree at 20 bytes per character; then the cost of searching a pattern of length {m} with and without LCP.
L4.answer: n=1e8: SA 400 MB, SA+LCP 800 MB, tree 2 GB. n=3e9: SA 12 GB (needs 32-bit indices, which just fit), SA+LCP 24 GB, tree 60 GB. Search without LCP is O(m log2 n): m=20, n=3e9 -> 20*31.5 = 630 character comparisons; m=100 -> 3148. With LCP it is O(m + log n): 20+31.5 = 52, or 100+31.5 = 132. Roughly a 12x to 24x reduction in comparisons.
L4.explanation: The 3 gigabase case is the human genome and the memory figures are why read aligners use an FM-index rather than a plain suffix array: a BWT plus wavelet tree brings it to a few GB, small enough for a workstation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kasai's algorithm computes LCP in $O(n)$ using the fact that $h$ can drop by at most {d} when moving from suffix $i$ to suffix $i+1$. Explain why, and why that bounds total work.
L4.answer: If suffix i shares h characters with its sorted-order predecessor, then suffix i+1 - which is suffix i with the first character removed - shares at least h-1 characters with the suffix that is suffix-i's-predecessor-minus-its-first-character, which cannot appear later in sorted order than suffix i+1's own predecessor. So h drops by at most 1 per step. Over n steps h decreases at most n times in total, and since h is bounded by n it can also increase at most 2n times overall; each increase costs one character comparison, so total work is O(n).
L4.explanation: This is an amortised argument with h as the potential function, and it is the same shape as the dynamic-array proof. Without it, computing LCP naively is O(n^2) and the whole suffix-array approach becomes impractical on large texts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A text of length {n} characters has a suffix array whose LCP array (the longest common prefix of each pair of adjacent suffixes in sorted order) sums to {L}. Using the identity that every repeated substring is exactly one shared-prefix overlap counted by some LCP entry, how many distinct substrings does the text contain?
L4.answer: Substrings counted with multiplicity total n(n+1)/2 (one of each length starting at each position). Each LCP entry counts exactly the substrings duplicated by the shared prefix with the previous suffix in sorted order, so distinct substrings = n(n+1)/2 - sum(LCP). Example: the text banana has n=6 and LCP array 1,3,0,0,2 (sum 6), giving 21-6=15 distinct substrings, which matches direct enumeration. For n=20, L=15: 210-15=195.
L4.explanation: This turns the LCP array, normally a search accelerator, into a counting tool: every duplicate substring is captured exactly once as a shared-prefix overlap with the suffix immediately before it in sorted order, so the LCP sum is precisely the number of duplicates to remove from the n(n+1)/2 total.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LCP-accelerated suffix-array binary search (Manber-Myers) locates a pattern of length {m} in a text of n = {n} characters using about m + log2(n) character comparisons. Compute that number.
L4.answer: log2(n) for n=1000 is about 9.97, for n=1e6 about 19.93, for n=1e9 about 29.90. Add m: n=1000,m=8 -> 17.97; n=1e6,m=32 -> 51.93; n=1e9,m=64 -> 93.90. Each is far below the unaccelerated m*log2(n) bound for the same pattern and text.
L4.explanation: This is the Manber-Myers result: carrying the LCP already established with the search boundaries means each binary-search step needs only the characters past that LCP, not a full re-comparison, turning O(m log n) into O(m + log n).

L4.prompt_tpl: Kasai's algorithm processes suffixes in text order (i, i+1, i+2, ...), not sorted order (SA[0], SA[1], SA[2], ...). Suppose an implementation instead walked SA in sorted order and tried to carry h from one rank to the next the same way. Would the O(n) amortised bound still hold? Explain what breaks.
L4.answer: No. The bound rests on h_{i+1} >= h_i - 1, which holds because suffix i+1 is suffix i with exactly one leading character removed, so it keeps at least h_i - 1 of the shared prefix. Adjacent SA ranks have no such relationship: SA[k] and SA[k+1] are suffixes at essentially arbitrary text positions with no guaranteed overlap between their LCP-with-predecessor values. Walking in rank order loses the one fact that bounds the drop in h, so each LCP would need to be recomputed from scratch, giving O(n) per entry and O(n^2) overall -- back to the naive bound Kasai's algorithm exists to avoid.
L4.explanation: The text-order traversal is not an implementation detail: it is the entire argument. This is the same lesson as the potential method generally -- the bound belongs to the specific sequence of states visited, not to the data structure alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: Model a suffix-tree search for a pattern of length {m} as costing one cache miss per edge traversal, about {m} misses (pointer chasing). Model an LCP-accelerated suffix-array binary search over n = {n} suffixes as costing one cache miss per comparison step, about log2(n) misses. For n = {n}, compute the suffix array's cache-miss estimate.
L4.answer: n=1e6: log2(1e6) is about 19.93, so about 20 cache misses, versus the tree's 50 or 300 -- far fewer, since the array's cost depends on log n regardless of pattern length. n=1e9: log2(1e9) is about 29.90, about 30 misses, still well under m=50 or 300.
L4.explanation: Both structures do O(log n)-ish or O(m)-ish work, but on real hardware pointer chasing through tree edges is one cache miss per step with no prefetch help, while the array's steps are also misses but there are only log n of them -- the reason arrays win in practice even at matched asymptotics.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must check, as text streams in one character at a time, whether any of {k} fixed patterns has just completed a match ending at the current position. Would you reach for Aho-Corasick or a suffix array with LCP, and why? Name the property of the other concept's automaton that makes it fit a streaming setting a suffix array does not.
L4.answer: Aho-Corasick. It builds one automaton over the {k} patterns up front, then processes the stream in amortised O(1) per character using failure links, needing no future characters and no rebuild as input arrives. A suffix array is built over one fixed text to answer substring queries about that text; it is not maintained incrementally as characters stream in, and rebuilding it per character would cost far more than O(1) amortised. Suffix arrays fit the reverse shape: one large fixed text, many patterns queried against it after the fact.
L4.explanation: Same underlying goal, string matching, but the two structures are built around opposite fixed points: Aho-Corasick fixes the pattern set and streams the text, a suffix array fixes the text and takes arbitrary pattern queries. Picking the wrong one costs an asymptotic factor, not just constants.
