L0.body:
Build a trie of all patterns, then add:
  fail(v)   = the node for the longest proper suffix of v's string that is also a
              trie node. Computed by BFS: fail(child) = goto(fail(v), c).
  output(v) = patterns ending at v, PLUS output(fail(v))   <- suffix-link chain

  goto(v, c): follow fail links until a child on c exists. Precompute into a full DFA
              -> one array lookup per input character, no branching.

  O(sum of pattern lengths) to build, O(n + z) to scan n characters with z matches.
  Cost is INDEPENDENT of the pattern count. 5000 patterns x 12 chars: 60k nodes.
L0.cloze: The failure link of a node points to the node for the longest proper {{c1::suffix}} of its string that is also in the trie, and it is computed by {{c2::BFS}} over the trie. A node's output set must include the outputs along its {{c3::failure link}} chain. Scanning costs $O(n + z)$, {{c4::independent}} of the number of patterns.

concepts.L1: A trie of all patterns augmented with failure links, forming a finite automaton that matches every pattern in one left-to-right pass. Building costs the total pattern length; scanning costs $O(n + z)$ for $n$ input characters and $z$ matches, regardless of how many patterns there are.
concepts.L2: The output set must follow the failure chain, and forgetting this is the standard bug: if `he` and `she` are both patterns, the node for `she` must report `he` as well, because `he` is a suffix of `she`.
concepts.L3: The cost being independent of the pattern count is the property that makes it infrastructure. Snort and Suricata match tens of thousands of intrusion signatures against every packet; ClamAV matches its signature database against every file. Running $k$ separate Boyer-Moore searches costs $O(kn)$, which at $k = 10^{4}$ and gigabit line rate is impossible; Aho-Corasick costs one array lookup per input byte. The memory trade is real: materialising the goto table densely costs $|\Sigma|$ pointers per node - 60,000 nodes times 256 times 4 bytes is 61 MB - so implementations use sparse or double-array representations.

L4.prompt_tpl: An intrusion detector matches {k} signatures averaging {L} bytes against a {rate} stream. Compare Aho-Corasick against running the patterns individually, and give the automaton's node count and dense-table memory.
L4.answer: Nodes <= k*L: 60,000 or 600,000. Dense goto table at 256 entries of 4 bytes per node: 61 MB or 614 MB - the latter forces a sparse representation. Scanning: Aho-Corasick is O(n + z), one lookup per byte, so 125 MB/s of input needs 1.25e8 lookups/s - comfortable. Individually: O(k*n) = 5000 or 50000 passes over the same bytes, 6.25e11 or 6.25e12 byte operations per second. Impossible by four to five orders of magnitude.
L4.explanation: The dense-table memory is the real engineering constraint and the reason production matchers use double-array tries or bitmapped nodes. Hyperscan goes further, compiling pattern sets to SIMD literal matchers with an NFA fallback, but the Aho-Corasick structure is the baseline every such system is measured against.

L4.prompt_tpl: An Aho-Corasick implementation reports a match for `{p1}` but never for `{p2}` when scanning text containing `{p1}`. Both are in the pattern set. Diagnose.
L4.answer: The output set is not following the failure links. A node's reported patterns must be the patterns ending exactly there UNION the output set of its failure node, computed transitively during the BFS that builds the links. Without it, only the longest match ending at each position is reported and every pattern that is a proper suffix of another is silently lost.
L4.explanation: This is the canonical Aho-Corasick bug and it is invisible unless the pattern set contains a pattern that is a suffix of another. For a security scanner that is a vulnerability, not a defect: an attacker who knows the signature set can hide a short signature inside a longer one.

L4.prompt_tpl: A pattern set with no shared prefixes has total length (sum of all pattern lengths) m = {m} characters, so the trie has exactly m nodes below the root. The BFS that computes every node's failure link visits each node exactly once. Give the number of node visits this BFS performs.
L4.answer: The BFS visits each of the m trie nodes exactly once, so the visit count equals m: 480, 12,000, or 60,000. This is the concrete meaning of 'build cost is the total pattern length' - it is a single linear pass over the trie, not a pass per pattern.
L4.explanation: This is the base fact behind 'cost independent of pattern count': construction touches each trie node once regardless of how many patterns produced it. It is also why the automaton is worth building once and reusing across many scans.

L4.prompt_tpl: Build the Aho-Corasick trie for the classic pattern set he, she, his, hers (Aho and Corasick's own 1975 example). Consider the node reached from the root by reading the two characters s, h - i.e. the node for the string 'sh'. Its failure link points to the node for which string?
L4.answer: h
L4.explanation: Proper suffixes of 'sh' are 'h' and the empty string. 'h' is a trie node (root's child on 'h', shared by he/his/hers), so fail('sh') = the node for 'h'. This is the failure-link rule applied by hand, on the algorithm's own textbook example.

L4.prompt_tpl: A matcher holds k = {k} patterns of any lengths, scans an input of n = {n} bytes, and reports z = {z} total pattern occurrences. Aho-Corasick's scanning cost is O(n + z), independent of k. Give the exact value of n + z for this run.
L4.answer: n + z, with k playing no part: (n=1000, z=0) gives 1000; (n=1000, z=12) gives 1012; (n=50000, z=0) gives 50000; (n=50000, z=12) gives 50012 - the same regardless of whether k is 10 or 200,000.
L4.explanation: The point of the template is that k never enters the formula. Whether the automaton encodes 10 patterns or 200,000, the scan still costs one array lookup per byte plus one step per reported match.

L4.prompt_tpl: The goto function can be realized two ways: (a) on a miss, follow failure links until a match or the root - no extra space beyond the trie; or (b) precompute a full transition table so every state has one entry per alphabet symbol, giving a true array lookup with no branching. For an alphabet of size sigma = {sigma} and a trie with m = {m} non-root nodes (m + 1 states counting the root), give the number of table entries method (b) must fill in.
L4.answer: sigma*(m+1): byte alphabet (sigma=256) with m=500 needs 128,256 entries; m=60,000 needs 15,360,256. A 4-symbol DNA alphabet with the same tries needs only 2,004 and 240,004. Method (a) costs O(m) to build regardless of sigma, with an amortized O(1) (not worst-case O(1)) scan step per character; method (b) costs O(sigma*m) to build but gives a genuine worst-case O(1) lookup per character - the model the L0/L3 'one array lookup per character' claim silently assumes.
L4.explanation: This is the word-RAM assumption the concept's O(n+z) scan bound leans on: it is only a strict per-character O(1) if the full sigma-way table is materialized, at O(sigma*m) build cost and space - see The word RAM model and what it quietly assumes. With the failure-link fallback instead, per-character cost is O(1) only in the amortized sense.

L4.prompt_tpl: During a scan of n = {n} characters using the failure-link-fallback form of goto (no precomputed full table), the automaton's depth in the trie rises by at most 1 per successful goto step and falls by at least 1 per failure-link traversal, and never goes below 0. Using depth as a potential function, give the maximum possible total number of failure-link traversals across the whole scan.
L4.answer: At most n: 500, 10,000, or 1,000,000. Total depth increase across the scan is at most n (one +1 per character), depth starts and ends at or above 0, so total decrease - and hence the number of failure-link traversals, each worth at least one unit of decrease - cannot exceed total increase, which is at most n.
L4.explanation: This is the same potential-method argument used elsewhere in this curriculum (see The potential method, and Amortized vs average vs worst case) to turn a per-step worst case into a linear total: no single character is cheap, but the whole scan is O(n) because expensive characters are paid for by the depth they had already banked.

L4.prompt_tpl: Restrict Aho-Corasick to a single pattern of length {m} characters: the trie degenerates to a chain, no branching. Explain why the resulting failure-link function is exactly the KMP failure (border) function for that pattern, and name the Whetstone concept this connects to.
L4.answer: Both are defined the same way: the failure value at a prefix is the length of the longest proper suffix of that prefix that is also a prefix of the same string. On a chain trie every node's string is a prefix of the one pattern, so 'longest proper suffix that is also a trie node' reduces exactly to 'longest proper suffix that is also a prefix of the pattern' - the KMP border definition. Example: for 'aabaa', the border at the full string has length 2 ('aa' is both a prefix and a suffix), matching KMP's own prefix-function trace. This connects to String algorithms, where the KMP failure function is covered directly.
L4.explanation: Aho-Corasick is the k-pattern generalization of KMP, not a different idea: with one pattern its failure links and KMP's failure function coincide by construction, and the goto/fail traversal during a scan is exactly the KMP shift rule.

L0.cloze: Reservoir sampling keeps element $i$ with probability {{c1::k/i}} and evicts a uniformly chosen incumbent, so every element of a stream of unknown length $n$ ends in the sample with probability exactly {{c2::k/n}}. {{c3::Las Vegas}} algorithms are always correct with random runtime; {{c4::Monte Carlo}} algorithms have fixed runtime and may be wrong.

concepts.L1: Reservoir sampling, randomized quickselect, Karger's min cut, Miller-Rabin. Las Vegas (always correct, random runtime) vs Monte Carlo (fixed runtime, probably correct).
concepts.L2: Reservoir sampling over a stream of unknown length is one of the highest-value small algorithms in practice — sampling logs, sampling traces, sampling training data — and it's a two-line implementation most people can't reconstruct.
concepts.L3: The induction for reservoir sampling is short and worth being able to produce. Assume after $i$ items each is in the reservoir with probability $k/i$. Item $i+1$ is admitted with probability $k/(i+1)$. An incumbent survives if either the new item is rejected, probability $1 - k/(i+1)$, or it is admitted but evicts one of the other $k-1$ slots, probability $\frac{k}{i+1}\cdot\frac{k-1}{k}$. Summing: $\frac{k}{i}\left(1 - \frac{k}{i+1} + \frac{k-1}{i+1}\right) = \frac{k}{i}\cdot\frac{i}{i+1} = \frac{k}{i+1}$. The invariant holds, so the sample is uniform at every prefix without ever knowing $n$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Reservoir sampling with $k = {k}$ over a stream of $n = {n}$ items. Give the probability any specific item is in the final sample, the expected number of times the reservoir is written, and the memory used.
L4.answer: Probability = k/n: 1e-6 or 1e-5. Expected writes = k + sum_{i=k}^{n-1} k/(i+1) = k(1 + H_n - H_k), well approximated by k(1 + ln(n/k)). k=1e3, n=1e9: 1000*(1 + ln(1e6)) is approximately 14,815 writes out of a billion items. k=1e4: 10000*(1 + ln(1e5)) is approximately 125,129. Memory is O(k) items regardless of n.
L4.explanation: About 15,000 writes across a billion items is the striking number: the reservoir stabilises quickly because the acceptance probability k/i decays. The whole cost is one random number per item, which is why the algorithm runs at line rate on log pipelines.

L4.prompt_tpl: Miller-Rabin with {t} independent rounds on a composite. Give the error bound, and compare it to the probability of an undetected memory error over the same computation.
L4.answer: Error <= 4^-t. t=20: 9.1e-13. t=40: 8.3e-25. t=64: 2.9e-39. Measured DRAM soft-error rates (Schroeder et al. 2009 field study) are on the order of $2\times10^{-11}$ per bit-hour (25,000-70,000 FIT per megabit), not the 1e-14 to 1e-16 this item previously stated. For a Miller-Rabin round touching on the order of $10^4$-$10^5$ bits of working memory for well under a millisecond, the chance of an undetected bit flip during that window is itself on the order of $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-13}$ - so the crossover with the algorithm's own error is still roughly around t=20-25, but that conclusion now rests on an explicit, rough memory-and-time estimate rather than a bare per-bit rate mistaken for a probability.
L4.explanation: This is the useful framing for Monte Carlo error: not 'is it certain' but 'is it more certain than the hardware'. The 4^-t bound is also pessimistic for random candidates - the average-case error for a random odd number is far smaller, which is why primality testing in key generation uses relatively few rounds.

L4.prompt_tpl: Karger's min-cut algorithm always performs exactly n - 2 edge contractions and returns some cut of the graph; that cut is the true global minimum cut only with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)). Classify this algorithm as Las Vegas or Monte Carlo, and justify in one sentence.
L4.answer: Monte Carlo
L4.explanation: Fixed running time (n-2 contractions, every run) with a possibly wrong answer is exactly the Monte Carlo definition - contrast with randomized quicksort, which is Las Vegas: its running time varies but the output is always correctly sorted.
options: Las Vegas
Monte Carlo
Neither - it is deterministic

L4.prompt_tpl: A Miller-Rabin composite test runs t = {t} independent rounds. Give the exact upper bound on the probability it incorrectly reports 'probably prime'.
L4.explanation: This is the textbook worst-case bound: for any odd composite, at most 1/4 of the candidate bases in [1, n-1] fail to expose it as composite, so t independent random bases each carry error at most 1/4, and independence multiplies the bounds.

L4.prompt_tpl: Karger's algorithm contracts random edges until 2 vertices remain, on a graph with n = {n} vertices; a single run returns a true global minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)). Compute this lower bound exactly for n = {n}.
L4.explanation: If the min cut has c edges, every vertex has degree at least c, so the graph has at least cn/2 edges and a uniformly random edge is a min-cut edge with probability at most 2/n at each contraction step; multiplying (1 - 2/i) over i = n down to 3 telescopes to exactly 2/(n(n-1)).

L4.prompt_tpl: A junior engineer simplifies reservoir sampling by replacing `j = random.randint(0, i)` with `j = random.randint(0, k - 1)`, keeping `if j < k: res[j] = x` unchanged. What breaks, and why does the sample stop being uniform?
L4.answer: j is now always in [0, k-1], so the condition j < k is always true: every later item is unconditionally admitted and overwrites a uniformly random one of the k slots, instead of being admitted with the decaying probability k/(i+1). An item already in the reservoir now survives one more step with constant probability (k-1)/k instead of the correct 1 - 1/(i+1), so its survival probability decays geometrically like ((k-1)/k)^(n-k) rather than harmonically like k/n on a long stream: early items are purged almost certainly and the 'sample' degenerates toward a window of the most recent k items.
L4.explanation: The bug is easy to miss because the code still keeps exactly k items and still looks like reservoir sampling - it just samples the wrong distribution. Uniformity needs the acceptance probability to shrink as i grows, which k/(i+1) does and a fixed range [0, k-1] cannot.

L4.prompt_tpl: A single run of Karger's algorithm on an n-vertex graph misses the global minimum cut with probability at most 1 - 2/(n(n-1)). Using (1-p)^R <= e^(-p R), derive the number of independent runs R, rounded up, needed to drive the failure probability of all R runs to at most 1/n, for n = {n}.
L4.explanation: Standard amplification for one-sided error: independent failure probabilities multiply, and C(n,2) ln n repetitions is the textbook trial count for confidence 1 - 1/n. 'Max flow and min cut', in this same section, gives the deterministic algorithm that finds the exact min cut in one shot instead of repeating this randomized contraction O(n^2 log n) times.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Miller-Rabin test using t = {t} rounds has one-sided error at most 4^-t. Derive the smallest number of extra rounds delta needed so the new bound, 4^-(t+delta), is at most the old bound times 2^-{b} (that is, delta more bits of confidence), rounded up to a whole round.
L4.answer: 4^-(t+delta) <= 4^-t * 2^-b means 4^-delta <= 2^-b, and since 4^-delta = 2^(-2*delta), that is 2*delta >= b, so delta = ceil(b/2) - independent of t. b=8: delta=4. b=16: delta=8. b=32: delta=16.
L4.explanation: Each extra round halves-and-squares the error (multiplies it by 1/4 = 2^-2), so gaining b bits of confidence always costs ceil(b/2) more rounds regardless of the starting t - the same 'independent trials multiply, so tail probability drops exponentially in trial count' idea that 'Concentration, and where the randomness lives', later in this section, develops into Chernoff-style bounds.

concepts.t: Concentration, and where the randomness lives

L0.body:
Markov     P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a                         needs only X >= 0
Chebyshev  P(|X - mu| >= k*sigma) <= 1/k^2             needs the variance
Chernoff   P(X >= (1+d)mu) <= exp(-d^2 * mu / (2+d))   needs INDEPENDENCE, gives
                                                       exponential decay

n = 1e6 fair coin flips, mu = 5e5:
   Chebyshev, k=20 (deviation 10,000): <= 1/400 = 0.25%
   Chernoff,  d=0.02 (deviation 10,000): <= exp(-0.0004*5e5/2.02) = 1.0e-43
Same event. The independence assumption is worth 40 orders of magnitude.
L0.cloze: Markov needs only {{c1::non-negativity}}, Chebyshev needs the {{c2::variance}}, and Chernoff needs {{c3::independence}} and pays back {{c4::exponential}} decay. On $10^{{6}}$ fair coin flips, Chebyshev bounds a 2 percent deviation at $0.25$ percent while Chernoff bounds it at about $10^{{-43}}$.

concepts.L1: Three tail bounds of increasing strength and increasing assumption. Markov needs only that the variable is non-negative. Chebyshev needs the variance. Chernoff needs independence and rewards it with a bound that decays exponentially rather than polynomially.
concepts.L2: Randomised quicksort and hash-table lookup have guarantees that sound alike and are categorically different. Quicksort's randomness is in the algorithm: the pivot comes from your generator, so the $O(n\log n)$ expectation holds for every input, including one chosen by an adversary who has read your source.
concepts.L3: Put numbers on the difference between Chebyshev and Chernoff. For $10^{6}$ fair coin flips, $\mu = 5\times 10^{5}$ and $\sigma = 500$. A deviation of 10,000 is $20\sigma$, so Chebyshev gives $1/400 = 0.25$ percent. Chernoff with $\delta = 0.02$ gives $\exp(-0.0004 \cdot 5\times 10^{5}/2.02) = 10^{-43}$. Forty-one orders of magnitude, purchased entirely with the independence assumption - which is exactly why the assumption is the thing to check. For randomised quicksort, a pivot lands in the middle half with probability $1/2$, and each such split shrinks the subproblem by a factor of at least $3/4$, so $\log_{4/3} n = 48$ good splits suffice at $n = 10^{6}$.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $n = {n}$ independent fair coin flips, bound the probability that the count of heads deviates from the mean by more than {dev}, using Chebyshev and using Chernoff.
L4.answer: sigma = sqrt(n)/2. n=1e6: sigma=500, mu=5e5. 1% deviation = 5000 = 10 sigma: Chebyshev 1/100 = 1e-2; Chernoff exp(-0.0001*5e5/2.01) = exp(-24.9) = 1.5e-11. 2% = 10000 = 20 sigma: Chebyshev 2.5e-3; Chernoff 1.0e-43. n=1e4: sigma=50, mu=5000. 1% = 50 = 1 sigma: Chebyshev 1 (vacuous); Chernoff exp(-0.0001*5000/2.01) = 0.78. 2% = 100 = 2 sigma: Chebyshev 0.25; Chernoff 0.37.
L4.explanation: Note that at n=1e4 Chernoff is barely better and sometimes worse than Chebyshev - the exponential only bites once mu*d^2 is large. Concentration is a large-n phenomenon, which is why sketches need large register counts and why small-sample estimates deserve suspicion.

L4.prompt_tpl: An adversary knows your source code, including the hash function and the sorting routine, for a service handling {n} items per request. Which of randomised quicksort and a fixed-seed hash table still has its guarantee, and why?
L4.answer: Randomised quicksort keeps its guarantee. Its randomness comes from the process's generator, not from the data, so the expectation over pivot choices holds for every input - the adversary can read the code and still cannot predict the pivots. The fixed-seed hash table loses its guarantee entirely: its O(1) was an average over inputs, and the adversary supplies colliding keys, giving Theta(n^2) work - 1e8 or 1e12 operations per request. The fix is to move the randomness into the algorithm by seeding the hash per process.
L4.explanation: This is the practical statement of 'where does the randomness live'. Las Vegas randomisation inside the algorithm converts an average-case bound into a guarantee that survives an adversary; randomness assumed about the input does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A non-negative random variable has mean {mu}. By Markov's inequality, what is the upper bound on P(X >= {a})? Give the bound as a decimal.
L4.answer: Markov's inequality gives P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a = mu/a. mu=10, a=100: 0.1. mu=40, a=150: 0.267. mu=90, a=300: 0.3.
L4.explanation: Markov needs only that X is non-negative - no variance, no independence, no shape assumption at all, which is exactly why the bound is this loose: it is the weakest statement provable from non-negativity alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: By Chebyshev's inequality, a random variable deviates from its mean by at least {k} standard deviations with probability at most what? Give the bound as a decimal.
L4.answer: Chebyshev gives P(|X-mu| >= k*sigma) <= 1/k^2. k=4: 0.0625. k=5: 0.04. k=10: 0.01.
L4.explanation: This is Markov's inequality applied to the non-negative variable (X-mu)^2, using only the variance - no independence needed, which is why it still holds even for correlated variables.

L4.prompt_tpl: For n = {n} independent fair coin flips (mu = n/2), Chernoff's bound gives P(X >= (1+delta)*mu) <= exp(-delta^2*mu/(2+delta)). With delta = {delta}, what is the numeric bound? Give the bound as a decimal; scientific notation is fine.
L4.explanation: Scaling n up 10x at fixed delta scales the exponent 10x, since the exponent is linear in mu - this is the shape of exponential decay, and it is what makes Chernoff useless at small n and overwhelming at large n.

L4.prompt_tpl: A student wants to bound P(X <= a) for a random variable X that represents a stock-price change (it can be positive or negative), with E[X] = {mu}. They write P(X <= a) <= E[X]/a directly from Markov's inequality. What is wrong with this step, and what would make it valid?
L4.answer: Markov's inequality requires the variable to be non-negative; a stock-price change can be negative, so E[X]/a does not bound P(X<=a) as written - and it is also the wrong tail, since Markov naturally bounds P(X>=a) from above. To use it validly, apply Markov to a non-negative transform of X, such as Y=|X| or a shifted variable, and restate the bound in terms of Y.
L4.explanation: Non-negativity is not a technicality: Markov's proof writes E[X] as the integral of P(X>=t) over t from 0, which only equals E[X] when X cannot go negative. Skip that and the 'bound' need not even be true.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Count-Min sketch bounds each row's overestimate using Markov's inequality, giving per-row failure probability at most 1/e. The sketch reports the minimum estimate across d independent rows, so it fails only if every row fails. What is the smallest integer depth d that drives the overall failure probability to at most {delta}?
L4.answer: Independent rows all fail with probability (1/e)^d, so d must satisfy (1/e)^d <= delta, i.e. d >= ln(1/delta). delta=0.01: d=ceil(4.605)=5. delta=0.001: d=ceil(6.908)=7. delta=0.0001: d=ceil(9.210)=10.
L4.explanation: This is randomized quicksort's own trick, generalized: take an estimator with weak, independent confidence and repeat it, so failure probabilities multiply instead of add. See Count-Min sketch for where this exact depth number gets used.

L0.body:
approximation ratio  ALG(I) <= rho * OPT(I) for every instance I
  PTAS (1+eps)-approx, poly in n for fixed eps; FPTAS also poly in 1/eps.

competitive ratio (online)  ALG(sigma) <= c * OPT_offline(sigma) + b
  No deterministic paging algorithm beats k-competitive with a cache of k pages - a lower bound on all of them.
  LRU is k-competitive. So is FIFO. LIFO (evict the page you just loaded) is NOT - same rules, unbounded ratio.
  randomised marking: O(log k)-competitive - randomisation genuinely helps here.
  resource augmentation: LRU with cache 2k is 2-competitive against OPT with cache k.
L0.cloze: An approximation ratio bounds $\mathrm{{ALG}}/\mathrm{{OPT}}$ on {{c1::every}} instance; an {{c2::FPTAS}} is additionally polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$. No deterministic paging policy with a cache of $k$ pages can beat {{c3::k}}-competitive, and LRU meets that bound exactly, while {{c4::resource augmentation}} is the model that explains why LRU is nevertheless fine in practice.

concepts.L1: Approximation ratios, PTAS/FPTAS. Competitive ratio for online problems. LRU is not competitive against an offline optimum by a constant factor, which is why it's analyzed in the resource-augmentation model.
concepts.L2: Online algorithm analysis is the honest framework for cache eviction and scheduling, and it explains why 'LRU is optimal' is false but 'LRU is fine' is true.
concepts.L3: No deterministic online paging algorithm can beat $k$-competitive against the offline optimum: an adversary who knows your policy always requests the page you just evicted, faulting every request, while Belady's offline optimum evicts the page used furthest in the future and faults at most once per $k$. LRU meets that bound exactly - and so does FIFO, which means the ratio alone does not distinguish policies that differ obviously in practice; it is not automatic either, since LIFO (evict the page you just loaded) is just as deterministic and demand-paging but has an unbounded ratio. Resource augmentation repairs the discrimination problem: LRU with a cache of $2k$ is 2-competitive against the optimum with $k$, a bound LIFO cannot match at any cache multiple. 'LRU is optimal' is false; 'LRU is fine' is a theorem in that model.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that no deterministic online paging algorithm can beat $k$-competitiveness with a cache of $k = {k}$ pages, by constructing the adversary's request sequence.
L4.answer: Use k+1 distinct pages. The adversary always requests the one page not currently in the algorithm's cache - it knows the deterministic policy, so it knows which. Every request faults: n faults in n requests. The offline optimum, on the same sequence, evicts the page whose next use is furthest away, which guarantees at least k-1 subsequent requests hit before the next fault - so it faults at most n/k times. The ratio is k, and it is achieved, so k is tight.
L4.explanation: The construction needs only k+1 pages, which is why the bound is so easy to hit and so uninformative: it describes a working set one page larger than the cache, the single worst case for any policy. Real workloads are not adversarial and their working sets are not exactly k+1.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cache designer claims their new policy is provably better than LRU because it is {c}-competitive. Evaluate the claim for a cache of {k} entries.
L4.answer: The claim is impossible for a deterministic policy: the lower bound says no deterministic online paging algorithm is better than k-competitive, so 2- or 4-competitiveness with k=1024 or 65536 cannot hold. Three ways the claim could be salvaged, and each should be asked about: the policy is randomised (O(log k) is achievable, so 2 still is not); the comparison uses resource augmentation (LRU with 2k is 2-competitive against OPT with k, which is a different statement); or it is an empirical result on a trace, not a competitive-ratio theorem.
L4.explanation: Being able to reject the claim from the lower bound alone, without seeing the policy, is the point of knowing the model. The follow-up - 'competitive against what cache size, and is your algorithm randomised?' - is what turns it into a real conversation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A rho-approximation algorithm guarantees ALG(I) <= rho * OPT(I) on every instance. For rho = {rho} and OPT(I) = {opt}, what is the largest value ALG(I) is allowed to take under this bound?
L4.answer: The bound is ALG(I) <= rho*OPT(I), so the largest permitted value is rho*opt. rho=1.5, opt=100 gives 150. rho=2, opt=40 gives 80. rho=3, opt=250 gives 750.
L4.explanation: The approximation ratio is a worst-case multiplicative bound, not an average: it says the algorithm's cost never exceeds rho times optimal on any instance, so rho*opt is the ceiling, not a typical value.

L4.prompt_tpl: The classic k+1-page adversary sequence has n = {n} requests against a cache of k = {k} pages. Belady's offline optimum faults at most floor(n/k) times on it. What is floor(n/k) for these values?
L4.answer: OPT evicts the page whose next use is furthest away, which guarantees at least k-1 hits between faults, so it faults at most floor(n/k) times. k=4, n=900 gives floor(900/4)=225. k=16, n=5000 gives floor(5000/16)=312.
L4.explanation: Any deterministic online algorithm faults on all n requests of this sequence (the adversary always asks for the evicted page), while OPT's fault count is bounded by n divided by the cache size - that gap of a factor k is the whole lower-bound proof.

L4.prompt_tpl: LRU with a cache of h = {h} pages is h/(h-k+1)-competitive against Belady's optimum with a cache of k = {k} pages (h > k). Compute that ratio for h = {h} and k = {k}, to two decimal places.
L4.answer: Plug into h/(h-k+1). h=50, k=4: 50/47 = 1.06. h=100, k=16: 100/85 = 1.18. h=200, k=40: 200/161 = 1.24. Along the h=2k line this ratio (2k/(k+1)) approaches but never reaches 2 as k grows; for other h,k pairs the ratio can be far from 2 - e.g. h close to k pushes it back up toward k (h=50,k=40 gives 50/11 = 4.55, well above 2).
L4.explanation: This is the Sleator-Tarjan resource-augmentation bound, h/(h-k+1); setting h=2k gives 2k/(k+1), which is always below 2 but tends to it, so quoting a flat '2-competitive' for the 2k case is a valid, slightly loose upper bound.

L4.prompt_tpl: A note claims: 'LRU and FIFO are both k-competitive, and any deterministic demand-paging policy is k-competitive by the same kind of argument, so LIFO must be too.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning, for a cache of k = {k} pages.
L4.answer: k-competitiveness is not automatic for every deterministic demand-paging policy - it is proved separately for each one. LIFO (evict the page you just loaded) is deterministic and demand-paging, exactly like LRU and FIFO, but an adversary can force it to fault on almost every request of a k+1-page sequence while OPT, on the same sequence, faults roughly once every k-1 requests: LIFO's competitive ratio is unbounded, not k. The universal result is only the lower bound (no deterministic algorithm beats k); the matching upper bound has to be shown policy by policy, and it fails for LIFO and for least-frequently-used.
L4.explanation: The mistake is treating a lower bound (nothing beats k) as if it were also an upper bound every algorithm automatically meets. LRU, FIFO and flush-when-full happen to meet it; LIFO and LFU are the standard counterexamples that show the upper bound is not free.

L4.prompt_tpl: The knapsack FPTAS scales every item's value so the largest is about n/eps, rounds down to an integer, then reruns the value-indexed knapsack DP on the rounded values in roughly cubic time in n and 1/eps. For eps = {eps} and n = {n} items, explain why rounding keeps the DP's state space polynomial in n and 1/eps, and why the rounding error cannot cost more than a factor of (1+eps) in the returned value. Connect this to the DP formulation in Dynamic programming, structurally.
L4.answer: The exact knapsack DP (see Dynamic programming, structurally) indexes states by achievable total value, which can be as large as the sum of all item values - exponential in the input's bit length. Rounding each value down to a multiple of mu = eps*Vmax/n collapses the value axis to about n/eps distinct levels, so the same DP now runs in time polynomial in n and 1/eps (about O(n^3/eps)) instead of pseudo-polynomial in the raw values. Each item's value drops by less than mu when rounded, and any feasible solution uses at most n items, so the total value lost is under n*mu = eps*Vmax. Assuming every item individually fits in the knapsack (the usual preprocessing step of discarding any item whose weight alone exceeds capacity), the single most valuable remaining item is itself a feasible solution, so Vmax <= OPT and the lost value is under eps*OPT; since the DP finds the true optimum on the rounded instance, the unrounded value of the set it returns is at least OPT - eps*OPT = (1-eps)*OPT, which is what an FPTAS promises.
L4.explanation: This is the standard scale-and-round FPTAS technique: shrinking the value axis is what turns a pseudo-polynomial exact DP into a genuinely polynomial approximate one, at the cost of a controllable, provable (1-eps) factor - the same trade the concept's PTAS/FPTAS line states abstractly.

L0.body:
LSH      near points collide; L tables x k concatenated hashes, tuned for recall
IVF      k-means the corpus into nlist cells; probe nprobe cells at query time
PQ       D-dim vector -> M subvectors, each quantised to 256 centroids: M bytes/vec
HNSW     multi-layer navigable small-world graph; greedy descent from the top layer
         M = edges/node (16-64), efConstruction / efSearch = beam width
         memory ~ M * 2 * 4 bytes/node of links, ON TOP of the vectors
         1e8 x 768-dim fp32 = 307 GB of raw vectors; with PQ at M=96, 9.6 GB
L0.cloze: HNSW's memory is about ${{c1::M \cdot 2 \cdot 4}}$ bytes of graph links per node on top of the vectors themselves, and its search quality knob is {{c2::efSearch}}. Product quantisation splits a $D$-dimensional vector into $M$ subvectors, each coded to one of {{c3::256}} centroids, giving {{c4::M}} bytes per vector.

concepts.L1: LSH, then HNSW and IVF-PQ. HNSW builds a navigable small-world graph with hierarchical layers; product quantization compresses vectors for memory-bound search.
concepts.L2: This is now core infrastructure for retrieval-augmented systems, and it's absent from classical interview prep. Being fluent in the recall/latency/memory tradeoff here is directly relevant to any LLM-adjacent role.
concepts.L3: HNSW's layers are a skip list grafted onto a graph: each node's top layer is drawn from an exponential distribution with rate $m_{L} = 1/\ln M$, so a node reaches layer $l$ with probability decaying like $M^{-l}$, giving an expected $O(\log n)$ layers and a sparse top layer to start from. Greedy descent takes one long-range hop per layer before dropping down - the same trick a skip list uses on a line, applied to a graph. PQ's real payoff is asymmetric distance computation: precompute a $256 \times M_{PQ}$ table of query-to-centroid distances ($M_{PQ}$ subvectors, unrelated to HNSW's M above), then score every vector in $O(M_{PQ})$ lookups instead of $O(D)$ multiply-adds - compression buys query speed too. See Graph representations: adjacency list, CSR, and locality for why HNSW's pointer-chasing resists the layouts that make IVF's cell scan disk-friendly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A corpus of {n} vectors of dimension {D} in fp32. Give the raw memory, the memory under product quantisation with $M = D/8$ subvectors, and HNSW's link overhead at $M_{{\mathrm{{ graph }}}} = 32$.
L4.answer: Raw = n*D*4 bytes. n=1e7,D=768: 30.7 GB. n=1e8,D=768: 307 GB. n=1e7,D=1536: 61.4 GB. n=1e8,D=1536: 614 GB. PQ with M=D/8 subvectors at 1 byte each: D/8 bytes per vector - 96 or 192 bytes: n=1e7 -> 0.96 GB or 1.92 GB; n=1e8 -> 9.6 GB or 19.2 GB, a 32x reduction. HNSW links at 32*2*4 = 256 bytes per node: 2.56 GB at n=1e7, 25.6 GB at n=1e8 - on top of whatever the vectors cost.
L4.explanation: At n=1e8, D=768 the raw vectors alone exceed any single machine's RAM, so the choice is PQ or sharding, and PQ's 9.6 GB plus HNSW's 25.6 GB of links is the reason production systems combine them (HNSW over PQ codes) rather than using either alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: A retrieval-augmented system needs {r} recall@10 at p99 under {ms} ms over {n} documents, on a single machine. HNSW, IVF-PQ, or a flat exact index?
L4.answer: n=2 million: a flat exact index is 2e6 * 768 * 4 = 6.1 GB and one query is 2e6 distance computations - about 1.5 GFLOP, which is 5-20 ms with SIMD and multiple threads. At 99% recall requirements, exact is the honest choice and removes all tuning risk; HNSW cuts latency to under a millisecond if throughput matters. n=200 million: exact is 614 GB and impossible. IVF-PQ at 96 bytes per vector is 19.2 GB plus the coarse quantiser, fits, and reaches 95% recall with a suitable nprobe; 99% on a single machine at this scale needs re-ranking - retrieve 100 candidates with IVF-PQ, then rescore them against full-precision vectors fetched from disk.
L4.explanation: The re-ranking pattern is the standard answer to 'high recall on a compressed index': the approximate index only needs to get the true neighbour into the candidate set, and an exact rescore of 100 vectors is trivial. Naming it is what separates a real answer from a library recommendation.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LSH scheme has single-hash collision probability {p} for a truly similar pair, concatenates {k} hash functions per table (an AND), and uses {L} independent tables (an OR). What is the probability this pair collides in at least one of the L tables? Answer with that probability.
L4.explanation: k concatenated hashes make a table stricter (AND), cutting false positives but also cutting the true-neighbor hit rate to $p^{k}$; L independent tables then restore recall (OR). Raising k without raising L trades recall for query cost in exactly this formula.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fp32 vector of dimension {D} is split into {M} subvectors, each coded with {bits} bits (that is, 2^bits centroids per subquantiser). What is the compression ratio versus the raw fp32 vector - raw bytes divided by compressed bytes? Answer with that ratio.
L4.explanation: 8-bit codes (256 centroids, PQ8) and 4-bit codes (16 centroids, PQ4, two codes packed per byte) are both used in production; halving the code width doubles the compression ratio at fixed M, at the cost of a coarser codebook and a larger quantisation error.

L4.prompt_tpl: IVF splits a corpus of {n} vectors into {nlist} roughly balanced cells by k-means. A query probes {nprobe} of the cells. Assuming the cells are balanced, how many vectors does the query actually examine? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: vectors examined = n*nprobe/nlist (balanced-cell assumption). n=1e8,nlist=4096,nprobe=1: 24414. n=1e8,nlist=4096,nprobe=32: 781250. n=1e7,nlist=1000,nprobe=8: 80000. n=1e8,nlist=1000,nprobe=1: 100000.
L4.explanation: nprobe=1 examines the fewest vectors but has a real chance of missing the true nearest neighbor outright: it can sit just across a cell boundary, in the second-closest centroid's cell, which nprobe=1 never visits. Recall, not just latency, depends on nprobe.

L4.prompt_tpl: IVF splits a corpus of {n} vectors into {nlist} roughly balanced cells by k-means. A query probes only the single nearest centroid (nprobe = 1). Is the true nearest neighbor guaranteed to be among the vectors examined?
L4.answer: No: the true nearest neighbor can be assigned to a different cell whose centroid is only slightly farther from the query than the nearest one, and nprobe = 1 never visits that cell.
L4.explanation: A database vector is assigned to the cell whose centroid is nearest to it at index-build time, not to the cell nearest to a future query. A query sitting close to a Voronoi boundary can have its true nearest neighbor just across that boundary, in the second-closest cell - exactly the miss that raising nprobe above 1 is bought to fix.
options: Yes: a vector's true nearest neighbor is always assigned to the same cell as the query's nearest centroid, so nprobe = 1 is exact.
No: the true nearest neighbor can be assigned to a different cell whose centroid is only slightly farther from the query than the nearest one, and nprobe = 1 never visits that cell.
No: k-means guarantees every cell but the nearest is empty for any query, so nprobe = 1 already examines every vector that could be the answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LSH scheme has single-hash collision probability {p} for a truly similar pair and concatenates {k} hashes per table. How many independent tables L (rounded up to a whole table) are needed so that pair collides in at least one table with probability at least {r}? Answer with that number of tables.
L4.explanation: The table count needed to hit a recall target grows fast as k rises or r approaches 1: going from 90% to 99% recall at p=0.8,k=6 needs 16 tables, not 8. Shipping fewer tables than this is the usual reason an LSH index 'works in the demo, misses in production'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A corpus of {n} vectors must be served from SSD because it does not fit in RAM. Between IVF-PQ and HNSW, which is more naturally disk-friendly, and why does the answer trace back to the same locality argument as CSR versus adjacency lists for graphs?
L4.answer: IVF-PQ: each probed cell's codes are stored contiguously, so a probe is a sequential read of one block - disk-friendly by construction, the same reason CSR packs a graph's edges contiguously by source instead of chasing pointers. HNSW's neighbor lists point to node ids scattered anywhere in the index, so each hop is a random page fault; unlike a static graph, HNSW's edges are built incrementally and are not laid out for locality, so disk-based systems (DiskANN's Vamana graph) redesign the layout itself rather than page an ordinary HNSW graph from SSD.
L4.explanation: Naming DiskANN's Vamana graph, not just 'HNSW is bad on disk', shows the connection is structural: any proximity graph can be made disk-friendly if its edges are laid out contiguously the way CSR lays out a static graph - HNSW's build process just doesn't.

L0.cloze: Lock-free guarantees {{c1::some}} thread makes progress; wait-free guarantees {{c2::every}} thread finishes in a bounded number of its own steps. A CAS retry loop is {{c3::lock-free}} but not wait-free, because a specific thread can lose the race indefinitely. Wait-free constructions typically need a {{c4::helping}} mechanism.

concepts.L1: Lock-free: some thread makes progress. Wait-free: every thread makes progress in bounded steps. Wait-free is much harder and usually needs helping mechanisms.
concepts.L2: Most 'lock-free' production code is actually obstruction-free or has a lock somewhere in the reclamation path. The terminology is used loosely and using it precisely is a signal.
concepts.L3: The gap between the definitions is a per-thread starvation guarantee, and it costs a lot. A CAS retry loop is lock-free by construction: whoever wins the compare-exchange made progress, so the system as a whole advances. But a specific unlucky thread can lose every race, so its latency is unbounded - which is precisely the property a real-time or tail-latency-sensitive system needed the non-blocking structure for. Wait-freedom requires that a thread which is being starved gets its operation completed by someone else: it publishes a descriptor of what it wants done, and any thread that sees it performs the work on its behalf before proceeding. RCU sidesteps this for readers rather than solving it: a reader just dereferences a pointer, no atomic op, no retry loop, so it is wait-free by having nothing to contend over - writers tolerate stale readers instead of publishing help.

L4.prompt_tpl: A trading system requires a p{p} latency bound on every thread's enqueue operation. Is a lock-free queue sufficient? Justify from the definitions.
L4.answer: No. Lock-free guarantees only that some thread makes progress; a specific thread can lose the CAS race arbitrarily many times, so its individual latency is unbounded and no per-thread percentile is guaranteed. Sufficient options: a wait-free queue with a helping protocol (bounded steps per thread, worse average constant), or a single-producer design like a disruptor ring where the producer owns its cursor and never contends at all. In practice the second is what trading systems use.
L4.explanation: The disruptor answer is the interesting one: the strongest progress guarantee comes from removing the contention rather than from a cleverer non-blocking protocol. Single-writer-per-cursor makes the operation a plain store, which is trivially wait-free.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 'lock-free' stack pops a node, and the node is freed immediately by the popping thread. Under {n} concurrent threads it segfaults rarely. Name the two distinct bugs.
L4.answer: First: use-after-free in reclamation. Another thread may hold a pointer to that node from its own load of head and dereference node->next after the free. This needs hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation or RCU, none of which is in the pop loop. Second: ABA. A thread reads head = A, is descheduled; other threads pop A, pop B, and push A back (possibly a recycled allocation at the same address); the first thread's CAS on A succeeds and sets head to A->next, which is now stale. Tagged pointers or double-width CAS fix ABA; they do not fix the use-after-free.
L4.explanation: These are commonly conflated and they are independent: solving ABA with a version tag still leaves the reader dereferencing freed memory. This is exactly the preserved point that most 'lock-free' production code has a lock or an unbounded wait hiding in the reclamation path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A concurrent object has this property: if a thread runs completely alone (no other thread takes any step) from some point on, it is guaranteed to finish its operation - but under full contention from {n} threads, no such guarantee holds for any thread. Which point in Herlihy's progress hierarchy does this describe?
L4.answer: obstruction-free
L4.explanation: Obstruction-freedom is the weakest of the three: it only promises progress when a thread has no active contention at all. Lock-free needs no such isolation (some thread always advances even under full contention); wait-free needs every thread to finish regardless of contention.
options: obstruction-free
lock-free
wait-free

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with gcc -O2, {n} pthreads each call `__atomic_fetch_add(&counter, 1, __ATOMIC_RELAXED)` exactly {m} times on a shared int initialized to 0, then all join. Nothing else touches counter. What is the final value of counter after every thread has joined, no matter how the OS interleaves them? Answer with that single integer.
L4.answer: counter = n*m always. For n=8, m=2000: running the compiled program 5 times prints 16000 every time regardless of thread interleaving, because `__atomic_fetch_add` compiles to a single locked hardware instruction (lock xadd on x86-64) with no retry loop - it is wait-free by construction, unlike the CAS loop in this concept's L0.
L4.explanation: fetch_add is a single atomic read-modify-write instruction, so no increment can be lost or double-counted regardless of scheduling - the final count is always n times m, verified by running the compiled program repeatedly. This is why hardware RMW primitives are wait-free while a CAS retry loop is only lock-free.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a CAS retry loop, {n} threads contend for the same atomic pointer. Model each round as exactly one uniformly-random thread's compare-exchange succeeding, so a specific thread's success is geometric with probability 1/{n} per round. What is the expected number of rounds (attempts, counting the winning one) until that thread succeeds?
L4.answer: A geometric variable with success probability 1/n has expected trials 1/(1/n) = n. For n=8: 8 expected rounds total, including the winning attempt.
L4.explanation: Mean of a geometric distribution with success probability p is 1/p trials, including the success itself. With p = 1/n across n contending threads, that is n expected rounds. (A companion template asks for FAILED attempts only, which is n-1 - easy to conflate with this trials count.)

L4.prompt_tpl: Same {n}-thread CAS contention model: each round, exactly one uniformly-random thread succeeds, so a specific thread's success is geometric with probability 1/{n} per round. What is the expected number of that thread's FAILED compare-exchange attempts before it succeeds (not the total number of rounds)? Answer with the number of failed attempts.
L4.answer: Expected total trials is n (geometric mean 1/p with p=1/n), and exactly one of those trials is the success, so expected failures = n-1. For n=8: 8 expected trials, 7 of them failures on average before the thread wins the CAS.
L4.explanation: The trap is trials vs failures: E[trials] = n, but the question asks only for the failed attempts before the win, which is n-1, not n. Confusing the two is the classic off-by-one here. It also shows why lock-free gives no per-thread bound - the average is finite but the worst case is not: a thread can in principle lose every round forever.

L4.prompt_tpl: A queue used by {threads} threads is protected by a single mutex, but the lock is held for only a few nanoseconds and is almost always free when a thread requests it, so in practice no thread ever seems to wait. Does this make the queue lock-free? Answer using the definitions, and name a scheduling event that breaks the practical argument.
L4.answer: No. Lock-free is a worst-case structural guarantee, not a statement about typical latency: it requires the algorithm to contain no lock at all, so no thread can be blocked by another thread's scheduling. This queue still has a mutex, so if the lock holder is preempted (descheduled by the OS, a page fault, a signal handler) while holding it, every other thread attempting to enter the critical section blocks until that specific thread is rescheduled and finishes - the defining failure mode of blocking synchronization, however rarely it happens.
L4.explanation: Progress properties are about the worst case over all schedules, including adversarial ones, not the common case. A preempted lock holder is exactly the scenario lock-free algorithms are built to survive, since there they have no lock to be preempted while holding.

L4.prompt_tpl: Same {n}-thread CAS contention model as before: each round, exactly one of the {n} threads succeeds uniformly at random. A specific thread has just lost {k} consecutive rounds. Estimate first, then compute exactly: what is the probability of a run at least that unlucky, (1 - 1/{n}) raised to the power {k}? Give the decimal.
L4.answer: P = (1 - 1/n)^k. n=4,k=5: 0.75^5 = 0.2373. n=8,k=10: 0.875^10 = 0.2631. n=16,k=20: 0.9375^20 = 0.2751. The probability is never zero for any finite k - it shrinks but never hits a hard bound, which is exactly why lock-free alone cannot promise a specific thread a bounded number of retries.
L4.explanation: This is the estimate-then-verify point: intuition says repeated bad luck becomes basically impossible, but the geometric tail is only exponentially small, never zero, and for large n it decays slowly. A wait-free structure removes this tail entirely by bounding every thread's steps by construction, not by probability.

  rcu_read_lock();      // ~free         new = copy_and_modify(old);
  p = rcu_dereference(gp);               rcu_assign_pointer(gp, new);  // release store

  rcu_read_unlock();    // ~free         kfree(old);         // now provably unreachable

grace period = every CPU has passed a quiescent state since the update, so no
Reader cost on a non-preemptible kernel: literally zero instructions. Writer: milliseconds.
L0.cloze: An RCU reader pays approximately {{c1::zero}} cost and never blocks; the writer publishes a new version with a {{c2::release}} store and then waits for a {{c3::grace period}} before freeing the old one. A grace period ends when every CPU has passed a {{c4::quiescent}} state, so no pre-existing reader can still hold the pointer.

concepts.L1: Read-copy-update: readers never block and pay near-zero cost; writers copy, update, and defer reclamation until a grace period passes. The Linux kernel's dominant synchronization mechanism.
concepts.L2: RCU's cost model is inverted from a lock — reads are free, writes are expensive and deferred. That makes it right for read-mostly structures and wrong for anything else, and knowing when not to use it matters.
concepts.L3: The cost model is inverted from a lock and that inversion is the entire design constraint. A reader-writer lock makes readers pay an atomic operation on a shared cache line, so read-mostly workloads still generate coherence traffic proportional to reader count - on a 64-core machine, readers contend with each other even though they conflict with nothing. RCU makes the reader side free by never writing shared state at all: readers simply dereference a pointer, and correctness comes from the writer never destroying anything a reader might hold.

L4.prompt_tpl: A read-mostly structure sees {r} reads/s and {w} writes/s across 64 cores. Compare a reader-writer lock (about 40 cycles per reader acquire+release under contention) with RCU (zero reader cost, 5 ms grace period per write) on a 3 GHz core.
L4.answer: rwlock reader cost: 1e8 * 40 = 4e9 cycles/s, which is 1.3 cores of pure lock overhead; at 1e9 reads/s it is 4e10 cycles/s, over 13 cores - and this understates it, because the contended cache line serialises. RCU reader cost: zero. Writer side: at 10 writes/s, grace periods are irrelevant (RCU batches them, and callbacks are asynchronous). At 10,000 writes/s, each write copies the object and defers a free; the grace periods batch, but memory held pending reclamation grows to roughly 10,000 * 5 ms = 50 objects in flight, and the copy cost now dominates.
L4.explanation: The crossover is about write rate and object size, not about the grace period latency itself, because callbacks batch. RCU's failure mode at high write rates is memory growth from deferred frees plus copy cost, not reader latency.

L4.prompt_tpl: Code reads two RCU-protected pointers `a` and `b` inside one `rcu_read_lock()` section and asserts an invariant relating them, on a system with {n} writers. It fires occasionally. Explain.
L4.answer: RCU guarantees that each object a reader dereferences stays alive for the duration of the read-side critical section. It does not guarantee that two separate pointer reads see a consistent snapshot: a writer may publish a new `a` between the two dereferences, so the reader sees old `b` with new `a`. Even one writer is enough. The fix is to make the two fields reachable through a single pointer that is replaced atomically - publish a new container object holding both - so one rcu_dereference gets a consistent pair.
L4.explanation: This is the most common RCU misuse and it follows directly from the cost model: readers are free precisely because they take no lock and therefore establish no mutual exclusion across multiple objects. Multi-object atomicity must be designed into the pointer structure.

L4.prompt_tpl: A single writer thread performs {n} sequential updates to an RCU-protected pointer. Each update calls rcu_assign_pointer then synchronize_rcu before starting the next update, and one grace period takes {g} ms. With no batching, how many milliseconds does the writer spend in total waiting on grace periods? Answer with the number of milliseconds.
L4.answer: Total wait = n * g, since each update's synchronize_rcu must fully elapse before the next update starts. n=10, g=5 ms: 50 ms. n=500, g=20 ms: 10,000 ms (10 seconds) - which is exactly why real code batches many frees behind one shared grace period with call_rcu() or kfree_rcu() instead of waiting synchronously per update.
L4.explanation: Serialized synchronize_rcu calls add up because each grace period must fully elapse before the next update's memory is provably safe to reuse. This is the concrete cost that batched, asynchronous reclamation (call_rcu) exists to avoid.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a non-preemptible ({arch}) Linux kernel, which event is what RCU actually counts as a CPU passing through a quiescent state, so that a grace period covering that CPU can complete?
L4.answer: A voluntary context switch, the CPU entering the idle loop, or the CPU returning to user mode
L4.explanation: A quiescent state is any point where the CPU is provably not inside an RCU read-side critical section. Under non-preemptible RCU, rcu_read_lock disables preemption, so a context switch, idle, or user-mode execution each proves no critical section was interrupted there. A bare memory barrier or an interrupt proves nothing about read-side sections and does not count.
options: A voluntary context switch, the CPU entering the idle loop, or the CPU returning to user mode
The CPU executing a memory-barrier instruction such as mfence or dsb
The CPU servicing a hardware interrupt

L4.prompt_tpl: {r} reader threads simultaneously attempt to read the same shared, mutable data structure at the same moment. Under RCU, all r of them can be executing inside rcu_read_lock and rcu_read_unlock critical sections concurrently. If the same data structure were instead protected by a single plain mutex (so only one reader may hold it at a time), how many more readers execute concurrently under RCU than under the mutex, in the worst case? Answer with a count.
L4.answer: RCU concurrency: r (no reader-side synchronization at all). Mutex concurrency: 1 (only one holder at a time). Difference = r - 1. r=4: 3 more readers running concurrently under RCU. r=1000: 999 more.
L4.explanation: This is the inverted cost model made concrete: a mutex caps concurrent readers at exactly 1 through contention on shared state, but RCU has no reader-side synchronization at all, so RCU's concurrency exceeds the mutex's by r - 1 readers.

L4.prompt_tpl: A reader path runs rcu_read_lock, dereferences the protected pointer, and then - still inside that same critical section - calls synchronize_rcu before using the value and calling rcu_read_unlock. On a {n}-CPU system under load this hangs. What is wrong?
L4.answer: Calling synchronize_rcu from inside an RCU read-side critical section is illegal on every RCU flavor and can deadlock: synchronize_rcu blocks until all pre-existing readers - including the calling task's own still-open critical section - have passed a quiescent state, but that reader cannot reach a quiescent state until it finishes and calls rcu_read_unlock, which never happens because it is blocked inside synchronize_rcu. On a non-preemptible kernel this shows up concretely as preemption being disabled for the whole section, so the CPU cannot be scheduled away to let other quiescent-state-producing events occur; under preemptible RCU the same circularity exists directly, because the task's own rcu_read_lock nesting count never returns to zero. The fix is to end the critical section with rcu_read_unlock before calling synchronize_rcu, or to avoid a synchronous wait on the read path entirely.
L4.explanation: The Linux kernel's own RCU requirements documentation states this explicitly: a read-side critical section must never wait, directly or indirectly, on a synchronize_rcu call, because that creates exactly this circular wait between the section and the grace period it is inside.

L4.prompt_tpl: The lock-free stack from 'Lock-free vs wait-free' needs safe memory reclamation for popped nodes under {n} concurrent threads. Compare reclaiming with RCU against reclaiming with hazard pointers: which one lets a single reader block a writer's reclaim of one specific node indefinitely, and which one instead delays reclamation of an entire batch behind one global condition?
L4.answer: Hazard pointers: each reader publishes the exact pointer it currently holds in a well-known per-thread slot before dereferencing it; a reclaimer must scan every thread's hazard pointer before freeing a node, so one reader that keeps a node's hazard pointer set can block reclamation of that single node indefinitely, at the cost of a store on every read. RCU: reclamation of everything freed since the corresponding rcu_assign_pointer is instead gated on one global grace period elapsing, so no single reader blocks anything by itself - it only delays the whole batch of pending frees until every reader has passed a quiescent state, and reading costs nothing. RCU trades node-level precision for zero-cost reads; hazard pointers trade a per-read store for precise, node-level reclamation.
L4.explanation: Both solve the same use-after-free problem the lock-free stack's pop introduces, by different means: hazard pointers make protection explicit and per-object at read cost, RCU makes it implicit and global at zero read cost. Choosing between them is a real systems trade-off, not a naming difference.

prereqs: Lock-free vs wait-free

L0.body:
state-based (CvRDT): merge must be a JOIN on a semilattice -
     idempotent  m(x,x) = x     commutative m(x,y) = m(y,x)     associative
  G-Counter  : vector of per-replica counts; merge = element-wise max; value = sum
  OR-Set     : add tags each element with a unique id; remove records observed tags
               concurrent add+remove -> ADD WINS, because the remove saw only old tags
op-based (CmRDT): operations must commute; needs exactly-once causal delivery
  RGA / LSEQ : sequence CRDTs for collaborative text

Convergence: guaranteed.  Intention preservation: NOT guaranteed.
L0.cloze: A state-based CRDT's merge must be {{c1::idempotent}}, commutative and associative - a join on a {{c2::semilattice}} - so retries and reordering are harmless. In an OR-Set a concurrent add and remove resolves as {{c3::add wins}}. Convergence is guaranteed; {{c4::intention preservation}} is not.

concepts.L1: Conflict-free replicated data types. State-based (join-semilattice, merge is idempotent/commutative/associative) or operation-based (commutative operations). G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set, RGA and LSEQ for sequences.
concepts.L2: CRDTs guarantee convergence, not correctness. Everyone converges to the same state; that state may not be the one any user intended. Collaborative text editing needs intention preservation, which is why OT persisted alongside CRDTs.
concepts.L3: The three merge algebra properties each buy a specific operational freedom, and it is worth naming which. Idempotence means a message may be delivered twice, so the transport needs only at-least-once, not exactly-once. Commutativity means messages may arrive in any order, so no sequencing or vector-clock ordering is required. Associativity means partial merges in any grouping are safe, so a tree of gossiping replicas can aggregate however it likes. Together they make the merge a join on a semilattice, and the convergence proof is one line: every replica's state is the least upper bound of the updates it has seen, and once all replicas have seen all updates their least upper bounds are equal.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team implements a distributed counter as a single integer per replica, merged by taking the {op}. Increments are lost. Explain and give the correct structure.
L4.answer: Max on a scalar is idempotent, commutative and associative, so it converges - but it converges to the wrong value. If replica A increments to 5 and replica B independently increments to 3, the merge is 5, and B's three increments are gone. The fix is a G-Counter: a vector with one slot per replica, each replica only incrementing its own slot, merged element-wise by max, with the value being the sum. Now no replica's increments can be overwritten by another's.
L4.explanation: This is the sharpest illustration that the semilattice properties guarantee convergence and nothing about correctness. The scalar-max counter is a perfectly valid CRDT that computes the wrong function. Per-replica slots are what make max the right join.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two users concurrently edit a shared document: one types '{a}' at position 5, the other deletes the character at position 5. The CRDT converges. Why is that not the same as being correct?
L4.answer: Convergence means every replica ends in the same state, which the merge algebra guarantees. It says nothing about whether that state reflects what either user intended: the insertion may end up attached to a character that no longer exists, landing in a position neither user was looking at, and both users see the same surprising result. Intention preservation - that the effect of an operation matches its meaning in the context where it was issued - is a separate property that CRDTs do not provide and that OT was explicitly designed for.
L4.explanation: The practical consequence is that production collaborative editors layer intention heuristics on top of a CRDT (or use OT) rather than relying on convergence alone. Naming the distinction is what the preserved note is pointing at.

L4.prompt_tpl: A G-Counter has 3 replica slots. Node X's locally known vector is [{x1}, {x2}, {x3}], node Y's is [{y1}, {y2}, {y3}], and node Z's is [{z1}, {z2}, {z3}] (same slot order everywhere). X merges in Y's vector, then merges in Z's vector. What is the counter's value at X afterward (the sum of the element-wise maximum of all three vectors)?
L4.answer: Merge is element-wise max per slot, then value = sum of the merged vector. With X=[4,2,1], Y=[6,3,0], Z=[3,5,2]: slot 1 = max(4,6,3)=6, slot 2 = max(2,3,5)=5, slot 3 = max(1,0,2)=2. Value = 6+5+2 = 13.
L4.explanation: G-Counter merge is idempotent, commutative and associative element-wise max, so X can apply Y's and Z's vectors in either order, or even re-apply one twice, without over-counting. Only the sum of the merged (maximum) vector is the counter's value - never the sum of any single replica's own raw vector, which would undercount whatever it has not yet heard about.

L4.prompt_tpl: A PN-Counter spread across 3 replicas has already fully converged. Its P vector (increments) is [{p1}, {p2}, {p3}] and its N vector (decrements) is [{n1}, {n2}, {n3}]. What is the counter's current value?
L4.answer: Each of P and N is itself a G-Counter, so its own value is the sum of its (already merged) slots. With P=[10,8,6] (sum 24) and N=[2,1,3] (sum 6), the PN-Counter's value is sum(P) - sum(N) = 24 - 6 = 18.
L4.explanation: A PN-Counter is two independent G-Counters, P for increments and N for decrements, each merged the ordinary way (element-wise max, value = sum of the merged vector); the composite value subtracts one sum from the other. A decrement is never folded in as a negative increment to the same vector, because max would then silently swallow a decrement that happened after a larger increment.

L4.prompt_tpl: A state-based CRDT's merge function is idempotent, commutative and associative. Which single one of those three properties is what lets the replication layer use plain at-least-once message delivery instead of building a de-duplication or exactly-once layer?
L4.answer: Idempotence
L4.explanation: Idempotence means merging the same state twice, m(x,x) = x, changes nothing, so a duplicate delivery of the same update is harmless. Commutativity removes the need for ordering, not deduplication, and associativity makes partial, differently-grouped merges safe; neither one says anything about a message arriving more than once.
options: Idempotence
Commutativity
Associativity

L4.prompt_tpl: A team builds a Last-Writer-Wins Register: each replica stores a (value, timestamp) pair, and merge keeps whichever pair has the larger timestamp (ties broken by replica id). They argue this is a valid state-based CRDT because merge is idempotent, commutative and associative, and in production it does converge. During a network partition, replica A's clock runs {skew} seconds slow; an update A makes after seeing B's update still loses the merge, because A's timestamp is the smaller one. Is the team's CRDT claim correct? What does the merge algebra actually guarantee here, and what does it not guarantee?
L4.answer: The claim is correct as far as it goes: LWW-Register's merge (max over (timestamp, replica-id) pairs) really is idempotent, commutative and associative, so the merge algebra does guarantee convergence - every replica ends up with the same (value, timestamp) pair. What it does not guarantee is that the winning write is the one that should have won causally. A physical clock is not a causality witness: A's update happened after B's in real, causal terms but carries a smaller timestamp because A's clock is skewed, so B's stale value wins and A's newer write is discarded with no conflict ever surfacing. This generalizes the same point the L2 layer makes about intention preservation: the semilattice properties prove convergence, never correctness, and LWW-Register is the sharpest case because it looks causally aware (it carries a timestamp) while actually being causality-blind.
L4.explanation: LWW-Register is a genuine CvRDT - the merge really is a join on a semilattice of (timestamp, id) pairs - so the team is not wrong that it converges. The error is treating 'valid CRDT' as 'correct outcome': convergence only says all replicas agree, not that they agree on the causally right value. This is why production LWW implementations use logical or hybrid clocks, not wall-clock time, for the timestamp.

L4.prompt_tpl: Both CRDTs and RCU (Read-Copy-Update) let some participants proceed without blocking on a writer: CRDT replicas accept local writes with zero coordination; RCU readers traverse the structure with no lock at all. Yet RCU still serializes writers against a single copy (typically via a mutex) before the pointer swap, while CRDT replicas can be written by independent, fully uncoordinated writers. What is the real reason for that difference?
L4.answer: CRDT merges are a commutative, associative join, so the order in which two writes are applied cannot change the result
L4.explanation: RCU's constraint is about a single mutable copy: two writers building two different next-versions from the same old copy is a genuine race, so RCU still serializes writers, usually via a lock, against each other - only reader/writer concurrency is lock-free there. A CRDT sidesteps this because its merge is commutative and associative by construction, so two replicas' independent writes can both stand and be combined afterward; no serialization is ever required.
options: CRDT merges are a commutative, associative join, so the order in which two writes are applied cannot change the result
CRDTs run over faster networks than RCU-protected structures run on
RCU is only used for read-heavy workloads, so it never has to handle concurrent writers

prereqs: Merkle trees
Concentration, and where the randomness lives
